en.explanation: ～後で means "after doing something" or "after something". With verbs, the た-form comes before 後で; with nouns, の comes before 後で.
en.formation: Verb た-form + 後で / Noun + の後で
en.notes: 後で on its own can also mean "later": 後で電話します (I'll call later). ～てから is an alternative with a similar meaning.
examples[].german: Let's go for a drink after work.
After I ate, I went for a walk.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 前に means "before" work, not "after".
仕事のながら is not a valid connection.
仕事のてから is not a valid connection.

en.explanation: In Japanese, counters (suffixes) are used after numbers, depending on the shape or type of the thing being counted. The most important N5 counters are ～つ (general), ～人 (people), ～本 (long things), ～枚 (flat things), ～匹 (small animals), ～台 (machines/vehicles).
en.formation: Number + counter + の + Noun / Noun + を + Number + counter + Verb
en.notes: ～つ (hitotsu, futatsu...) is the general counter and works up to 10. After that you use the specific counter. With some counters the numbers change: 三本 = さんぼん, 一匹 = いっぴき.
examples[].german: Three apples, please.
There are five students.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The translation calls for three apples, not one.
The translation calls for three apples, not two.
The translation calls for three apples, not four.

en.explanation: ～だけ means "only" or "just" and limits something. It can be used after nouns, verbs and numbers.
en.formation: Noun + だけ / Verb + だけ
en.notes: だけ limits neutrally; しか～ない puts more stress on how little there is or that it's the only thing (only, just ... and nothing else).
examples[].german: I only drink water.
I only ate a little.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: まで expresses "even water" here instead of "only water".
A direction does not mark the drink.
しか requires a negative verb form.

en.explanation: で marks the place where an action takes place, or the means by which something is done. It can also indicate a cause or a material.
en.formation: Noun + で
en.notes: Difference from に: で marks the place of an activity (図書館で勉強する), while に marks the place of existence (図書館にいる).
examples[].german: I study at the library.
I go by bus.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The place where 勉強します happens is marked with で.
へ would require a movement.
The library is not the thing being studied.

en.explanation: ～でした is the past form of です. It means "was" or "were".
en.formation: Noun + でした / な-adjective + でした
en.notes: でした is used for nouns and な-adjectives. For い-adjectives in the past, ～かったです is used, not ～いでした.
examples[].german: Yesterday was Sunday.
It was really tough.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Nouns don't take the verb ending ます.
Nouns don't take the い-adjective past.
This denies that it was Sunday.

en.explanation: ～でしょう expresses a guess and means "probably" or "I suppose...". It is less certain than a direct statement, but more certain than かもしれない.
en.formation: Verb/い-adj. (plain form) + でしょう / な-adj./Noun + でしょう
en.notes: でしょう is often used in weather forecasts. With rising intonation (でしょう？) you are seeking confirmation: そうでしょう？ (Right?).
examples[].german: It will probably be warm tomorrow.
He has probably gone home already.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 暖かいでした is not a regular adjective form.
An い-adjective does not take ました.
The guess comes after 暖かい, not 暖かいく.

en.explanation: です is the polite form of the copula and means "to be". It is used after nouns and な-adjectives to make polite statements.
en.formation: Noun + です / な-adjective + です
en.notes: です is not used as a copula with い-adjectives; it is only added for politeness: 暑いです. With verbs, ます is used, not です.
examples[].german: I am Tanaka.
This is a pen.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: A name does not take the verb ending ます.
A name is not an い-adjective.
This negates the identity.

en.explanation: どんな is a question word that asks about the kind or nature of something. It comes directly before a noun and means "What kind of...?".
en.formation: どんな + Noun
en.notes: どんな belongs to the こそあど series: こんな (this kind, like this one here), そんな (that kind, like that one there), あんな (that kind, like that one over there), どんな (what kind?).
examples[].german: What kind of music do you like?
What kind of person is he/she?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Before a noun, the attributive どんな is used here.
だれ asks about a person, not a kind of music.
どこ asks about a place, not a kind of music.

en.explanation: へ marks the direction of a movement. It is pronounced "e", not "he". With verbs of motion it is interchangeable with に, but it puts more emphasis on the direction than on the destination.
en.formation: Noun + へ
en.notes: へ emphasizes the direction of the movement, while に emphasizes the destination. In everyday speech, に is often preferred.
examples[].german: I'm going to Japan.
Let's walk south.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Japan is the destination here, not the traveler.
の does not link a noun to 行きます here.
Japan is the travel destination here, not a route passed through.

en.explanation: が marks the grammatical subject of a sentence and emphasizes who or what performs the action. It is often used to introduce new information or to put special emphasis on the subject.
en.formation: Noun + が
en.notes: が is used after question words (誰が、何が) and before certain predicates such as 好き、欲しい、分かる、ある、いる.
examples[].german: There is a cat. / A cat is here.
Who came?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: います does not take a direct object here.
へ marks a destination of movement, not a cat that exists.
の would need a following noun to modify.

en.explanation: ～がある is used to express the existence of inanimate things (objects, plants, buildings, events). The polite form is ～があります.
en.formation: Noun + がある / があります
en.notes: ある is used for inanimate things, いる for living beings (people, animals). ある is also used for events.
examples[].german: There is a book on the desk.
There's a test tomorrow.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: A book is not a living being.
あります does not take a direct object.
This denies that the book is there.

en.explanation: が is used as a conjunction to connect two clauses with contrasting or complementary content. It means "but" or "however". Don't confuse it with the subject particle が.
en.formation: Sentence 1 + が、+ Sentence 2
en.notes: が as a conjunction is more formal than けど. It is often used for polite lead-ins: ～ですが... (It's that..., but...).
examples[].german: Japanese is difficult, but interesting.
I'm sorry, but please say it once more.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This gives a reason instead of the intended contrast.
ですます doubles the polite ending, which is not allowed.
を does not connect contrasting statements here.

en.explanation: ～が欲しい expresses the wish to own or get something. It is conjugated like an い-adjective and only used for your own wishes.
en.formation: Noun + が欲しい(です)
en.notes: 欲しい is for things (nouns), たい is for actions (verbs). For other people, you use ～欲しがっている.
examples[].german: I want a new computer.
What do you want?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The thing you want is not marked with に.
This negates the wish.
欲しい does not form its past with でした.

en.explanation: ～がいる is used to express the existence of living beings (people, animals). The polite form is ～がいます.
en.formation: Noun + がいる / がいます
en.notes: Rule of thumb: anything that can move by itself uses いる. Plants and cars use ある, even though they are "alive" or move.
examples[].german: There are children in the park.
I have three siblings.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: People are described with いる here.
います does not take a direct object here.
This denies that they are there.

en.meaning: should; it would be better to...
en.explanation: ～ほうがいい is used to give advice. It means "You should..." or "It would be better if...". For positive advice you use the た-form, for negative advice the ない-form.
en.formation: Verb た-form + ほうがいい (should do) / Verb ない-form + ほうがいい (should not do)
en.notes: Positive advice: た-form + ほうがいい. Negative advice: ない-form + ほうがいい. This form can sound direct; with superiors it's better to use ～たらどうですか.
examples[].german: You should eat more vegetables.
You shouldn't eat late at night.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: いい requires が in this evaluation.
に does not replace が here.
This advises against eating more vegetables.

en.explanation: To negate an い-adjective, the い is replaced by くない. The polite form is ～くないです or ～くありません.
en.formation: い-adjective (without い) + くない(です)
en.notes: Exception: いい (good) → よくない (not good). The adjective いい changes to よ- in all conjugated forms.
examples[].german: It's not hot today.
This movie isn't interesting.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Negating an い-adjective requires くない.
This would be the affirmative past.
This would be the negative past instead of today's state.

en.explanation: For the past form of an い-adjective, the い is replaced by かった. The polite form is ～かったです.
en.formation: い-adjective (without い) + かった(です)
en.notes: Exception: いい (good) → よかった (was good). Remember: いい → よくない → よかった → よくなかった.
examples[].german: It was cold yesterday.
The trip was fun.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: い-adjectives form the past with かった.
くでした is not a past form.
This would be "not cold" instead of "was cold".

en.explanation: For the negative past form of an い-adjective, the い is replaced by くなかった. The polite form is ～くなかったです.
en.formation: い-adjective (without い) + くなかった(です)
en.notes: Exception: いい (good) → よくなかった (was not good).
examples[].german: The test wasn't difficult.
It wasn't very tasty.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means "was difficult".
The negative form needs く before なかった.
This is non-past, not the past that is asked for.

en.explanation: い-adjectives end in い and can come directly before a noun or be used as a predicate. In the polite predicate form, です is added.
en.formation: い-adjective + です / い-adjective + Noun
en.notes: きれい (beautiful) and 有名 (famous) look like い-adjectives, but they are な-adjectives! There, the い is part of the word stem.
examples[].german: This book is interesting.
I like big dogs.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: い-adjectives do not form the past with でした.
The regular negative is おもしろくないです.
This means "not interesting".

en.explanation: 一番 (いちばん) means "most" or "number one" and is used for superlatives. It comes before the adjective.
en.formation: (Noun + の中で) + Noun + が一番 + Adjective
en.notes: For questions you use: ～の中で何/どこ/誰が一番～ですか。 (What/Where/Who is the most ~?)
examples[].german: Of all fruits, I like apples best.
The highest mountain in Japan is Mt. Fuji.
Who's the tallest in the class?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 一つ counts one item, not the top rank.
好き requires が here, not を.
に does not mark the preferred item here.

en.explanation: ～じゃないです or ～ではありません is the negative of です. It means "is not" or "am not". じゃない is more colloquial, ではありません is more formal.
en.formation: Noun + じゃないです / ではありません
en.notes: じゃ is the short form of では. Both forms are correct: じゃないです (colloquial) and ではありません (formal).
examples[].german: I'm not a student.
This isn't mine.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Nouns are not negated with くない.
This is not a standalone copula negative after a noun.
だったです is not the regular polite negative here.

en.explanation: ～じゃなかったです or ～ではありませんでした is the negative past form of です. It means "was not".
en.formation: Noun + じゃなかったです / ではありませんでした
en.notes: The four forms make up a system: です → じゃない → でした → じゃなかった. This system applies to nouns and な-adjectives.
examples[].german: That person wasn't a teacher.
The weather wasn't good.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This says the person was a teacher instead of denying it.
A noun is not negated with くなかった.
This is non-past instead of the past that is asked for.

en.explanation: か is attached to the end of a sentence to form a question. In polite Japanese, か replaces the question mark. The word order does not change.
en.formation: Sentence + か
en.notes: In polite speech, か is used without a question mark. In informal Japanese, か can be left out; the question is then formed with rising intonation.
examples[].german: Are you a student?
What will you eat?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a question after です.
に does not form a question after です.
へ does not form a question after です.

en.explanation: ～かもしれない expresses an uncertain guess. It means "maybe" or "it might be that...". The polite form is ～かもしれません.
en.formation: Verb/い-adj. (plain form) + かもしれない / な-adj./Noun + かもしれない
en.notes: Level of certainty: かもしれない (maybe, ~30%) < でしょう (probably, ~70%) < と思います (I think, personal opinion).
examples[].german: It might rain.
That person might be Japanese.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The fixed form for possibility is かもしれません.
This is not a form of the possibility expression.
No な is inserted after a verb here.

en.explanation: から marks the starting point of an action in time or space. It means "from" or "starting at". When it comes after a verb at the end of a sentence, it can also mean "because".
en.formation: Noun + から
en.notes: As a particle, から means "from/starting at"; as a conjunction after a verb it means "because". See also the conjunction から under sentence structures.
examples[].german: It starts at nine o'clock.
I came from Tokyo.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: まで names an end point, not the start at nine.
へ indicates a direction, not a starting time.
始まります has no direct object here.

en.explanation: から after a verb or adjective means "because". It gives the reason for the action described in the main clause. The reason comes before から.
en.formation: Sentence (reason) + から、+ Sentence (result)
en.notes: から (because) is more subjective than ので. から can also come at the end of a sentence to add a reason afterwards: 行きません。高いですから。
examples[].german: It's hot, so let's open the window.
I have a test tomorrow, so I'm studying today.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: のため is not a correct connection after 暑い.
No な is inserted after 暑い.
This sets up a contrast instead of the stated reason.

en.explanation: ～方 (かた) means "the way you do something". It is attached to the verb stem and forms a noun.
en.formation: Verb stem + 方(かた)
en.notes: 方 is read かた when it means "way, manner". The result is a noun: 食べ方 (way of eating), 書き方 (way of writing).
examples[].german: Please tell me how to read this kanji.
I don't know how to use it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ながら does not form a noun for the way of reading here.
読みます cannot come directly before を.
読みたい would need to be nominalized here; を cannot follow it directly.

en.explanation: ～けど is the colloquial version of が (but). The more formal form is ～けれども. It connects two clauses with contrasting content.
en.formation: Sentence 1 (plain) + けど、+ Sentence 2
en.notes: Level of formality: けど (most casual) → けれど → けれども (formal) → が (most formal). けど can also come at the end of a sentence and leave it open.
examples[].german: It's expensive, but it's tasty.
I want to go, but I don't have time.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This gives "expensive" as a reason instead of a contrast.
This gives a reason instead of "although it's expensive".
のため is not a correct connection after the い-adjective here.

en.meaning: feast / hospitality / treating someone to a meal (always with ご)
en.explanation: ご馳走 means "feast" or "lavish meal" and is best known from the expression ご馳走様でした (thank you for the meal). The ご prefix is mandatory – 馳走 without ご is not used. The kanji 馳走 literally mean "running around," alluding to the host going to great lengths to obtain ingredients.
en.formation: ご + 馳走（ちそう）— prefix mandatory
en.notes: ご馳走様でした is one of the most important Japanese table manners – you say it after every meal, whether at home, in a restaurant or when you have been treated. Its counterpart before eating is いただきます. ご馳走する means "to treat someone (to a meal)" and is a useful everyday expression.
examples[].german: Thank you for the meal. (said after eating)
Today it's my treat. (I'm paying.)
What a wonderful feast!
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: いただきます is said before the meal and does not come before でした.
This is a goodnight greeting, not thanks for the meal.
This is a daytime greeting, not thanks for the meal.

en.explanation: ご遠慮なく is an inviting phrase that encourages the other person to act without inhibition or reserve. 遠慮 means "reserve/restraint" and なく is the negation. With the polite prefix ご it becomes a respectful invitation to feel at ease.
en.formation: ご遠慮なく + verb (ください / お申し付けください etc.)
en.notes: ご遠慮なく is often used in restaurants, when entertaining guests and in customer service. The phrase reflects Japanese culture, in which guests often hesitate out of politeness. With ご遠慮なく you encourage them to give up this reserve.
examples[].german: Please help yourself without holding back.
If there is anything at all, please do not hesitate to say so.
Please feel free to use it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This asks for restraint instead of helping oneself freely.
The fixed adverbial form is ご遠慮なく.
の cannot come before the request here.

en.explanation: ご飯 is the standard word for "cooked rice" and for "meal" in general. The ご prefix is completely mandatory here – 飯（めし）without a prefix is a coarse, masculine variant that is avoided in polite speech. ご飯 is one of the most important examples of a ご-美化語.
en.formation: ご + 飯（はん）— prefix mandatory in normal speech
en.notes: ご飯 is used both for "rice" and for "meal" (朝ご飯 = breakfast, 昼ご飯 = lunch, 晩ご飯 = dinner). 飯（めし）without ご sounds coarse and is mainly used by men in informal speech. ご飯 is proof that rice is at the center of Japanese food culture.
examples[].german: Have you eaten?
The food is ready!
What do you eat for breakfast?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This asks about medicine instead of the meal.
This asks specifically about sweets instead of the meal.
This asks specifically about meat instead of the meal.

en.explanation: ご住所 is the polite form of 住所 (address). The ご prefix is used because 住所 is a Sino-Japanese word. As with お名前, ご住所 is mainly used when asking for another person's address or politely asking someone to fill it in on a form.
en.formation: ご + 住所（じゅうしょ）— prefix when asking others
en.notes: ご住所 follows the same pattern as お名前: you use the polite prefix when referring to the other person's details. You talk about your own address without the prefix: 住所は東京です。Forms often have ご住所 printed on them to show politeness toward the person filling them in.
examples[].german: Could you tell me your address?
Please write your address here.
Has your address changed?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This asks for the name instead of the address.
This asks for the phone number instead of the address.
This asks about work instead of the address.

en.explanation: ご家族 is the polite word for another person's family. The ご prefix is used here because 家族 is a Sino-Japanese word (漢語). Important: ご家族 is only used for the family of the person you are talking to or of third parties – for your own family you simply say 家族.
en.formation: ご + 家族（かぞく）— prefix for other people's families
en.notes: The distinction between ご家族 (for others) and 家族 (for yourself) is a basic principle of keigo: you honor what belongs to others and speak modestly about what is your own. Similarly: ご主人 (your husband) vs. 主人/夫 (my husband), ご両親 (your parents) vs. 両親/父と母 (my parents).
examples[].german: Is your family well?
Please give my regards to your family.
Are you here with your family?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means the address, not the family.
This means the name, not the family.
This means work, not the family.

en.meaning: polite forms of address and titles
en.explanation: Japanese honorific titles (敬称) are an important part of the keigo system. 様 (sama) is the most polite general form of address, 殿 (dono) is used in official documents, and 各位 (kakui) addresses a group. Using these forms correctly is essential in business.
en.formation: Name + 様 (standard) ／ Name + 殿 (official) ／ 各位 (to all)
en.notes: 様 is the safest choice in business correspondence. 殿 is mainly used in internal documents and certificates and is considered outdated in emails. 各位 replaces ～の皆様 in formal circulars. For outside companies: 御中 (onchū) for the company, 様 for individuals.
examples[].german: Mr./Ms. Tanaka, thank you for your call.
To all employees: today's meeting has been cancelled.
To the Head of the Human Resources Department (in official documents)
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The object particle does not make a form of address here.
The attributive particle does not fit the form of address here.
ます cannot be attached directly to the honorific suffix.

en.meaning: there is no excuse; I am deeply sorry
en.explanation: 申し訳ございません is the most formal standard apology in Japanese. 申し訳 literally means "excuse/justification" and ございません is the keigo negative of ある. Literally, the phrase says: "There is no excuse (for my behavior)". It is considerably more formal than すみません or ごめんなさい.
en.formation: 申し訳ございません (fixed phrase) / 大変申し訳ございません (stronger) / 誠に申し訳ございません (strongest)
en.notes: The levels of intensity are: 申し訳ございません → 大変申し訳ございません → 誠に申し訳ございません. In the less formal variant, ございません is replaced by ありません. In business, this phrase is expected for every mistake or inconvenience.
examples[].german: I am terribly sorry to have kept you waiting.
I sincerely apologize for causing you trouble.
I am very sorry. We are currently out of stock.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite negative form is ございません.
This is not a verb form.
Two negative endings cannot be combined like this.

en.explanation: お弁当 is the polite form of 弁当 (lunch box). The お prefix is widespread here and usual in most everyday situations. 弁当 without お is used in compounds such as 弁当箱 (bentōbako, lunch box container) or in matter-of-fact contexts (menus, business descriptions).
en.formation: お + 弁当（べんとう）— prefix usual in everyday speech
en.notes: In everyday life, お弁当 is almost always used with お, especially in spoken language. On signs and menus in shops you sometimes see 弁当 without お. Bento culture is deeply rooted in Japan, and お弁当 is an everyday word that every learner of Japanese should know.
examples[].german: I brought a bento today.
Let's go buy a bento.
I make a bento every day.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means a souvenir gift, not the bento meal.
This means money, not the bento meal.
This means flowers, not the bento meal.

en.explanation: 美化語 refers to the use of the prefixes お (for native Japanese words) and ご (for Sino-Japanese words) to beautify words and make them sound more polite. Unlike respectful language (sonkeigo) and humble language (kenjōgo), 美化語 is not directed at a particular person but makes speech more elegant in general.
en.formation: お + native Japanese word ／ ご + Sino-Japanese word
en.notes: Some words have お/ご so firmly built in that they are hardly used without it (お茶, ご飯, お金). For others it is optional and signals the level of politeness. Loanwords (katakana) normally do not take お/ご, with exceptions such as おトイレ (colloquial).
examples[].german: Shall I make some tea?
The weather has gotten nice, hasn't it?
The meal is ready!
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: An object particle cannot stand between the prefix and 天気.
な cannot stand between the prefix and 天気.
ます cannot be attached to the prefix.

en.explanation: お茶 is one of the best-known examples of 美化語, where the お prefix is so firmly attached that it is practically mandatory. 茶 without お sounds unnatural; it appears without お almost only in compounds such as 茶道 (sadō, tea ceremony) or 緑茶 (ryokucha, green tea).
en.formation: お + 茶（ちゃ）— prefix practically mandatory
en.notes: お茶 is a prime example of a word in which the お prefix has become mandatory. Even in casual speech, people say お茶 and not 茶 on its own. The word shows how 美化語 can become a fixed part of the vocabulary over time.
examples[].german: Would you like some tea or something?
I'll make some tea, okay?
I drink tea every morning.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This offers water instead of tea.
This offers coffee instead of tea.
This offers alcohol instead of tea.

en.explanation: お金 is the standard word for "money" in Japanese. The お prefix is mandatory here – 金 (かね) on its own is hardly used and sounds crude or rude. 金 is used without お only in compounds such as 金額 (kingaku, amount of money) or 金持ち (kanemochi, rich person).
en.formation: お + 金（かね）— prefix mandatory
en.notes: お金 is one of the words where the お prefix is so deeply rooted that many Japanese people no longer perceive it as an honorific prefix at all. Even in colloquial speech and in rude contexts, お金 is used with お.
examples[].german: I don't have enough money.
I'm saving money.
Please don't worry about the money.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means water, not money.
This means time, not money.
This means rice, not money.

en.meaning: sorry to have kept you waiting; thank you for your patience
en.explanation: お待たせいたしました is a polite phrase used when you have kept someone waiting. It combines お待たせする (to make someone wait) with いたしました (kenjōgo past of しました). You hear this phrase constantly in restaurants, shops, on the phone and in all service situations.
en.formation: お待たせいたしました (fixed phrase) / 大変お待たせいたしました (after a longer wait)
en.notes: In Japan, お待たせいたしました is said reflexively, even if the wait was very short. The less formal version is お待たせしました (without いた). 大変 is added when the wait was longer than usual.
examples[].german: Sorry to have kept you waiting. Here is your order.
Thank you very much for your patience. I will show you to your seat.
Sorry to have kept you waiting on the phone. This is Suzuki from the sales department.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates having caused the wait.
This is not a polite past form.
This is not a verb form.

en.explanation: お祭り is the usual word for "festival" in Japanese. The お prefix is firmly built in here – 祭り（まつり）without お is used in some compounds such as 夏祭り（なつまつり, summer festival）or 火祭り（ひまつり, fire festival）, but as a standalone word people almost always say お祭り.
en.formation: お + 祭り（まつり）— prefix mandatory as a standalone word
en.notes: お祭り has its origins in the worship of the gods (祭る = to worship, to pay homage to the kami). The お prefix originally showed reverence for the religious character of the festival. In compounds such as 夏祭り or 花祭り, the お is dropped.
examples[].german: There's a festival this weekend, you know.
I wore a yukata at the festival.
The children are looking forward to the festival.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means work, not a festival.
This means time off, not a festival.
This means a meal, not a festival.

en.meaning: gift brought back from a trip / souvenir (always with お)
en.explanation: お土産 is the standard word for a gift brought back from a trip, or a "souvenir." The お prefix is practically mandatory here – 土産（みやげ）on its own is used almost only in compounds such as 土産物（みやげもの）or 土産話（みやげばなし, travel stories）. The culture of buying お土産 is deeply rooted in Japan.
en.formation: お + 土産（みやげ）— prefix practically mandatory
en.notes: In Japan it is customary to bring お土産 back from trips for colleagues and friends. Train stations and airports have large お土産 sections. The word is practically never used without お and is an excellent example of a culturally deep-rooted 美化語.
examples[].german: I bought souvenirs from my trip.
This is a souvenir from Kyoto. Here you go.
It took me a long time to choose souvenirs.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means a meal, not a travel souvenir.
This means medicine, not a travel souvenir.
This means water, not a travel souvenir.

en.explanation: お水 is the polite form of 水 (water). The お prefix is optional here but common in most everyday situations, especially in restaurants, when offering drinks or when politely asking for water. Without お, 水 sounds rather matter-of-fact or blunt.
en.formation: お + 水（みず）
en.notes: In everyday life お水 is almost always used with お, especially by women and in polite speech. In scientific or technical contexts, 水 without the prefix is more common. In restaurants, お水 is the standard term.
examples[].german: Water, please.
Shall I bring you some water?
There's some cold water, you know.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The translation calls for water, not tea.
The translation calls for water, not rice.
The translation calls for water, not money.

en.explanation: お腹 is the standard everyday word for "belly" or "stomach." The お prefix is mandatory here – 腹（はら）on its own is used in some idioms (腹が立つ = to get angry), but for the body part people always say お腹. Especially in the well-known phrase お腹が空いた (I'm hungry), お is indispensable.
en.formation: お + 腹（なか）— prefix mandatory in everyday speech
en.notes: お腹 is another example where the お prefix has fused so firmly with the word that it is no longer perceived as a polite form. The reading なか (instead of はら) is used only with お. 腹（はら）without お sounds masculine and coarse.
examples[].german: I'm hungry.
I'm full.
My stomach isn't feeling well.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: A name does not get hungry.
Tea does not get hungry.
Money does not get hungry.

en.explanation: お名前 is the polite form of 名前 (name). The お prefix is used especially when asking for another person's name or talking about the name of a respected person. When talking about your own name, お is left out: 名前は田中です。
en.formation: お + 名前（なまえ）— prefix usual for other people
en.notes: お名前 shows the difference between 美化語 and 尊敬語: when you mean the other person's name, お serves as a mark of respect (尊敬語 function). When talking about names in general, it is 美化語. You give your own name without お, since you do not honor yourself.
examples[].german: Your name, please.
What is your name? (very polite)
Please write your name here.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This asks for the address instead of the name.
This does not ask about the name.
This does not request the name.

en.explanation: お手洗い is the standard polite word for "toilet" or "restroom." Literally it means "hand-washing" (手を洗う). The お prefix is mandatory here – 手洗い alone is hardly ever used in the sense of "toilet." お手洗い is the preferred form in polite speech and the usual word on signs in public buildings.
en.formation: お + 手洗い（てあらい）— prefix mandatory
en.notes: Japanese has several words for "toilet" with different levels of politeness: トイレ (neutral, most common), お手洗い (polite), 化粧室（けしょうしつ, "powder room," very polite, in department stores), お手水（おちょうず, traditional/religious). お手洗い is the safest choice in polite conversation.
examples[].german: Where is the restroom?
I'll just go to the restroom. (very polite)
The restroom is over there.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This asks about the exit instead of the restroom.
This asks about paying the bill instead of the restroom.
This asks about a meal instead of the restroom.

en.meaning: thank you for your hard work / good work (very formal)
en.explanation: お疲れ様でございます is the most formal version of お疲れ様です, used as a greeting among colleagues and as acknowledgment of work done. The でございます form makes it particularly respectful; it is used toward superiors and in formal situations.
en.formation: お疲れ様でございます (set phrase) ／ お疲れ様でした (after finishing a piece of work)
en.notes: お疲れ様でございます is used as the standard opening in internal company emails (like お世話になっております with external contacts). Toward superiors, お疲れ様です is the minimum; ご苦労様です should only be used toward subordinates.
examples[].german: Thank you for your hard work. I am sending you the minutes of today's meeting.
Thank you for your hard work in handling this for so long.
Hello (internal greeting). This is Tanaka; would you have a moment?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is ございます.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite past ends in ました.

en.meaning: change / money given back (always with お)
en.explanation: お釣り is the standard word for "change" (money). The お prefix is mandatory here – 釣り（つり）on its own means "fishing" or "angling" and is not used without お in the sense of "change." お釣り is an indispensable word for everyday life in Japan, especially when shopping.
en.formation: お + 釣り（つり）— prefix mandatory in the sense of "change"
en.notes: You hear お釣り constantly at Japanese checkouts. Although cashless payment is spreading in Japan, cash is still widely used. The checkout phrase お釣りは○○円です is part of everyday language. Without お, 釣り means only "fishing."
examples[].german: Please check your change.
Keep the change.
Out of 1,000 yen. Your change is 300 yen.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means a name, not the change.
This means an address, not the change.
This means luggage, not the change.

en.meaning: rules for using お (native Japanese) and ご (Sino-Japanese)
en.explanation: The basic rule for 美化語 prefixes is: お goes before 和語 (native Japanese words, mostly with kun readings), ご before 漢語 (Sino-Japanese words, mostly with on readings). There are exceptions, however: some 漢語 take お instead of ご (e.g. お電話, お料理, お返事), and katakana words (loanwords) usually take no prefix.
en.formation: お + 和語（kun reading）／ ご + 漢語（on reading）／ watch out for exceptions
en.notes: The distinction 和語→お / 漢語→ご is a helpful rule of thumb but not an absolute law. Many frequently used 漢語 take お (お電話, お料理, お食事, お返事, お天気). Loanwords (katakana) normally take no prefix – おコーヒー or おビール are considered colloquial/jokey. When in doubt, it helps to memorize common combinations.
examples[].german: Flowers, water, sake → native Japanese words → お
Family, address, opinion → Sino-Japanese words → ご
Telephone, cooking, reply → Sino-Japanese, but exceptions with お

en.meaning: you've been put through / I'm taking over the call
en.explanation: お電話代わりました is the standard phrase you say when you take over a call from a colleague. It signals to the caller that a new person is on the line and is followed by a self-introduction.
en.formation: お電話代わりました + [Department]の[Name]でございます。
en.notes: This phrase is said automatically after the call has been put through. When you transfer a caller yourself, you say: ただいま担当に代わります (I'll put you through to the person in charge now) or 少々お待ちくださいませ (please wait a moment).
examples[].german: You've been put through. This is Yamada from the sales department.
You've been put through. This is Satō, the person in charge. Sorry to keep you waiting.
You've been put through. I'll now take your inquiry.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite past requires the stem 代わり.
Politeness endings cannot be doubled.
This negates the takeover of the call, which has already happened.

en.explanation: お電話ありがとうございます is the standard opening when answering business calls. It is used together with the company name and your own name. Japanese telephone etiquette has fixed formulas that every businessperson must master.
en.formation: お電話ありがとうございます。[Company名]の[名前]でございます。
en.notes: Japanese telephone etiquette follows fixed rules: 1) greet the caller with the company name, 2) ask what the call is about, 3) confirm the customer's name (お名前を頂戴できますか), 4) transfer the call or offer a callback. 恐れ入りますが is used as a cushion word before questions.
examples[].german: Thank you for calling. This is Suzuki from ABC Trading.
Thank you for calling. How may I help you?
Thank you for calling. I'll put you through to the person in charge, so please hold for a moment.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form of thanks is ありがとうございます.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite past ends in ました.

en.meaning: allow me to inform you (formal announcement)
en.explanation: ご案内申し上げます is a formal opening phrase for official announcements, invitations and notices. It combines ご案内 (information/guidance) with 申し上げます (to say, humble) and is used in business circulars, letters of invitation and official notifications.
en.formation: ご案内申し上げます ／ ～につきまして、ご案内いたします
en.notes: ご案内申し上げます is the standard opening for formal business announcements and letters of invitation. It often appears after the subject line of an official email or at the beginning of an informational letter.
examples[].german: Please allow us to inform you as follows.
Please allow us to inform you of our business hours over the year-end and New Year holidays.
Please allow us to inform you of the launch of our new product.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the announced information.
ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.meaning: should you have any questions; if anything is unclear
en.explanation: ご不明な点がございましたら is a polite standard phrase that signals to the recipient that you are available for follow-up questions. ございましたら is the formal version of あったら (if there is). This phrase is typically used at the end of business emails or explanations.
en.formation: ご不明な点がございましたら + お気軽にお問い合わせください (or similar)
en.notes: This phrase is almost obligatory in business emails and typically comes shortly before the closing formula. Variants are: ご質問がございましたら (if you have questions) and ご不明点等ございましたら (if anything is unclear or the like).
examples[].german: Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact us.
If anything is unclear, please contact Satō, who is in charge.
Should you have any questions at all, please do not hesitate to let us know.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The conditional is ございましたら.
を and ご do not form an existence construction here.
The て-form is not combined with たら.

en.meaning: I realize you are busy, but ...
en.explanation: お忙しいところ恐縮ですが is a variant of the cushion phrase お忙しいところ恐れ入りますが in which 恐縮です (to feel ashamed/humbled) is used instead of 恐れ入ります. Both forms are interchangeable in business emails and introduce a request that might cause the recipient some trouble.
en.formation: お忙しいところ恐縮ですが + request ／ ご多忙のところ恐縮ですが (variant)
en.notes: 恐縮ですが and 恐れ入りますが are interchangeable in everyday business. 恐縮ですが has a slightly stronger undertone of guilt. Intensifying it with 大変 or making it more formal with 存じます are the usual ways to step it up.
examples[].german: I know you're busy, but could you please sign this?
I'm very sorry to trouble you when you're so busy, but could you send me the documents?
I'm sorry to impose on you when you're busy, but I would ask you to take care of this.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます cannot be attached directly to 恐縮.
を cannot be attached to the clause connection.
No な comes before the copula です here.

en.meaning: I would be grateful for a quick message
en.explanation: ご一報いただければ幸いです is a polite request for a short reply. 一報 means "a message/notice," and the whole phrase politely asks the recipient to get in touch briefly. It is used in business emails when you are waiting for an answer or confirmation.
en.formation: ご一報ください / ご一報いただければ幸いです / ご一報くださいますようお願いいたします
en.notes: ご一報 is used as a less demanding alternative to ご連絡 (getting in touch) and signals that only a short confirmation message is expected, not a detailed letter.
examples[].german: Once your schedule is settled, I would be grateful for a quick message.
Please let us know when you have arrived.
If you notice anything, please let us know.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The conditional is いただければ.
ます cannot be attached directly to 幸い.
を cannot complete this request.

en.meaning: please take care of your health
en.explanation: ご自愛ください is a traditional closing formula in letters and emails that asks the recipient to look after their health. 自愛 literally means "self-love/self-care." This phrase is used especially when the seasons change and in more personal business letters.
en.formation: ご自愛ください / ご自愛くださいませ / くれぐれもご自愛ください (emphatic)
en.notes: ご自愛ください is used to close personal and semi-business letters. It goes particularly well with seasonal greetings (時候の挨拶). It is used less often in purely factual business emails.
examples[].german: The cold days continue, so please take extra good care of yourself.
Given the season, I pray that you take good care of yourself.
Please look after yourself and take care of your health.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ください is not attached to する.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite past requires the correct stem.

en.explanation: ご確認ください is a polite request asking the recipient to check or confirm something. It is used very often in business emails and documents. The prefix ご in front of the Sino-Japanese word 確認 makes the phrase respectful.
en.formation: ご確認ください / ご確認いただけますでしょうか (even more polite, as a question)
en.notes: ご確認ください is one of the most frequent phrases in business emails. The more polite question form ご確認いただけますでしょうか is used when you do not want to ask the recipient directly.
examples[].german: Please check the attached file.
Could you please check the schedule?
Please check the following and reply.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This is a statement instead of a request.
This is not a request form.
This negates a past check instead of asking for one.

en.meaning: I would be grateful if you could consider it
en.explanation: ご検討いただければ幸いです is an extremely polite request asking the recipient to consider a proposal or an offer. The combination of ご検討 (consideration), いただければ (if I could receive the favor) and 幸いです (it would be a joy) produces a phrase that combines maximum politeness with modesty.
en.formation: ご検討いただければ幸いです / ご検討いただけますと幸いです (variant)
en.notes: This phrase is often used at the end of business proposals and offers. The variant with 存じます instead of です at the end sounds even more humble. 前向きに (positively/favorably) is often added to encourage a positive consideration.
examples[].german: I would be grateful if you could consider this plan.
I am sending you the quote; I would be grateful if you could consider it.
I would be most grateful if you could give it favorable consideration.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を cannot end the request.
ます cannot be attached directly to 幸い.
The conditional is いただければ.

en.meaning: I'm sorry we could not meet your expectations
en.explanation: ご期待に沿えず申し訳ございません is a formal apology used when turning something down in business. 期待に沿う means "to meet expectations," and the negative 沿えず expresses that one was unable to do so. This form is more polite than a direct refusal.
en.formation: ご期待に沿えず / ご希望に添えず + 申し訳ございません / 大変残念ですが
en.notes: This phrase is the standard opening for business refusals. It softens the refusal and shows regret. In Japan, refusals are almost never stated directly but are always introduced with cushioning formulas like this one.
examples[].german: We are truly sorry that we were unable to meet your expectations.
I'm very sorry that we cannot accommodate your wishes, but we will have to pass this time.
It pains me not to be able to meet your request, but I'm afraid we are unable to do so.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This affirms that the expectations are met.
The point of reference requires に.
な cannot be attached here.

en.meaning: I would be grateful for your reply
en.explanation: ご返信いただけますと幸いです is a standard request for a reply in business emails. It is more polite than ご返信ください and less urgent than ご返信くださいますようお願い申し上げます. The と conditional together with 幸いです expresses a wish.
en.formation: ご返信 + いただけますと / いただければ + 幸いです / 幸いに存じます
en.notes: In business emails, a deadline for the reply is always given. 幸いです is softer than お願いいたします and gives the recipient more leeway. 助かります (that would help me) is a slightly more informal but frequently used alternative.
examples[].german: I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy, but I would be grateful for a reply within this week.
I would be grateful if you could check it and then reply.
If possible, it would be a great help if you could reply by next Monday.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
ます cannot be attached directly to 幸い.
を cannot complete this request.

en.meaning: thank you for your message / for getting in touch
en.explanation: ご連絡いただきありがとうございます is a standard thank-you formula at the start of an email reply when the other person has gotten in touch. It shows appreciation for the contact and is one of the most frequently used opening phrases in business.
en.formation: ご連絡いただきありがとうございます ／ ご連絡くださりありがとうございます
en.notes: This phrase is used at the beginning of reply emails, directly after お世話になっております. 早速の (prompt) is added when the reply came quickly. ご丁寧に (courteous/thorough) emphasizes appreciation for a detailed message.
examples[].german: Thank you for your prompt message.
Thank you for getting in touch despite being so busy.
Thank you very much for your kind message.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The thanks must be preceded here by the connecting stem or て-form.
The polite form of thanks is ありがとうございます.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.explanation: ご了承ください (ごりょうしょうください) is used to ask the recipient politely for understanding or acceptance of a situation that may not be ideal. 了承 means "consent/understanding". This phrase is often used when announcing a restriction, change or inconvenience.
en.formation: ご了承ください / ご了承いただけますようお願いいたします (even more polite)
en.notes: ご了承ください is found very often on notice signs, in terms and conditions and in notifications. It is often used together with あらかじめ (in advance). Not to be confused with ご容赦ください, which contains a stronger apology.
examples[].german: Please understand this in advance.
Please understand if the item is out of stock.
There will be noise due to construction work. We ask for your understanding.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: A statement about granting does not form the request here.
る cannot be attached to ます.
ください is not attached to the dictionary form.

en.explanation: ご査収ください (ごさしゅうください) is a very formal phrase used mainly in business emails when you are sending documents, files or papers. 査収 literally means "to examine and accept". It asks the recipient to check what was sent and accept it.
en.formation: ご査収ください / ご査収のほどよろしくお願いいたします (even more formal)
en.notes: ご査収ください is used almost exclusively in written business communication and sounds unnatural in spoken language. It is one of the most formal phrases for sending something in Japanese.
examples[].german: I have attached the invoice; please review it.
I am sending you the report. Please kindly review it.
I have enclosed the contract; I respectfully ask you to review and accept it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ください is not attached to する.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite past needs the verb stem.

en.meaning: thank you for taking the trouble to come
en.explanation: ご足労いただきありがとうございます is a formal thank-you formula used when someone has taken the trouble to come in person. 足労 literally means "leg work / effort of the feet" and expresses appreciation for the effort of coming.
en.formation: ご足労いただき / おかけいたしまして + ありがとうございます / 申し訳ございません
en.notes: ご足労 is used especially when a customer or business partner comes to your own office. It shows appreciation for the physical effort of the journey. The phrase is used at reception and at the start of meetings.
examples[].german: Thank you for taking the trouble to come today.
I'm sorry to have put you to the trouble of coming when you are so busy.
I feel humbled that you took the trouble to come.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The thanks requires a connecting stem or て-form.
The polite form of thanks is ありがとうございます.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.meaning: may I ask what your business is?
en.explanation: ご用件をお伺いいたします is a standard phrase on the phone or at reception for asking what a visitor or caller needs. It combines ご用件 (business/matter, honorific), お伺い (to ask, humble) and いたします (to do, humble) into a triply polite construction.
en.formation: ご用件をお伺いいたします ／ どのようなご用件でしょうか (as a question)
en.notes: This phrase is standard at reception desks and on the phone. At reception it is typically followed by お約束はいただいておりますか (do you have an appointment?) or 少々お待ちくださいませ (please wait a moment).
examples[].german: May I ask what this is regarding?
How may I help you?
Excuse me, but could you tell me what this is regarding?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: もよろしい is preceded by the て-form.
もよろしい is preceded by the て-form.
The finite polite form does not fit before もよろしい here.

en.explanation: ご容赦ください (ごようしゃください) is a very formal apology phrase that is stronger than ご了承ください. 容赦 means "leniency/forgiveness". You use this phrase when asking forgiveness for an omission, an inconvenience or a mistake. It expresses deeper regret than other forms of apology.
en.formation: ご容赦ください / 何卒ご容赦くださいますようお願い申し上げます (very formal)
en.notes: ご容赦ください is often combined with 何卒 (nanitozo = earnestly) to strengthen the urgency of the request. This phrase is more formal and more apologetic than ご了承ください.
examples[].german: Please forgive the late reply.
Please excuse me for contacting you so suddenly. I earnestly ask for your forgiveness.
We apologize for the inconvenience and kindly ask for your forgiveness.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ください is not attached to する.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite past needs the verb stem.

en.meaning: as always / all along / continually (formal email opening)
en.explanation: 平素より is a formal adverb used as an opening in business letters and emails. It means "all along" or "as always" and introduces thanks for the business relationship so far. It is more formal than いつも (always).
en.formation: 平素より + 大変お世話になっております / 格別のお引き立てを賜り
en.notes: 平素より is the most formal opening for business letters and emails. In everyday email communication, いつもお世話になっております is enough. 格別のお引き立て (special patronage) and ご愛顧 (customer loyalty) are common additions in official letters.
examples[].german: Thank you very much for your continued support.
We sincerely thank you for your continued special patronage.
We extend our heartfelt thanks for your continued patronage of our products.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a time expression here.
な does not connect to the thanks that follow here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 平素.

en.meaning: in closing / last but not least (letter ending)
en.explanation: 末筆ながら is a formal closing formula in business letters that literally means "although it is the last line." It introduces a final wish, a wish for good health or an additional request. This formula shows that the writer is aware of the hierarchy.
en.formation: 末筆ながら + ご自愛ください / ますますのご発展をお祈り申し上げます
en.notes: 末筆ながら is used only in written communication. The formula implies modesty: the personal wish is placed at the end because it is secondary to the business content. ご自愛ください (please take care of your health) is the most common closing formula.
examples[].german: In closing, I wish you all the best of health.
In closing, I wish your company continued prosperity.
In closing, given the season, please take good care of yourself.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: な cannot be attached here.
を does not form a closing connection here.
ます cannot be attached to ながら.

en.meaning: please let us know / please tell me
en.explanation: お申し付けください is a polite customer-service phrase that signals to the other person that you are available at any time for inquiries, requests or instructions. 申し付ける means "to instruct/to charge someone with," and with the respectful (sonkeigo) frame お～ください it becomes a deferential request.
en.formation: お申し付けください ／ 何なりとお申し付けください (emphatic)
en.notes: 何なりとお申し付けください is one of the most popular customer-service phrases and is often heard in hotels, restaurants and upscale retail. It sounds more welcoming and respectful than ~~ください alone.
examples[].german: Please don't hesitate to tell me anything you need.
If anything is unclear, please feel free to let us know at any time.
If you have any further requests, please let us know.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ください is not attached to the dictionary form.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite past requires the correct stem.

en.meaning: earnestly / at all costs / please, by all means
en.explanation: 何卒 is a formal adverb that strengthens a request and expresses great urgency or seriousness. It means "at all costs" or "please, by all means" and is used in business emails, letters and formal requests to underline the importance of the request.
en.formation: 何卒 + よろしくお願いいたします / ご理解ください / ご容赦ください
en.notes: 何卒 is used almost exclusively in written business communication. It is one of the most important intensifiers in business letters. 何卒よろしくお願いいたします is the strongest standard closing formula in emails.
examples[].german: I earnestly ask for your understanding.
I earnestly ask you to consider this matter.
I humbly ask for your support.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form an adverbial request here.
な cannot connect to the request here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 何卒.

en.explanation: ～の件につきまして is the formal business version of ～について (regarding). つきまして is the ます-form of the formal verb つく (to relate to) in the て-form. This phrase is used to introduce the subject of a business message.
en.formation: Noun + の件につきまして / Noun + につきまして
en.notes: ～の件につきまして is especially common in email subject lines and at the start of business messages. The shorter form ～につきまして can also be used without 件.
examples[].german: I am contacting you regarding the quote from the other day.
Regarding next month's meeting, there is something I would like to discuss with you.
Regarding the change in the delivery date, I would like to offer my apologies.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The finite form cannot be connected with ご連絡いたします here.
The reference requires に.
まして is not attached to the dictionary form.

en.explanation: ご笑納ください (ごしょうのうください) is used when you give someone a gift or an enclosure and literally means "please accept it with a smile." It expresses modesty about the gift and asks the recipient to accept it graciously.
en.formation: ご笑納ください / お納めください (less formal) / ご笑納いただければ幸いです
en.notes: The Japanese culture of giving gifts includes traditional modest set phrases: つまらないものですが (it's nothing special), ほんの気持ちです (it's just a small token), 粗品ですが (it's just a little something). ご笑納 goes with all of these lead-ins.
examples[].german: It's just a small token of my appreciation, but please kindly accept it.
It's nothing special, but I would be glad if you would accept it.
It's just a small gift, but please accept it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ください is not attached to する.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite past requires the verb stem.

en.meaning: I'm sorry to trouble you when you are busy
en.explanation: お忙しいところ恐れ入りますが is a fixed business courtesy formula used before a request. It shows consideration for the other person's time and introduces a request respectfully.
en.formation: お忙しいところ恐れ入りますが + request/inquiry
en.notes: This formula is especially common in business emails and phone calls. Variants: お忙しい中 (onaka), ご多忙のところ. 恐れ入ります on its own means "excuse me" or "thank you very much" and is an important business phrase.
examples[].german: I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy, but could you please check this?
Sorry to bother you when you're busy, but could you spare me a little of your time?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます requires the verb stem 入り.
を does not link the request to the introduction here.
な does not form a link to the request here.

en.meaning: please do not hesitate to contact us
en.explanation: お気軽にお問い合わせください is an inviting standard phrase that signals to the recipient that they can get in touch without any worries. お気軽に means "freely/casually" and お問い合わせ is the polite form of 問い合わせ (inquiry). This phrase is often used at the end of business emails and on websites.
en.formation: お気軽に + お問い合わせください / ご連絡ください / お申し付けください
en.notes: This phrase is everywhere on Japanese websites, in brochures and in business emails. It corresponds to the English "Don't hesitate to contact us" and is less formal than other business phrases.
examples[].german: If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact us.
Please feel free to contact us. We look forward to hearing from you.
If there is anything at all, please do not hesitate to let us know.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ください does not follow the dictionary form here.
This is not a request form.
This explicitly asks people not to make inquiries.

en.explanation: お願い申し上げます is the most formal version of お願いします and is used in official requests, business letters and formal inquiries. 申し上げる (to say/to offer, humble) gives the request the highest level of humility.
en.formation: お願い申し上げます ／ 何卒お願い申し上げます (earnestly) ／ ～くださいますようお願い申し上げます
en.notes: お願い申し上げます is more formal than お願いいたします. In emails it is often used at the end, especially combined with 何卒 (earnestly). The progression: お願いします < お願いいたします < お願い申し上げます.
examples[].german: I earnestly ask for your kind support.
I humbly request your attendance.
I humbly ask for your indulgence.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the request.
ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.meaning: business greeting formula (thank you for your continued support)
en.explanation: お世話になっております is the most important business greeting formula in Japan. It is used at the beginning of emails, phone calls and meetings with business partners and expresses gratitude for the existing business relationship.
en.formation: お世話になっております (fixed formula, invariable) ／ variant: いつもお世話になっております
en.notes: This formula is used almost automatically at the beginning of every business email or phone call. On first contact, you say instead: 初めまして or お世話になります (future form). 大変お世話になりました is used when saying goodbye or at the end of the year.
examples[].german: Thank you as always for your support. This is Tanaka from ABC Corporation.
Thank you for your continued support. I am getting in touch about the matter from the other day.
Thank you so much for everything you have done for me. (when saying goodbye)
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is おります.
The expression uses に.
This negates the ongoing support.

en.meaning: excuse me, but... / I'm sorry, but...
en.explanation: 恐れ入りますが is a polite introductory phrase (クッション言葉) used before a request, a question or a potentially unwelcome matter. It softens what follows and shows consideration for the other person. This form is indispensable in Japanese business life.
en.formation: 恐れ入りますが + request/question/matter
en.notes: 恐れ入りますが belongs to the so-called クッション言葉 (cushion words), which are used in Japanese to soften requests and questions. Other cushion words are: お手数ですが、申し訳ございませんが.
examples[].german: Excuse me, but could you tell me your name once more?
I'm sorry, but could you fill this in here?
Excuse me, but could you wait a moment?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます needs the stem 入り.
を cannot connect to the following request here.
な does not connect with the following request here.

en.meaning: I'm sorry for the trouble, but...
en.explanation: お手数をおかけしますが is a polite cushion word (クッション言葉) used before a request that may cause the recipient trouble or effort. お手数 means "trouble/effort" and おかけする is the humble form of かける (to cause). This phrase shows consideration and gratitude for the other person's effort.
en.formation: お手数をおかけしますが + request / お手数ですが + request (shorter)
en.notes: お手数をおかけしますが is one of the most common cushion words in business emails. It is used before practically any request that creates work for the recipient. The shorter form お手数ですが is also very widespread.
examples[].german: Sorry for the trouble, but I would ask you to sign the documents.
I'm sorry for the trouble, but could you please check it once more?
I apologize for the trouble and ask you to kindly take care of this.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます needs the stem し.
を does not connect the request here.
な does not connect the introduction with the request here.

en.meaning: I would humbly like to be allowed to...
en.explanation: ～させていただきたく存じます is one of the most polite forms in Japanese for expressing an action you intend to take. It combines させていただく (to be allowed to) with たく (to want) and 存じます (to think, kenjōgo). This triple humble form is used in very formal business situations.
en.formation: Verb させ-form + ていただきたく存じます
en.notes: This form is sometimes criticized as excessively polite (過剰敬語), but it is quite common in Japanese business culture, especially when addressing customers or people of higher status. The slightly shorter form ～させていただきたいと思います is a less formal alternative.
examples[].german: I would like to pay you a visit next week, if I may.
I would like to be allowed to explain the details of the project to you.
I would like to have the opportunity to meet with you once.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: いただく needs the て-connection.
The adverbial form of たい is たく.
ます needs the verb stem.

en.meaning: is that so? / oh, I see (very formal)
en.explanation: 左様でございますか is the most formal version of そうですか (is that so?). 左様 (さよう) is the formal equivalent of そう (so), and でございます raises it to the highest level of politeness. This phrase is used in upscale customer service and very formal business situations.
en.formation: 左様でございますか (as a confirmation / listening signal)
en.notes: 左様でございますか is used mainly in the hotel industry, by airlines and in premium customer service. In ordinary business, そうでございますか or そうですか is enough. Knowing this form shows an N1-level understanding of the keigo system.
examples[].german: Oh, I see. Understood.
Is that so? Please accept my sincere apologies for that.
I see. I will check right away.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます cannot be attached directly to 左様.
The polite form is ございます.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.meaning: excuse me; I'll take my leave (formal)
en.explanation: 失礼いたします is a versatile formal phrase used in various situations: when entering or leaving a room, when hanging up the phone, when interrupting an activity or when saying goodbye. いたします is the kenjōgo form of します and makes the phrase especially polite.
en.formation: 失礼いたします (fixed phrase) / 失礼いたしました (past: apology for something that already happened)
en.notes: お先に失礼いたします is the standard phrase when you leave the office before your colleagues. On the phone, you say 失礼いたします before hanging up. The past form 失礼いたしました is used as an apology for a rudeness already committed.
examples[].german: Excuse me for leaving before you. (said when leaving work for the day)
Well then, goodbye. (as a farewell on the phone)
Excuse me for disturbing you. I have come to deliver the documents.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is いたします.
This negates the leave-taking.
This is not a verb form.

en.meaning: I am contacting you in haste; a quick, urgent note
en.explanation: 取り急ぎご連絡いたします is a standard business phrase used when you want to pass on important information quickly without following the usual elaborate politeness structure. 取り急ぎ means "in haste" or "hurriedly" and at the same time apologizes for the brevity of the message.
en.formation: 取り急ぎ + ご連絡いたします / ご報告いたします / お知らせいたします
en.notes: 取り急ぎ is often used as an apology for a short email. The shortened form 取り急ぎご報告まで (just a quick report) is also used frequently and is somewhat more informal.
examples[].german: A quick note to let you know: the date of the meeting has changed.
Just a quick report for now.
I will send you the details later, but I wanted to let you know quickly in advance.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates making contact.
ます needs the stem いたし.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.meaning: I humbly ask for your kind consideration (formal closing phrase)
en.explanation: よろしくお願いいたします is the formal version of よろしくお願いします and one of the most important phrases in Japanese business life. It is used as a closing phrase in emails, in first introductions, after requests and in almost all business communication. いたします (kenjōgo of します) makes the phrase especially respectful.
en.formation: よろしくお願いいたします (fixed formula) / 何卒よろしくお願いいたします (even more formal)
en.notes: Almost every business email in Japan ends with a variation of よろしくお願いいたします. With 何卒 (nanitozo) in front, the request becomes more urgent and more formal. This phrase has no direct English equivalent.
examples[].german: I ask for your continued kind support.
I sincerely ask you to kindly deal with this matter.
I ask for your continued valued cooperation.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is お願いします.
いたすます is not a polite verb form.
This negates the request.

en.explanation: 頂戴する (ちょうだいする) is a formal kenjōgo form of もらう (to get/receive). It expresses humbly that you receive something from a person of higher status. Compared with いただく, 頂戴する sounds somewhat more formal still and is often used in business and in the restaurant industry.
en.formation: 頂戴する (fixed verb, conjugated like する) / 頂戴いたす (even more polite)
en.notes: 頂戴 is also used as a standalone word without する in children's language (ちょうだい = please give me). In business, お名刺を頂戴できますか is a standard formula when exchanging business cards.
examples[].german: Might I have your business card?
Thank you for giving me your time.
I am contacting you because I would like to hear your opinion.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
The polite past ends in ました.
The polite negative is not formed with ないました.

en.explanation: 愚見 and 拙見 are kenjōgo nouns with which you modestly call your own opinion a "foolish view" or "clumsy view". These forms of self-deprecation are typical of polite Japanese communication and appear in formal discussions and writing.
en.formation: 愚見 / 拙見 + ですが / ではございますが / を述べさせていただきます
en.notes: Similar self-deprecating forms: 拙著 (my humble book), 拙作 (my humble work), 愚息 (my foolish son = my son), 愚妻 (my foolish wife = my wife). Some of these forms are now outdated, but 愚見 and 拙見 are still used.
examples[].german: This is only my humble opinion, but I think this proposal is the best option.
Allow me to state my humble view.
In my humble opinion, there seems to be room for reconsideration.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: な does not fit before ではございますが here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 愚見.
を does not fit before ではございますが here.

en.explanation: 拝聴する is the kenjōgo form of 聞く (to hear/listen). The kanji 拝 expresses humility. You use this form to say humbly that you are listening to a speech, a lecture or the words of a respected person.
en.formation: 拝聴する (fixed verb, conjugated like する) ／ 拝聴いたす (even more polite)
en.notes: 拝聴する belongs to the group of 拝～する kenjōgo verbs alongside 拝見する、拝借する、拝読する. They all use the kanji 拝 (to bow) and express the utmost humility.
examples[].german: I humbly listened to the professor's lecture.
It is an honor to have heard your valuable words.
I would humbly like to hear your opinion.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the listening.
The polite past needs the stem いたし.
The polite endings cannot be doubled.

en.explanation: 拝読する (はいどくする) is the kenjōgo form of 読む (to read). It is used to say humbly that you have read something written or sent by a respected person. The kanji 拝 signals humility.
en.formation: 拝読する (fixed verb, conjugated like する)
en.notes: 拝読する belongs to the group of 拝～する kenjōgo verbs (拝見する、拝借する、拝読する). They all express that you carry out the action humbly toward a person of higher status.
examples[].german: I have read your book (humble).
I have read your email. I will consider your proposal.
I read the report and learned a great deal from it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the reading.
ます needs the stem いたし.
The polite endings cannot be doubled.

en.explanation: 拝受する is a very formal kenjōgo form of 受け取る (to receive). It is used mainly in written business communication to humbly confirm receipt of documents, shipments or messages.
en.formation: 拝受する / 拝受いたしました (acknowledgment of receipt)
en.notes: 拝受する is used almost exclusively in business emails and letters. It sounds more formal than いただきました and is the usual form for acknowledging receipt in Japanese business correspondence.
examples[].german: I have humbly received the materials.
I have received the documents you sent.
I have received the quote and will review it internally.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the receipt.
The polite past needs the stem いたし.
The polite endings cannot be doubled.

en.meaning: humble form of 見る (to see/look at)
en.explanation: 拝見する is the humble (謙譲語) form of 見る (to see). The kanji 拝 means "to bow" and therefore expresses special deference. It is used when looking at something that belongs to a higher-ranking person.
en.formation: 拝見 + する (ます-form: 拝見します / 拝見いたします)
en.notes: 拝見する is often raised further with いたす to 拝見いたす. Similar expressions with 拝: 拝読する (to read, humble), 拝借する (to borrow, humble), 拝聴する (to listen, humble).
examples[].german: May I have a look at your business card?
I have looked through the documents.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: もよろしい requires the て-form before it.
The ます-form does not fit before も.
The dictionary form does not fit before もよろしい.

en.explanation: 拝借する (はいしゃくする) is the kenjōgo form of 借りる (to borrow). The kanji 拝 expresses humility and reverence. You use this form when you yourself borrow something from a person of higher status, lowering your own action and thereby showing respect indirectly.
en.formation: 拝借する (fixed verb, conjugated like する)
en.notes: 拝借する is used not only for physical objects but also abstractly (e.g. お時間を拝借する = to be allowed to take up someone's time). With いたします at the end it becomes even more polite.
examples[].german: Might I use your restroom?
Could I borrow a little of your time?
I will humbly borrow these documents.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The て-form comes before もよろしい.
The て-form comes before もよろしい.
The finite polite form does not fit before もよろしい.

en.meaning: to bring; to serve (humble, restaurant service)
en.explanation: お持ちする is the kenjōgo form of 持っていく / 持ってくる: you bring something to the guest and present your own action humbly. お持ちいたします is one step more formal still. In restaurants and hotels, both forms are standard. 配膳する ("serving food"), on the other hand, is not keigo but a neutral technical term; it only becomes polite as 配膳させていただきます.
en.formation: お + verb (ます-stem of 持つ) + する / いたす ／ お持ちしてもよろしいでしょうか
en.notes: Japanese restaurants use keigo throughout. Standard phrases such as お持ちいたします, ご注文はお決まりでしょうか and お皿をお下げしてもよろしいでしょうか are part of the basic vocabulary of service staff.
examples[].german: Here is your meal. (waiter's language)
May I bring you dessert?
I will bring your drinks. Please wait a moment.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the bringing.
The polite past needs the stem いたし.
The polite endings cannot be doubled.

en.explanation: 弊社 is the humble term for your own company. The kanji 弊 means "abuse/disadvantage" and expresses self-deprecation. This form is indispensable in business correspondence and is the opposite of 御社/貴社 (your company, respectful).
en.formation: 弊社 (spoken/written) ／ 弊店 (our shop) ／ 弊局 (our office) ／ 弊誌 (our magazine)
en.notes: In spoken business Japanese, 当社 (tōsha = our company) is also used, which sounds less humble but more neutral. 弊社 is the standard kenjōgo form in written communication. In emails to customers, 弊社 is almost always used.
examples[].german: Thank you for your interest in our company's products.
At our company, we are thorough about quality control.
The person in charge at our company will contact you again.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This refers to the other person's company instead of your own.
This refers to the other person's company instead of your own.
な does not fit before の製品 here.

en.meaning: humble form of もらう / 食べる / 飲む
en.explanation: いただく is the humble (謙譲語) form of もらう (to receive) as well as of 食べる (to eat) and 飲む (to drink). It expresses gratitude and humility when receiving or consuming something.
en.formation: Directly replaces もらう / 食べる / 飲む (ます-form: いただきます)
en.notes: いただきます before a meal is one of the best-known Japanese expressions. ～ていただく is an important construction for expressing humbly that someone does something for you.
examples[].german: Thank you for the food (said before eating). (lit.: I humbly receive.)
I received this book from the teacher.
Could I have some tea?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is いただきます.
This negates receiving instead of starting the meal.
This is not a polite verb form.

en.meaning: humble form of する (to do)
en.explanation: いたす is the humble (謙譲語) form of する (to do). It is used to express one's own actions humbly toward a higher-ranking person.
en.formation: Directly replaces する (ます-form: いたします)
en.notes: いたす is also used as 丁重語 (courteous language) without specific reference to a higher-ranking person, e.g. in public announcements or formal notices. 失礼いたします is one of the most common business phrases.
examples[].german: I will do it.
I will check.
Excuse me (for disturbing you). / Goodbye.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is いたします.
This negates doing it.
This is not a polite verb form.

en.explanation: かしこまりました is the most polite way to say "understood" or "certainly". It is used in customer service, hotels, restaurants and formal business situations. It is considerably more formal than 分かりました and shows that you respectfully accept the instruction or request.
en.formation: かしこまりました (fixed form, past form of かしこまる)
en.notes: The politeness levels for "understood" are: 分かった → 分かりました → 承知しました → かしこまりました. かしこまりました is the highest level and is used almost exclusively by service staff toward customers.
examples[].german: Certainly. I will bring it right away.
Understood. I will take care of the change.
A reservation for 2 p.m., correct? Certainly.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite past is かしこまりました.
This is not a verb form.
This refuses the request instead of accepting it.

en.meaning: humble form of 行く / 来る (to go / to come)
en.explanation: 参る is the special humble (謙譲語) form of 行く (to go) and 来る (to come). It is used to express one's own movement humbly toward a higher-ranking person.
en.formation: Directly replaces 行く / 来る (ます-form: 参ります)
en.notes: 参る is also used colloquially to mean "to give up" or "to be worn out" (参った！= I give up!). In a keigo context it is exclusively the humble form of 行く/来る.
examples[].german: I'll be right there.
I will come to your company tomorrow.
I came by taxi.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is 参ります.
This negates coming.
This reports the past instead of coming right away.

en.meaning: on the occasion of ... / when the opportunity arises ...
en.explanation: ～の折には is a formal expression meaning "on the occasion of" or "when the opportunity arises." 折 (おり) means "occasion/moment" and is used in elevated language instead of 時 (とき). This form appears in formal invitations and polite letters.
en.formation: Noun + の折には / ～した折には / お近くにお越しの折には
en.notes: 折 is preferred in formal correspondence and sounds more elegant than 時 or 場合. The phrase お近くにお越しの折には is a classic courtesy formula at the end of business letters and New Year's cards.
examples[].german: If you are ever in the area, please do drop by.
If you are ever in Tokyo, I would be glad to hear from you.
I look forward to our next opportunity to meet.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a time connection here.
な cannot be attached here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 折.

en.meaning: very humble form of 言う (to say/tell)
en.explanation: 申し上げる is the most formal humble form of 言う. It is used when telling something directly to a higher-ranking person and expresses the greatest humility.
en.formation: Directly replaces 言う (ます-form: 申し上げます)
en.notes: 申し上げる is more formal than 申す and is used especially in business letters, emails and formal speeches. Common set expressions: お礼を申し上げる, お詫び申し上げる, お願い申し上げる.
examples[].german: There is one thing I would like to tell you.
I would like to express my thanks.
I sincerely apologize.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: たい modifies こと without な.
たい follows the verb stem.
This negates the wish to tell.

en.meaning: humble form of 言う (to say)
en.explanation: 申す is the humble (謙譲語) form of 言う (to say). It is used to express humbly that you yourself are saying something, especially in self-introductions and general statements.
en.formation: Directly replaces 言う (ます-form: 申します)
en.notes: 申す is less formal than 申し上げる. In self-introductions on the phone or in business, ～と申します is the standard form. 申す can also be used as 丁重語 (courteous language) without specific reference to a higher-ranking person.
examples[].german: My name is Tanaka.
May I say a word?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is 申します.
This negates giving the name.
This is not a polite verb form.

en.meaning: to call (humble); to make a phone call (humble)
en.explanation: お電話を差し上げる is the kenjōgo form of 電話をかける (to call). 差し上げる (さしあげる) is the humble form of あげる (to give) and expresses that you "offer" the act of calling to a person of higher status. This form is used in business communication.
en.formation: お電話を差し上げる / お電話いたす (alternative)
en.notes: Recently there has been debate about whether お電話を差し上げる is appropriate, since 差し上げる (to give) implies that the call is a gift. Some consider the alternative お電話いたします more neutral. Both forms are nevertheless accepted in business.
examples[].german: I will call you later.
Might I call you tomorrow morning?
I will call you back, so please wait a moment.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the announced call.
ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.explanation: お目にかかる is the kenjōgo form of 会う (to meet). Literally it means something like "to come before the eyes (of a respected person)". You use this form to express your own act of meeting humbly and thereby show respect to the other person.
en.formation: お目にかかる (fixed expression, conjugated as a godan verb)
en.notes: お目にかかる is more formal than お会いする and is used especially at first meetings or in very polite contexts. The phrase お目にかかれて光栄です is a classic greeting formula.
examples[].german: It is an honor to meet you.
I look forward to the day we meet again.
We have met once before, at a party.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The finite past does not connect with 光栄です here.
ます needs the stem かかり.
The finite polite form does not connect with 光栄です here.

en.explanation: お目にかける is the kenjōgo form of 見せる (to show). Literally it means "to offer to the eyes (of a respected person)". You use this form when you humbly show or present something to a person of higher status.
en.formation: お目にかける (fixed expression, conjugated as an ichidan verb)
en.notes: お目にかける is the counterpart of お目にかかる (to meet). かける = to offer, かかる = to meet. These two forms are often confused, so it is important to know the difference.
examples[].german: I would like to show you the new design.
It is an embarrassing piece of work, but let me show it to you.
I believe I will be able to show you the finished product soon.
