examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The plain verb form comes before こと.
The て-form cannot modify こと attributively here.
ます is not attached to かける.

en.explanation: 御礼申し上げる is one of the most formal expressions of thanks in Japanese. It combines 御礼 (thanks, respectful) with 申し上げる (to say, humble). This form is used in official acknowledgments, business letters and on ceremonial occasions.
en.formation: 御礼 / お礼 + 申し上げます ／ 厚く御礼申し上げます (intensified)
en.notes: 厚く (warmly/sincerely) and 心より (from the heart) are common intensifiers. 略儀ながら (although it is only an informal way) is used when apologizing for thanking in writing rather than in person.
examples[].german: I thank you most sincerely. (very formal)
I thank everyone who gave us their cooperation from the bottom of my heart.
For now, though it is only in writing, I would like to express my thanks.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the thanks.
ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.meaning: humble form of いる (to be, to be present)
en.explanation: おる is the humble (謙譲語) form of いる (to be, to be present). It is used to talk humbly about your own whereabouts or state.
en.formation: Directly replaces いる (ます-form: おります) ／ ～ております (humble progressive form)
en.notes: ～ております is the humble form of ～ています and is used very frequently in business. On the phone, your own side is always described with おる, the other side with いらっしゃる.
examples[].german: Tanaka is out of the office at the moment.
I live in Tokyo.
We have been expecting you.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is おります.
This reports the past instead of current absence.
This negates being out.

en.meaning: to look up (humble) / to search for (humble)
en.explanation: お調べする and お探しする are the humble (kenjōgo) forms of 調べる (to look up/to investigate) and 探す (to search for). They follow the standard humble pattern お + verb stem + する and are often used in customer service when you look something up for a customer.
en.formation: お調べする / お調べいたす ／ お探しする / お探しいたす
en.notes: These forms are standard vocabulary in retail and customer service. They follow the universal お～する/お～いたす pattern, which can be applied to practically any verb (with exceptions such as the special keigo verbs).
examples[].german: I'll look into it for you right now, so please wait a moment.
I'll check the stock for you.
Shall I look for the item you would like?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the announced checking.
ます requires the stem いたし.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.explanation: お～する, or the even humbler form お～いたす, is the standard humble (謙譲語) verb form. It is used to lower one's own actions in relation to a higher-ranking person.
en.formation: お + Verb (ます-stem) + する / いたす ／ ご + Sino-Japanese noun + する / いたす
en.notes: お～いたす is humbler than お～する. With Sino-Japanese words, ご is used instead of お (e.g. ご説明する). Used only for your own actions that affect another person.
examples[].german: I'll carry your luggage for you.
I will contact you later.
Let me show you the way.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: お～する needs the verb stem 持ち.
This negates the carrying.
The polite ending is します.

en.meaning: to humbly go; to call on (someone)
en.explanation: 参上する is a very formal kenjōgo form of 行く (to go) / 訪ねる (to visit) that expresses that you respectfully go to a person of higher status. It sounds more formal than 参る and is used in elevated business language and on official occasions.
en.formation: 参上する (fixed verb, conjugated like する) ／ 参上いたす (even more polite)
en.notes: 参上する is more formal than 参る and 伺う. In modern business language 伺う is used more often, but 参上する is found in official letters of invitation and on traditional occasions.
examples[].german: I will call at your company tomorrow.
I have just arrived.
I have come in response to your kind invitation.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the announced visit.
ます needs the stem いたし.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.meaning: humble form of あげる (to give)
en.explanation: 差し上げる is the humble (謙譲語) form of あげる (to give). It is used to express humbly that you give something to a higher-ranking person.
en.formation: Directly replaces あげる (ます-form: 差し上げます)
en.notes: 差し上げる can seem excessive when used in everyday situations. ～て差し上げる (doing something for someone) can sound condescending and should be used with care.
examples[].german: I presented the teacher with flowers.
May I offer you something?
I would like to give you a souvenir.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This is not a polite past.
This negates the presenting.
This is not a past form.

en.meaning: my humble book; my humble manuscript
en.explanation: 拙著 and 拙稿 are kenjōgo nouns for your own literary or academic works. The kanji 拙 means "clumsy/awkward" and is a form of self-deprecation. You use these forms when mentioning your own work in conversation with others.
en.formation: 拙著 (my book) ／ 拙稿 (my manuscript) ／ 拙作 (my work) ／ 拙論 (my paper)
en.notes: These forms are used especially in academic and literary circles. In contrast, for other people's works you use respectful forms such as ご著書 (your book), ご高著 (your great book), 大著 (your extensive work).
examples[].german: Thank you for reading my humble book.
I would be grateful if you would look over my humble manuscript.
It is only my humble paper, but I hope it can serve as a reference.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: な does not fit before をお読み here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 拙著.
The following を would be doubled, which is not allowed.

en.explanation: 奉る is a classical (文語) kenjōgo form expressing that you humbly offer or dedicate something to a person of the very highest status. In modern language it is found in religious contexts, ceremonial acts and fixed expressions such as 謹んで申し上げ奉ります.
en.formation: 奉る (godan verb) ／ Verb (連用形) + 奉る (classical)
en.notes: 奉る is archaic in modern everyday language, but alive in certain contexts: Shintō ceremonies (奉納 = ritual offering), New Year's greetings and imperial occasions. The form 謹んで～奉る is the most polite in the entire Japanese keigo system.
examples[].german: I offer a prayer to the gods.
I respectfully present this item to His Majesty.
I most respectfully extend my New Year's greetings.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the offering.
ます needs the verb stem.
The polite past needs the verb stem.

en.explanation: 謹んで is an adverb that expresses the highest respect and humility. It is used before formal acts such as apologies, congratulations and condolences and strengthens the humility of the statement that follows. It is indispensable in formal correspondence.
en.formation: 謹んで + verb (申し上げます / お詫び申し上げます / お祝い申し上げます)
en.notes: 謹んで is found on New Year's cards (年賀状), in letters of condolence and in formal business letters. 謹賀新年 (Happy New Year, respectful) on New Year's cards contains the same kanji 謹.
examples[].german: I offer my most humble apologies.
I respectfully extend my New Year's greetings.
Please accept my deepest condolences.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The attributive past does not form an adverbial connection here.
The finite form does not form a connection here.
The て-form of 謹む is 謹んで.

en.meaning: humble form of 行く / 聞く / 訪ねる
en.explanation: 伺う is the humble (謙譲語) form of 行く (to go), 聞く (to ask, to hear) and 訪ねる (to visit). It is used to express humbly that you visit someone, ask something or hear about something.
en.formation: Directly replaces 行く / 聞く / 訪ねる (ます-form: 伺います)
en.notes: 伺う is one of the most versatile keigo verbs, since it can replace three different verbs. お伺いする is a double honorific form that is frequently used in practice.
examples[].german: May I visit you tomorrow?
There's one thing I'd like to ask.
I have already heard about it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The て-form is needed before もよろしい here.
The ます-form does not fit before もよろしい.
The dictionary form does not fit before もよろしい.

en.meaning: to receive; to hear; to accept (humble)
en.explanation: 承る (うけたまわる) is a very formal kenjōgo form that serves as the humble version of 聞く (to hear), 受ける (to receive) and 引き受ける (to take on). It is often used in customer service and in formal business situations to express that you are taking an order, a request or information.
en.formation: 承る (fixed verb, conjugated as a godan verb)
en.notes: 承る is one of the most formal kenjōgo verbs and is used especially in the service industry. It sounds more professional than お聞きする or お受けする.
examples[].german: I have taken your order.
I will take your reservation. May I have your name, please?
May I ask what this is regarding?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates taking the order.
The polite past needs the stem 承り.
The polite endings cannot be doubled.

en.meaning: humble form of 知っている (to know someone)
en.explanation: 存じ上げる is the humbler form of 存じる and is mainly used to express humbly that you know a person. It is more respectful than 存じる.
en.formation: Directly replaces 知っている (for people) (ます-form: 存じ上げております)
en.notes: 存じ上げる is mainly used for people, while 存じる tends to be used for things and facts. The negative 存じ上げません is a polite way of saying that you don't know someone.
examples[].german: I know Professor Yamada.
I have known your name for a long time.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This denies knowing the person.
おります needs the て-connection.
The polite past ends in ました.

en.meaning: humble form of 知る / 思う (to know / to think)
en.explanation: 存じる is the humble (謙譲語) form of 知る (to know) and 思う (to think, to believe). It is used to express humbly that you know something or hold an opinion.
en.formation: Directly replaces 知る / 思う (ます-form: 存じます / 存じております)
en.notes: 存じる refers to things and facts. For people, 存じ上げる is used. 存じております is the usual business form for "I know".
examples[].german: I am aware of that matter.
I think so too.
I don't know. (humble)
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is おります.
This negates the knowing.
存じる forms the て-form 存じて.

en.explanation: 贈呈する is a very formal form of あげる (to give) or プレゼントする (to give as a present) used for official presentations. It expresses that you solemnly and respectfully present something to a person, e.g. an award, a gift or a certificate.
en.formation: 贈呈する (fixed verb) ／ ～を贈呈いたします
en.notes: 贈呈する is used at ceremonies, award presentations and official occasions. Unlike 差し上げる, which is common in everyday business life, 贈呈する has a ceremonial character.
examples[].german: We will now present a commemorative gift.
We will now present the trophy to the winner.
Allow me to present you with a bouquet of flowers.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the announced presentation.
ます needs the stem いたし.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.explanation: お～遊ばす is an extremely elevated sonkeigo form that is historically associated with the speech of aristocratic women (女性語). It is used to describe the actions of a very high-ranking person with the greatest respect. In modern language it is rare and considered archaic.
en.formation: お + verb (ます-stem) + 遊ばす ／ ～遊ばせ (imperative)
en.notes: お～遊ばす was in use in refined women's speech until the postwar period. Today you hardly ever hear it, except in historical dramas or very traditional contexts. Knowing this form is useful for understanding classical Japanese literature.
examples[].german: Madam has gone out.
Please take all the time you need. (very elevated)
What are you reading? (highest respect)
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the going out.
The polite past needs the stem 遊ばし.
The polite endings cannot be doubled.

en.meaning: correct use of phrases that acknowledge someone's effort
en.explanation: お疲れ様です and ご苦労様です both mean "thank you for your hard work," but they follow different usage rules. お疲れ様です can be used toward anyone (including superiors), whereas ご苦労様です is only appropriate toward subordinates or equals. This distinction is a common keigo pitfall.
en.formation: お疲れ様です (universal) ／ ご苦労様です (only toward people below you or equals)
en.notes: The rule that ご苦労様です should not be used toward superiors is less strict among younger Japanese people, but it is still observed in the business world. When in doubt, お疲れ様です is always the safe choice. Some companies no longer use ご苦労様 internally at all.
examples[].german: Thank you for your hard work, sir/ma'am. I've brought the report. (to the department head)
Thanks for your hard work. (said to a delivery person)
Thank you for your hard work today as well.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます cannot be attached directly to 様.
る cannot be attached to the copula です.
No な comes before the copula です here.

en.meaning: to read; to look at (very respectful)
en.explanation: ご高覧 is a very formal sonkeigo form of 見る (to see/read) used in business letters and formal invitations. 高覧 literally means "high gaze" and expresses the highest respect toward the reader or viewer.
en.formation: ご高覧 + ください / いただく / 賜る
en.notes: ご高覧 is used almost exclusively in very formal written communication. Similar elevated sonkeigo nouns are ご高配 (gracious consideration), ご厚意 (kind intention), ご高説 (learned opinion).
examples[].german: I would be grateful if you would kindly take a look at it.
I respectfully ask that you read this book.
Please take a look at the project proposal. (very formal)
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This particle combination does not fit before いただければ.
な does not fit before いただければ here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 高覧.

en.meaning: respectful form of 見る (to see/look)
en.explanation: ご覧になる is the special respectful form of 見る (to see). It is used to describe respectfully that a higher-ranking person looks at or reads something.
en.formation: ご覧 + になる (ます-form: ご覧になります)
en.notes: ご覧ください is the shortened and very common polite form for "please look". You often see it in museums, in presentations and in business emails.
examples[].german: Have you looked at these documents?
Please take a look.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The honorific expression uses に.
This is not a polite past.
This is not a verb form.

en.meaning: to be so kind as to do something (Sino-Japanese)
en.explanation: ご + Sino-Japanese noun + くださる is the respectful form expressing that a person of higher status is so kind as to carry out an action for the speaker. It is the Sino-Japanese counterpart of お～くださる and is used in formal business and written contexts.
en.formation: ご + Sino-Japanese noun + くださる / くださいますよう
en.notes: ご指導ご鞭撻を賜りますよう is one of the most formal request formulas in Japanese and is often found in official welcoming speeches and New Year's greetings. ご鞭撻 (gobentatsu) literally means "urging on with the whip" and figuratively stands for encouragement.
examples[].german: I respectfully ask for your understanding.
Thank you very much for your kind cooperation.
I respectfully ask for your guidance and encouragement.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます needs the stem ください.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite past ends in ました.

en.meaning: to use; to make use of (respectful)
en.explanation: ご利用になる is the sonkeigo form of 利用する (to use). Because 利用 is a Sino-Japanese word, the prefix ご is used instead of お. You come across this form very often in public announcements, shops and service businesses.
en.formation: ご利用になる / ご利用ください (as a request)
en.notes: You hear ご利用ください all the time on trains, at airports and in shops. It is one of the most frequent sonkeigo forms in everyday Japanese life.
examples[].german: Would you like to use the elevator?
Thank you for using our service.
Please feel free to use it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The honorific expression uses に.
This is not a polite form.
This is not a verb form.

en.meaning: respectful form of 知っている (to know)
en.explanation: ご存じ is the respectful form of 知っている (to know). It is used as a noun or na-adjective to ask or say respectfully whether a higher-ranking person knows something.
en.formation: ご存じ + です / ですか (negative: ご存じない / ご存じありません)
en.notes: Strictly speaking, ご存じ is a noun, but it is used like a stative verb. The spelling ご存知 (with 知) also exists, but ご存じ is the standard spelling.
examples[].german: Do you know this word?
As you know, new rules take effect from next month.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 存じ, as a nominal honorific form, does not take ます before です here.
No な comes before です here.
を cannot stand before です here.

en.meaning: respectful form of いる / ある / 行く / 来る
en.explanation: いらっしゃる is the special respectful form of the verbs いる (to be, to be present), 行く (to go) and 来る (to come). It is used to talk about where a respected person is or about their coming and going.
en.formation: Directly replaces いる / ある / 行く / 来る (ます-form: いらっしゃいます)
en.notes: One of the most important keigo verbs. The imperative form いらっしゃいませ is used as a greeting in shops. The ます-form is いらっしゃいます (not いらっしゃります).
examples[].german: Is Tanaka-sensei in?
Will you be coming to the party tomorrow?
The customer/guest has arrived.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is いらっしゃいます.
This is not a verb form.
This asks about past rather than current presence.

en.meaning: respectful form of くれる (to give, to me/us)
en.explanation: くださる is the respectful form of くれる and expresses that a higher-ranking person gives something to the speaker or the speaker's group, or does something for them. It emphasizes the recipient's gratitude.
en.formation: Directly replaces くれる (ます-form: くださいます)
en.notes: The imperative form ください (please give / please do) is the most frequently used form of this verb. The ます-form is くださいます (not くださります).
examples[].german: The teacher gave me a dictionary.
The department manager gave me some advice.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite past is くださいました.
This negates the gift.
This is not a polite past form.

en.meaning: respectful form of 食べる / 飲む (to eat / to drink)
en.explanation: 召し上がる is the special respectful form of 食べる (to eat) and 飲む (to drink). It is used to talk respectfully about a higher-ranking person eating or drinking.
en.formation: Directly replaces 食べる / 飲む (ます-form: 召し上がります)
en.notes: Very polite and respectful. In less formal situations お食べになる can also be used, but 召し上がる is the preferred form in business contexts.
examples[].german: Please help yourself. / Please eat/drink.
Would you like some coffee?
The company president has already had lunch.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ください requires the て-form.
The ます-form does not fit before ください.
This asks the person not to eat.

en.meaning: to eat; to drink; to wear; to call (classical respect)
en.explanation: 召す is a versatile classical sonkeigo verb that serves as the respectful form of 食べる (to eat), 飲む (to drink), 着る (to put on), 呼ぶ (to call) and 乗る (to ride). In modern language it is found mainly in fixed expressions such as お召し物 (clothing, respectful).
en.formation: 召す (godan verb, ます-form: 召します)
en.notes: お召し物 (clothing, respectful) and お風邪を召す (to catch a cold, respectful) are the most common modern uses. 召し上がる (to eat/drink, respectful) is derived from 召す.
examples[].german: Have you caught a cold? (very polite)
Let me take your coat.
Will you be taking the car? (very polite)
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: いらっしゃる needs the て-connection here.
いらっしゃる needs the て-connection here.
The finite form does not fit before いらっしゃる here.

en.meaning: respectful form of する (to do)
en.explanation: なさる is the special respectful form of する (to do). It is used to talk respectfully about the actions of a higher-ranking person.
en.formation: Directly replaces する (ます-form: なさいます) ／ お + Noun + なさる
en.notes: The imperative form なさい is also used for instructions to children or subordinates (e.g. 早くしなさい). The ます-form is なさいます (not なさります).
examples[].german: What would you like to do?
The professor is doing research.
Please do as you like.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is なさいます.
This is not a verb form.
This is not a polite verb form.

en.explanation: 二重敬語 refers to the use of two keigo forms in a single verb construction. Although this is considered a grammatical error, some double keigo forms have become established in modern Japanese and are generally accepted, such as お召し上がりになる or お見えになる.
en.formation: お + special sonkeigo verb + になる (e.g. お召し上がりになる) ／ special sonkeigo verb + れる/られる
en.notes: The Japanese Council for Cultural Affairs (文化審議会) has classified some 二重敬語 forms as acceptable, including お召し上がりになる and お見えになる. Others, such as おっしゃられる, are considered errors but are widespread. For N1, recognizing and correctly assessing 二重敬語 is important.
examples[].german: Please go ahead and eat/drink. (double keigo, but accepted)
The teacher said so. (double keigo, often heard, but strictly speaking incorrect)
Have you seen it? (double keigo, widespread)

en.explanation: ご高配 is a very formal sonkeigo noun that expresses the kind consideration or support of a person or organization of higher status. It is used in formal business letters, official notices and ceremonial greeting formulas.
en.formation: ご高配 + を賜り / いただき + ありがとうございます ／ ご高配 + のほど + よろしくお願い申し上げます
en.notes: 平素より格別のご高配を賜り is one of the most standard opening formulas in formal Japanese business letters. It is more formal than お世話になっております and is used especially in official documents and corporate communication.
examples[].german: We sincerely thank you for your continued special patronage.
We ask for your continued kind support.
Thanks to everyone's kind support, it was completed successfully.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: な does not fit before を賜り here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 高配.
The following を would be doubled, which is not allowed.

en.meaning: to go; to come; to be (respectful)
en.explanation: おいでになる is a versatile sonkeigo form that serves as the respectful version of 行く (to go), 来る (to come) and いる (to be). Which meaning is intended becomes clear from the context. This form is used especially in refined conversation.
en.formation: おいでになる (fixed expression, conjugated as a godan verb)
en.notes: Depending on context, おいでになる can replace three different verbs (行く、来る、いる). It sounds somewhat softer and less formal than いらっしゃる, but is still considered full-fledged sonkeigo.
examples[].german: Will you be coming to tomorrow's meeting?
The company president is currently in Tokyo.
Where are you going?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます needs the stem なり.
The polite past ends in ました.
ない does not take ます attached to it.

en.explanation: ～なさいませ is the most polite imperative form and is used in high-end customer service. It combines なさる (sonkeigo of する) with the polite imperative ending ませ. This form is often found in department stores, hotels and traditional Japanese businesses.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + なさいませ ／ お + verb stem + なさいませ
en.notes: いらっしゃいませ is actually the ませ-form of いらっしゃる and the best-known use of this pattern. In department stores you regularly hear forms such as お選びなさいませ or お試しなさいませ.
examples[].german: Welcome. Please come in.
Please take all the time you need.
Please take care. (very polite)
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ませ is not attached to the dictionary form.
る cannot be attached to ませ.
The request is not attached to the past form.

en.explanation: お越しになる is an elegant sonkeigo form of 来る (to come). It is used to describe respectfully that a person of higher status is coming or visiting a place. This form is especially common in business language and in formal invitations.
en.formation: お越しになる (fixed expression) / お越しください (as a request)
en.notes: お越しください is used very often in event invitations and business emails. The combination お越しいただく is an especially polite hybrid of sonkeigo and kenjōgo.
examples[].german: What time did the teacher come?
Please do come and visit our company.
We have prepared parking for guests who have come from far away.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite past is なりました.
The plain past of なる is なった.
The polite negative is not formed with ないました.

en.explanation: お～ください is the basic polite request form in Japanese. You put お in front of the verb stem (ます-form without ます) and add ください. This form is used to ask someone respectfully for something. It is one of the first keigo forms learners should get to know.
en.formation: お + verb stem (ます-form without ます) + ください
en.notes: This is one of the most frequently used keigo forms in everyday life. With Sino-Japanese words, the prefix ご is used instead of お (e.g. ご連絡ください).
examples[].german: Please have a seat here.
Please wait a moment.
Please take care on your way home.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The request uses the stem 座り.
This is not a correct request.
This reports the past instead of asking the person to sit.

en.meaning: respectful request form / thanks for an action
en.explanation: お～くださる is used to express respectfully that a higher-ranking person does something for the speaker, or to make a polite request. It combines the respectful prefix お with くださる.
en.formation: お + Verb (ます-stem) + くださる ／ お + Verb (ます-stem) + ください
en.notes: お～ください is the most common form in everyday language. お～くださいませ sounds even more polite and is used in the service industry. With Sino-Japanese words, ご is used instead of お (e.g. ご確認ください).
examples[].german: Please wait. (very polite)
The teacher kindly taught me.
Thank you very much for getting in touch.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The honorific request requires the verb stem.
ませ requires the polite stem form before it.
This is not a request form.

en.explanation: お見えになる is an especially polite sonkeigo form used when a respected person appears or arrives. It is the respectful counterpart of 来る (to come) or 現れる (to appear) and is often used in business, especially when customers or important guests arrive.
en.formation: お見えになる (fixed expression, conjugated like a godan verb)
en.notes: お見えになる is used especially often at reception desks and in the hotel industry. It sounds more formal than いらっしゃる.
examples[].german: Department Manager Yamada has arrived.
When the customer arrives, please show them in right away.
The teacher has not arrived yet.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite past is formed with なりました.
The plain past of なる is なった.
This negates the arrival.

en.explanation: お求めになる is the sonkeigo form of 買う (to buy). It is used to talk respectfully about a purchase made by a customer or a person of higher status. This form is especially common in retail, department stores and customer service.
en.formation: お求めになる (お + 求め + になる)
en.notes: In department stores and upscale shops, お求めになる is used as standard instead of 買う. The shorter form お求めください is often used in advertising materials.
examples[].german: Where did you purchase this product?
We offer it at a price that makes it easy to buy.
You can also purchase this product online.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite past is なりました.
The plain past of なる is なった.
ない does not take ます attached to it.

en.explanation: お～になる is the standard respectful (尊敬語) verb form, used to describe the actions of a person higher in the hierarchy. It expresses respect toward the person performing the action.
en.formation: お + Verb (ます-stem) + になる
en.notes: Cannot be used with verbs that already have their own respectful form (e.g. いらっしゃる instead of お行きになる). Used only for other people's actions, never for your own.
examples[].german: The teacher has already gone home.
Did the company president read this book?
Please have a seat.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The honorific construction uses に.
This negates going home.
お～になる uses the verb stem.

en.explanation: 仰せになる is the highest sonkeigo form of 言う (to say) and expresses that a high-ranking person says or orders something. Today this form is used mainly in literary texts, historical contexts and very formal ceremonial situations.
en.formation: 仰せになる (fixed expression) ／ 仰せの通り (as you command)
en.notes: 仰せ on its own is also used as a noun (= instruction/command). The form 仰せつける means "to command/to order". In modern language おっしゃる is the usual sonkeigo form of 言う; 仰せになる is more archaic and ceremonial.
examples[].german: Please proceed exactly as the chairman has instructed.
I will do exactly as you say.
Please command me in whatever you wish.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The stem form does not modify とおり attributively here.
The polite past needs the stem なり.
No additional な comes before とおり here.

en.meaning: respectful form of 言う (to say)
en.explanation: おっしゃる is the special respectful form of 言う (to say). It is used when describing what a person higher in the hierarchy has said.
en.formation: Directly replaces 言う (ます-form: おっしゃいます)
en.notes: The past form is おっしゃった (not おっしゃいった). The ます-form is おっしゃいます. Frequently used in business situations.
examples[].german: I will do as the teacher said.
What did the department manager say?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The plain form is needed before とおり here; besides, the polite form is おっしゃいました.
This is not a past form.
This denies that the teacher said it.

en.meaning: please look at it indulgently (humble request)
en.explanation: ご笑覧 is an extremely polite form used to ask someone to look at your own work. 笑覧 literally means "to look at with a smile" and implies a request for indulgent consideration of your own (modestly presented) work. It is used in art, literature and formal invitations.
en.formation: ご笑覧 + ください / いただければ幸いです
en.notes: ご笑覧 is often used together with 拙作 (my humble work) or 拙著 (my humble book). It shows the typically Japanese modesty of downplaying your own work while elevating the viewer.
examples[].german: It is a humble piece of work, but I would be grateful if you would take a look at it.
Please be so kind as to take a look at my new work.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: な does not fit before いただければ here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 笑覧.
This particle combination does not fit before いただければ.

en.explanation: ～給う is a classical (文語) sonkeigo form that appears frequently in premodern Japanese literature. In modern language it occasionally turns up in literary texts, religious contexts and set expressions. It expresses the highest respect toward the person performing the action.
en.formation: Verb (連用形) + 給う ／ ～たまえ (imperative; today: a collegial request)
en.notes: In modern colloquial language, ～たまえ is sometimes used as a slightly condescending but comradely request among equals (especially by older men). Religious use in prayers is the most living use of the classical form.
examples[].german: Heaven helps those who help themselves.
Now, just listen. (slightly elevated, collegial tone)
O God, protect us.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
ない does not take ます attached to it.
This negates Heaven's help.

en.meaning: passive form as a respectful expression
en.explanation: The passive form (～れる / ～られる) can also be used as a respectful way of speaking. It is less formal than お～になる but very common in everyday use.
en.formation: 五段動詞: ～あ段 + れる ／ 一段動詞: ～stem + られる
en.notes: Can be confused with the passive. Context determines the meaning. Compared with お～になる, this form is somewhat less formal but easier to form.
examples[].german: What time will the department manager be coming?
The teacher has already gone home.
The company president spoke about this matter.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The honorific form of 来る is 来られます.
ます does not follow the dictionary form.
This asks about the past instead of the upcoming arrival.

en.explanation: 賜る is a very elevated sonkeigo form that can mean both "to receive from a person of higher status" and "to graciously grant". In modern business language it is used mainly in fixed expressions, especially in formal letters, speeches and on ceremonial occasions.
en.formation: 賜る (godan verb) ／ お/ご～賜る ／ ～を賜りますよう
en.notes: 賜る is one of the most elevated keigo verbs and is often found in letters of invitation, speeches of thanks and official documents. In everyday business communication it seems excessive, but it is appropriate on ceremonial occasions.
examples[].german: I respectfully ask for your guidance.
Thank you sincerely for your kind words.
We respectfully invite you and request the honor of your attendance.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます needs the stem 賜り.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite negative is not formed with ないました.

en.meaning: respectful progressive form (someone is doing something right now)
en.explanation: ～ていらっしゃる is the sonkeigo (respectful) form of ～ている. You use it to describe the ongoing state or current action of a person you are showing respect to. Here いらっしゃる replaces いる in the て-form construction.
en.formation: Verb て-form + いらっしゃる (いらっしゃいます in the ます-form)
en.notes: This form sounds more natural and more polite than the ～ている form. In spoken language, いらっしゃる is often shortened to いらっしゃいます.
examples[].german: The company president is waiting in the conference room right now.
Is the teacher back already?
The guest is waiting in the lobby.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Here いらっしゃる follows the て-form.
This negates the waiting.
The polite form is いらっしゃいます.

en.meaning: very polite form of です (to be)
en.explanation: ～でございます is the highest level of politeness for です. It belongs to 丁寧語 (polite language) and is used in very formal situations, in customer service and in business contexts.
en.formation: Noun / な-adjective + でございます ／ い-adjective (く-form) + ございます
en.notes: ありがとうございます actually contains ございます (from ある). With い-adjectives: 早い → 早うございます (archaic, rare). でございます is frequently used in hotels, restaurants and customer service.
examples[].german: This is the conference room.
The restroom is over there.
Thank you very much.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is ございます.
This denies identifying the room.
The copula starts with で here.

en.meaning: to receive the favor of someone doing something
en.explanation: お/ご～いただく is an important keigo construction that expresses that you receive the favor of a respected person doing something for you. With native Japanese verbs you use お + verb stem + いただく, with Sino-Japanese words ご + noun + いただく. This form is more humble than お/ご～くださる.
en.formation: お + verb stem + いただく / ご + Sino-Japanese noun + いただく
en.notes: お/ご～いただく and お/ご～くださる have similar meanings but a different perspective: いただく emphasizes humbly receiving (kenjōgo), くださる emphasizes the other person's generous giving (sonkeigo). In practice, いただく is used more often.
examples[].german: Thank you for coming despite your busy schedule.
I would be grateful for your understanding.
Could you send me the documents?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 送り is a native Japanese verb stem and forms お送り here.
に does not form the humble verb-stem construction.
An extra を does not fit between 資料を and 送り.

en.meaning: I would like to discuss something with you
en.explanation: ご相談させていただきたく is a polite phrase for expressing a wish to consult or discuss something. It is often used in business emails to open a conversation and conveys that you value the other person's expertise or opinion.
en.formation: ご相談させていただきたく + ご連絡いたしました / 存じます
en.notes: ご相談 is one of the most common openers for requests in the business world. The form signals to the recipient that a discussion is wanted without sounding demanding.
examples[].german: I am contacting you because I would like to discuss the new project with you.
There is one matter I would like to discuss with you.
There is something I'd like to discuss with you; could you spare me some time?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The adverbial form of たい is たく.
いただく requires the て-connection.
たい is attached to the stem いただき.

en.explanation: ございます is the most polite form of あります (there is). It belongs to 丁寧語 and is used to express the existence of something in a very polite way. This form is everywhere in customer service, in hotels and in upscale business language.
en.formation: Noun + がございます ／ Noun + でございます (= to be)
en.notes: ございます is the polite form of あります. ございます is not used for the existence of people (いらっしゃいます is used instead). The negative is ございません. With i-adjectives: 早い → 早うございます (rare today, except in ありがとうございます).
examples[].german: Do you have any questions?
There is a parking lot here.
There is something I would like to tell you.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite form is ございます.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite negative is ございません.

en.meaning: very polite request form (Could you please ...?)
en.explanation: ～ていただけませんか is a very polite request form that uses the humble form いただく in the negative potential. It is more polite than ～てくれませんか or ～てもらえませんか.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + いただけませんか ／ いただけないでしょうか (even more polite)
en.notes: Politeness levels of requests: ～てくれ < ～てください < ～てくれませんか < ～ていただけませんか < ～ていただけないでしょうか. The last form is the most polite and is used for very formal requests.
examples[].german: Could you please speak a little more slowly?
Would it be possible for you to check this document?
Could you please tell me your name?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: いただく follows the て-form.
This is not a polite verb form.
This is not a question form.

en.meaning: I would be grateful if you could ... (very polite request)
en.explanation: ～いただければと存じます combines the conditional form of いただく with 存じます (to think, humble), producing an extremely polite way of making a request. The construction implies: "If I could receive the favor of your ..., that would be my wish." It is often used in formal business emails.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + いただければと存じます ／ お/ご + Noun + いただければと存じます
en.notes: This form is slightly less direct than ～いただけますでしょうか and slightly more polite than ～いただければ幸いです. It is used especially in business emails when you express a wish without asking for something directly.
examples[].german: I would be grateful if you could attend.
I would be grateful if you could let me hear your opinion.
I would be grateful if you could check it and then reply.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The conditional is いただければ.
The content of the thought requires と.
ます requires the verb stem.

en.meaning: it can't be helped / it is unavoidable (formal)
en.explanation: いたしかたございません is the very formal version of 仕方がない (it can't be helped). いたしかた is the humble (kenjōgo) form of 仕方 (way/method), and ございません is the formal negative. This phrase is used in formal business situations to express regret about an unavoidable situation.
en.formation: いたしかたございません / いたしかたないことですが (as a lead-in)
en.notes: いたしかたございません is used especially when you have to explain to a customer or business partner why something is not possible. It sounds regretful but firm.
examples[].german: Since it is the rule, I'm afraid it can't be helped.
We apologize for the inconvenience, but it is unavoidable for safety reasons.
Since it is due to the weather, I believe it can't be helped.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This affirms that something can be done instead of expressing that it is unavoidable.
ません is not attached to the dictionary form.
The negative ending is not combined with ない a second time.

en.meaning: it could happen that... / there is a risk that...
en.explanation: ～かねません expresses that a (usually negative) possibility exists. Despite its similar form to ～かねます, it has a completely different meaning: while ～かねます means "cannot", ～かねません means "it could well happen". The double negation (かね + ません) results in an affirmation of the possibility.
en.formation: Verb stem (ます-form without ます) + かねません / かねない (informal)
en.notes: ～かねません is almost always used for negative possibilities (problems, risks, dangers). It would be unnatural to use it for positive possibilities. The difference between ～かねます (cannot) and ～かねません (could happen) is a common stumbling block for learners.
examples[].german: If we leave it like this, it could turn into a big problem.
This could lead to misunderstandings, so please handle it carefully.
There is a risk that we will not be able to meet the delivery deadline.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This expresses inability instead of an impending risk.
ません is not attached to the dictionary form.
The negative ending is not combined with ない a second time.

en.meaning: to be unfortunately unable to; to regret being unable to
en.explanation: ～かねます is a polite form of refusal used to express that you unfortunately cannot do something. It sounds softer and more diplomatic than ～できません. This form is used especially in customer service and in business refusals to phrase the refusal respectfully.
en.formation: Verb stem (ます-form without ます) + かねます
en.notes: ～かねます is an indirect refusal and is considered more polite than ～できません. In Japanese business life direct refusals are avoided, which is why this form is very important. Not to be confused with ～かねません, which expresses a possibility.
examples[].german: I am very sorry, but I am unable to answer regarding that matter.
We are unfortunately unable to comply with your request.
We are unfortunately unable to accept the job at this price.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means "could well happen" and reverses the refusal.
ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
The polite past ends in ました.

en.explanation: 誠に is a formal adverb used in business language and keigo to express sincerity and seriousness. It intensifies the expressions of thanks, apologies and other polite expressions that follow it, giving them a more formal tone.
en.formation: 誠に + ありがとうございます / 申し訳ございません / 恐縮です
en.notes: 誠に is the more formal alternative to 本当に (really). In business emails and letters, 誠に is preferred. 大変 (very) and 誠に can both be used as intensifiers, but 誠に sounds more sincere and more formal.
examples[].german: I sincerely thank you.
I am truly and deeply sorry.
I'm truly sorry to trouble you, but I would ask you to take care of this.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The adverbial expression is 誠に.
を does not form an adverbial intensifier of the thanks here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 誠.

en.meaning: would it be possible for you to ...? (very polite question)
en.explanation: ～いただけますでしょうか is one of the most polite question forms in Japanese. It combines the potential form of いただく with the polite conjectural form でしょうか. This three-layer politeness construction is used in formal business requests.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + いただけますでしょうか ／ お/ご + Noun + いただけますでしょうか
en.notes: Politeness levels of requests: ～てくれますか < ～ていただけますか < ～ていただけませんか < ～ていただけますでしょうか. Some language purists consider ～いただけますでしょうか to be 二重敬語 (double keigo), but the form is firmly established in business practice.
examples[].german: Would it be possible for you to send me the documents?
Could you let me know a date and time that suits you?
Would it be possible for you to call me back?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite negative is not formed with ないました.

en.meaning: the thing is ... / I was wondering ... (polite lead-in)
en.explanation: ～のですが (or the even more polite ～のでございますが) is used to politely introduce a request, question or explanation. The が at the end signals that something more is to follow, which makes the statement indirect and therefore more polite. This form is fundamental to polite communication in Japanese.
en.formation: Verb/Adjective + のですが / のでございますが ／ Noun + なのですが
en.notes: Ending a sentence with が (without continuing it) is typically Japanese and expresses that the speaker leaves the situation open and gives the listener room to respond. It is one of the basic mechanisms of indirect communication in Japanese.
examples[].german: I'd like to make a reservation...
There's something I'd like to ask you...
I'd like to ask you to change the delivery date...
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます cannot be attached directly to の.
たい requires の here, not な.
The explanatory construction does not use the combination のでだが.

en.meaning: humble progressive (I am / we are doing ...)
en.explanation: ～ております is the polite, humble progressive form that replaces ～ている. It combines the て-form with おります (the humble form of いる). In business it is the standard form for politely describing your own state or activity.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + おります
en.notes: ～ております is the standard form on the phone and in emails when talking about yourself or your own company. 承知しております is the standard business reply for "understood / I am aware."
examples[].german: I am aware. / I understand.
I look forward to seeing you. / I'll be waiting for you.
We are currently proceeding with the investigation.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Attaching おります requires the て-form.
ます requires the stem おり.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.meaning: I feel ashamed / I feel awkward (out of gratitude/guilt)
en.explanation: 恐縮です expresses that you feel ashamed or unworthy and is used both for gratitude and for apologies. 恐縮 literally means "shrinking with fear." The phrase is slightly more formal than 恐れ入ります and is used especially in business correspondence.
en.formation: 恐縮です ／ 恐縮ですが (lead-in) ／ 恐縮に存じます (even more formal)
en.notes: 恐縮です is often combined with お忙しいところ or 大変. Unlike 恐れ入ります, 恐縮です has a stronger nuance of guilt. In emails, 恐縮ですが is a popular alternative to 恐れ入りますが.
examples[].german: I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy, but I would be grateful for a reply.
I'm terribly sorry to ask, but could I request a change of schedule?
I feel quite humbled (with gratitude) that you took the trouble to come all this way.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます cannot be attached directly to 恐縮.
を cannot be attached to this clause connection.
No な comes before the copula です here.

en.meaning: thank you very much / excuse me / I am honored
en.explanation: 恐れ入ります is a versatile polite phrase that expresses gratitude, apology or deference depending on the context. Literally it means "I am frightened/overwhelmed" and expresses that you feel unworthy of the other person's kindness or effort.
en.formation: 恐れ入ります (set phrase) ／ 恐れ入りますが (lead-in before a request)
en.notes: 恐れ入ります is used extremely often in business. Depending on the context, it can replace ありがとうございます and すみません while sounding more professional. The form with が at the end introduces a polite request.
examples[].german: I'm much obliged. You've been a great help.
Excuse me, but could you please say that once more?
I'm honored by your praise.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます requires the stem 入り.
る cannot be attached to ます.
The polite past ends in ました.

en.explanation: ～させていただく combines the causative (～させる) with the humble form いただく and expresses that you humbly ask for permission to do something. It implies gratitude for the permission granted.
en.formation: Verb (させ-form) + ていただく (ます-form: ～させていただきます)
en.notes: This form is very common in modern Japanese, but is also often overused. Language purists criticize its inflationary use (e.g. on TV shows: 歌わせていただきます). Correct use presupposes that permission from another person actually exists.
examples[].german: With your permission, I will take today off.
Allow me to explain.
Would it be all right if I checked this?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: いただく follows the て-form.
This negates the announced day off.
The causative form is 休ませる.

en.explanation: In modern business Japanese, ～させていただく is used for various purposes: announcements, refusals, notices of changes and official statements. Although the form literally asks for permission, it is often used formulaically for one-sided announcements.
en.formation: Verb (させ-form) + ていただきます ／ ～させていただくことになりました (announcing a decision)
en.notes: The inflationary use of ～させていただく is a much-debated topic among those who care about the Japanese language. Although purists criticize that no real permission is involved (e.g. with store closures), the form is firmly anchored in everyday business. ご遠慮させていただきます is the standard way of declining.
examples[].german: Please allow us to close the store as of today.
It has been decided that we will revise our prices.
Allow me to decline this time.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: いただく requires the て-connection.
ます requires the stem いただき.
This negates the announced closure.

en.explanation: 承知いたしました is a very formal way of answering "understood" and combines 承知 (knowledge/consent) with いたしました (the humble (kenjōgo) form of しました). In the politeness hierarchy it ranks between 分かりました and かしこまりました.
en.formation: 承知いたしました / 承知しました (slightly less formal)
en.notes: The politeness levels: 分かった → 分かりました → 承知しました → 承知いたしました → かしこまりました. 承知いたしました is the most common in everyday business, since かしこまりました tends to be reserved for customer service.
examples[].german: Understood. I will take care of it right away.
I have noted the change of schedule.
Regarding your request: understood.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The polite past requires the stem いたし.
Politeness endings cannot be doubled.
This negates the agreement.

en.meaning: would that be all right? / may I?
en.explanation: よろしいでしょうか is the polite form of いいですか (is that OK?). よろしい is the formal version of いい (good/fine), and でしょうか turns it into an even more polite question. This form is used constantly in business and customer service.
en.formation: よろしいでしょうか ／ ～してもよろしいでしょうか (asking permission)
en.notes: よろしいでしょうか is the standard polite form for confirmation questions in business. It is more polite than いいですか but less roundabout than よろしゅうございますでしょうか (extremely formal and old-fashioned).
examples[].german: Would it be all right if I took a little of your time?
Is this seat all right for you?
Would tomorrow at 3 p.m. be all right?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: An i-adjective does not take な.
ます cannot be attached directly to よろしい.
The past form ends in かった without an extra い.

en.explanation: ～ことができる expresses the ability to do something. The polite form is ～ことができます. It is an alternative to the potential form of the verb.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + ことができる
en.notes: This form is somewhat more formal than the potential form (話せる). The two are interchangeable, but ことができる is used more often in written language.
examples[].german: I can speak Japanese.
Can you read kanji?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: できる requires が in this construction.
The translation affirms the ability.
The translation states a present ability, not something that was possible in the past.

en.explanation: ～くなる and ～になる express a change of state ("something becomes something"). い-adjectives use ～くなる; な-adjectives and nouns use ～になる.
en.formation: い-adj. (without い) + くなる / な-adj. + になる / Noun + になる
en.notes: くなる/になる describes a natural or spontaneous change. For deliberate changes you use くする/にする.
examples[].german: My Japanese has gotten better.
It's gotten cold lately, hasn't it?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 上手 is a な-adjective and requires に.
This negates the change.
The polite past is なりました.

en.explanation: まだ means "still". With an affirmative form it means "still"; with a negative form it means "not yet".
en.formation: まだ + Verb/Adjective (affirmative or negative)
en.notes: To the question もう～ましたか (Have you already...?) you answer: はい、もう～ました (Yes, already) or いいえ、まだです (No, not yet).
examples[].german: It's still raining.
I haven't eaten yet.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means "soon" instead of "still".
This means "from now on" instead of "still".
This means "yesterday" instead of "still".

en.explanation: まで marks the end point in time or space. It is often used together with から to express a period of time or a distance.
en.formation: Noun + まで
en.notes: から～まで is a common pair: 月曜日から金曜日まで (from Monday to Friday).
examples[].german: I work until five o'clock.
I walk from the station to the school.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: から would mean "from five" instead of "until five".
へ does not mark an end point in time.
を marks neither the length of work nor the end time here.

en.explanation: ～前に means "before doing something" or "before something". With verbs, the dictionary form comes before 前に; with nouns, の comes before 前に.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + 前に / Noun + の前に
en.notes: The verb before 前に is always in the dictionary form, regardless of the tense of the main clause.
examples[].german: I brush my teeth before going to bed.
Please wash your hands before the meal.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: After the dictionary form 寝る, 寝た後で doesn't fit; besides, the meaning is "before".
ながら requires the stem 寝, not 寝る.
てから must attach to the matching て-form.

en.explanation: ～ません is the polite negative of a verb in the non-past. It expresses that you don't do something or won't do it.
en.formation: Verb stem + ません
en.notes: ません can also be used as a polite invitation: 一緒に行きませんか (Why don't we go together?).
examples[].german: I don't eat meat.
I'm not going to school today.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This would be an affirmative statement: I eat meat.
This would be the affirmative past.
This would be a suggestion, not a negation.

en.explanation: ～ませんでした is the polite negative in the past. It expresses that you did not do something.
en.formation: Verb stem + ませんでした
en.notes: This form is regular. You replace ます with ませんでした.
examples[].german: I didn't eat breakfast.
I didn't study yesterday.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This says breakfast was eaten.
This is the affirmative non-past.
This suggests having breakfast together.

en.explanation: ～ました is the polite past form of a verb. It expresses that an action was completed in the past.
en.formation: Verb stem + ました
en.notes: It's easy to form: you replace ます with ました. The verb stem stays the same.
examples[].german: I watched a movie yesterday.
I went to Japan.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 昨日 calls for the past for the completed action.
This would be non-past and negative.
The translation says the movie was watched.

en.explanation: ～ましょう expresses a suggestion ("Let's...") or an intention ("I'll..."). It is the polite volitional form.
en.formation: Verb stem + ましょう
en.notes: ましょう is a suggestion; ましょうか is a question about whether to do something together, or an offer.
examples[].german: Let's go together.
Let's take a break.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This is a negation, not a joint suggestion.
This reports something in the past.
This negates a past action.

en.explanation: ～ましょうか is used as a question to suggest doing something together ("Shall we...?") or to offer help ("Shall I...?").
en.formation: Verb stem + ましょうか
en.notes: When you offer someone help, ましょうか is more polite than just ましょう.
examples[].german: Shall I open the window?
Shall we have lunch together?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This reports a past action instead of offering help.
This negates the opening instead of offering help.
This reports that the window was not opened.

en.explanation: ～ます is the polite non-past form of a verb. It expresses actions in the present or future. This form is used in formal situations and with strangers.
en.formation: Verb stem + ます
en.notes: The ます-form is built from the verb stem (masu-stem). With group 1 (godan) verbs, the last syllable changes: 書く → 書きます, 飲む → 飲みます.
examples[].german: I study Japanese every day.
I'm meeting a friend tomorrow.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The translation is affirmative, not "I don't study".
The translation describes a present habit, not a completed past action.
This would be the negative past.

en.explanation: も replaces は, が or を and means "also" or "too". It shows that what is said also applies to the marked element. With amounts it can mean "even".
en.formation: Noun + も
en.notes: も replaces は, が and を, but is added on to other particles: にも、でも、からも, etc.
examples[].german: I'm a student too.
I like both cats and dogs.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The copula does not take an object here.
A direction does not express "also".
私の学生 would mean "my student" instead of me.

en.explanation: With an affirmative form, もう means "already". With a negative form it means "no longer" or "not anymore". It expresses that a change has taken place.
en.formation: もう + Verb (affirmative: already / negative: no longer)
en.notes: もう一度 (mō ichido) means "once more"; here もう has a different meaning. もう and まだ form a pair of opposites.
examples[].german: I've already done my homework.
I won't eat any more.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means "tomorrow" instead of "already".
This means "from now on" instead of "already".
This means "soon" instead of "already done".

en.explanation: ～んです is used to give an explanation, ask for an explanation, or emphasize a statement. It signals that the speaker wants to explain the context.
en.formation: Verb/い-adj. + んです / な-adj. + なんです / Noun + なんです
en.notes: んです (spoken form) and のです (written form) are interchangeable. ～んですか sounds more natural than ～ますか when you ask for the reason behind something.
examples[].german: What's wrong? / What happened?
It's just that I have a test tomorrow.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: A verbal statement is not connected with なです here.
にです is not an explanatory connection here.
をです is not an explanatory connection here.

en.explanation: Strongly emphasizes the reason for something, often with an emotional tone. This structure is used to underline that something happens specifically or solely because of a particular reason. Often expresses gratitude, pride or deep conviction.
en.formation: Verb ば-form + こそ / い-adjective-ければ + こそ / な-adjective/Noun + であればこそ
en.notes: Very emphatic. Strongly emphasizes the causal connection.
examples[].german: It's precisely because I trust you that I'm entrusting you with this work.
It's precisely because there were hardships that the joy of success is all the greater.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a link expressing a reason here.
な cannot be attached here.
ます cannot be attached directly to こそ.

en.explanation: Expresses that if something happens, everything is over or all efforts were in vain. This structure is used to describe a situation that is irreversible or final. Often carries a sense of resignation or warning.
en.formation: Verb ば-form + それまでだ / Verb たら-form + それまでだ
en.notes: Expresses finality or resignation. Warns of irreversible consequences.
examples[].german: If I fail the exam, that's the end of it.
If we give up, it's all over. Let's hang in there until the end.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The object particle does not end the sentence.
The attributive form does not end the sentence.
ます cannot be attached to も.

en.explanation: Emphasizes that, in addition to one thing, something even more surprising or extreme comes on top. Strengthens the statement.
en.formation:
Noun + ばかりか + Noun + まで
普通形 + ばかりか～まで
en.notes: Emphasizes the additional, surprising information.
examples[].german: He can speak not only Japanese but even Chinese.
She is good not only at studying but even at sports.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form an additive link here.
な cannot be attached here.
ます cannot attach to か.

en.explanation: Very formal and strong prohibition used mainly in written rules and regulations. This archaic structure is not common in modern spoken language. Often seen on signs or in official documents.
en.formation: Verb 辞書形 + べからず
en.notes: Very formal and archaic. Mainly found on signs or in written rules.
examples[].german: No entry.
One must not cause trouble for others.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This calls for entering instead of prohibiting it.
ます cannot be attached to ず.
ない cannot be attached to this classical negative form.

en.meaning: in order to, with the aim of
en.explanation: Expresses a purpose or intention, often in formal or literary contexts. This structure is a more formal alternative to ために. Used to describe that something is done with a particular goal.
en.formation: Verb 辞書形 + べく (する→すべく)
en.notes: Formal and literary. する becomes すべく.
examples[].german: I keep working hard in order to succeed.
An investigation was launched in order to uncover the truth.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The attributive form does not form a purpose link here.
This expresses a prohibition instead of an intention.
ます cannot be attached to べく.

en.explanation: Expresses that something is completely impossible or cannot be achieved. This very formal structure emphasizes absolute impossibility. Often used to express that something is far out of reach.
en.formation: Verb 辞書形 + べくもない (する→すべくもない)
en.notes: Very formal. Emphasizes absolute impossibility.
examples[].german: His talent is something someone like me could not possibly match.
This problem cannot possibly be solved by an amateur.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ない does not take an attached ます.
The polite past is not formed with ないました.
The expression requires も instead of を.

en.meaning: at least better than, at least
en.explanation: Expresses that a situation is not ideal, but at least better than an alternative. Emphasizes the positive in a negative situation.
en.formation:
普通形 + だけまし
Noun + だけまし
en.notes: Expresses relief despite negative circumstances.
examples[].german: Getting even a little is better than nothing.
At least nobody was hurt.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: No な comes before だ here.
を does not fit before だ here.
ます cannot attach directly to まし.

en.explanation: A very literary expression emphasizing that merely imagining something provokes a strong reaction. Used almost exclusively in written language.
en.formation:
Verb 辞書形 + だに
Noun + だに
en.notes: Very literary and archaic; rare in modern language.
examples[].german: Just imagining it is terrifying.
Just remembering it makes me angry.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form an adverbial link here.
な cannot be attached here.
ます cannot be attached directly to だに.

en.explanation: であれ expresses that something holds regardless of the circumstances or conditions. It can be used on its own or in the form であれ～であれ. This structure has a formal, written character.
en.formation: Noun + であれ / interrogative + であれ
en.notes: Often used with interrogatives such as 誰、何、どんな. Very formal.
examples[].german: Whoever it may be, they must follow the rules.
Whatever the reason, violence cannot be tolerated.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を cannot attach to である here.
な cannot attach to the concessive form here.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.explanation: であれ～であれ expresses that something holds regardless of which of several alternatives applies. It stresses that the result or consequence is the same in all cases. This form is very formal and is used mainly in written language.
en.formation: Noun + であれ + Noun + であれ
en.notes: More formal than ～でも～でも. Preferred in official contexts.
examples[].german: Day or night, please contact me anytime.
Whether male or female, people should be treated equally.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を cannot attach to である here.
な cannot attach to the concessive form here.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.explanation: Expresses that a situation or behavior is inappropriate because it does not correspond to the extreme situation mentioned. This structure is used to criticize something or argue that it is exaggerated or uncalled for. Often carries a sense of dissatisfaction or criticism.
en.formation: Noun + ではあるまいし / Verb 辞書形 + のではあるまいし
en.notes: Expresses criticism or dissatisfaction. Implies that the behavior is excessive.
examples[].german: You're not a child anymore, so don't cry over something like that.
It's not as if this were a war; there's no need to go that far.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ません is not attached to the dictionary form.
な cannot be attached here.
ます cannot be attached to まい.

en.meaning: even if it were ..., even if
en.explanation: Expresses that something applies regardless of the circumstances. A very formal expression.
en.formation:
Noun + であろうと
疑問詞 + であろうと
en.notes: Very formal; often found in written language.
examples[].german: Whoever it is, they must follow the rules.
However difficult it may be, I won't give up.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The volitional form of ある is あろう.
The concessive connection requires と, not を.
な cannot be attached here.

en.meaning: if not X, then what; nothing other than X
en.explanation: A rhetorical question that strongly emphasizes that something is definitely the case. Expresses conviction or indignation.
en.formation:
Noun + でなくてなんだろう
な-adjective + でなくてなんだろう
en.notes: Expresses strong conviction or rhetorical emphasis.
examples[].german: If this isn't a miracle, what is?
If that isn't betrayal, what is?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます cannot attach to だろう.
を cannot stand before だろう here.
The connective form of ない is なくて.

en.explanation: ですら is an emphatic particle expressing that even something unexpected or extreme is the case. It is stronger than でさえ and is used to express surprise or emphasis. It often introduces an extreme example.
en.formation: Noun + ですら
en.notes: More formal and emphatic than でさえ. Not common in colloquial speech.
examples[].german: He can't do what even a child can do.
Even his parents couldn't understand his behavior.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: な does not connect to できること here.
を cannot attach to the emphasis here.
ます cannot be attached to すら.

en.meaning: isn't it the case that; could it not be that
en.explanation: Expresses a cautious supposition or speculation. The speaker believes that something is probably the case.
en.formation:
普通形 + のではあるまいか
Noun/な-adjective + ではあるまいか
en.notes: A formal, literary expression, often found in written language.
examples[].german: Might he not be the culprit?
Isn't this the best way?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます cannot attach to the question particle.
The rhetorical question does not need な.
ません does not attach to the dictionary form.

en.meaning: no sooner ... than; the very moment that
en.explanation: Describes how, immediately after one action, the next one already happens, almost at the same time. Written language; for actual events, usually past ones, not for wishes or requests.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form / た-form) + が早いか
en.notes: Similar in meaning to ～や否や and ～なり (both N1) as well as ～たとたん (N3). が早いか puts particular emphasis on speed. The second clause is not in the volitional or imperative mood.
examples[].german: No sooner had the bell rung than the children rushed out of the classroom.
No sooner had he received his salary than he spent all of it.
The moment the shop opened, customers poured in all at once.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ばかりか means "not only ... but also" and does not express a sequence in time.
くせに ("even though") contains a reproach, not an immediate sequence.
ものなら ("if ... at all") is hypothetical and does not fit an actual event.

en.explanation: Expresses that once something happens, an irreversible or extreme consequence follows. This structure emphasizes finality and often negative consequences. Used to warn of serious or irreversible consequences.
en.formation: Verb 辞書形/た-form + が最後 / Verb たら-form + 最後
en.notes: Emphasizes irreversible, often negative consequences. A warning about a point of no return.
examples[].german: Once you tell him a secret, it spreads right away.
Once you go down that road, you can never come back.
Once you take this medicine, there's no going back to how things were.
Once you've had a fight with him, you can never make up.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a conditional link here.
な cannot be attached here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 最後.

en.meaning: presumptuous, seeming like ..., coming across as inappropriately ...
en.explanation: Expresses that something or someone comes across as something inappropriate or presumptuous. Has a negative connotation and indicates that the behavior or appearance does not suit the situation. A critical expression.
en.formation:
名詞 + がましい
名詞 + がましく
en.notes: Strongly negative connotation. Used to criticize inappropriate or presumptuous behavior.
examples[].german: It's an affected, contrived performance.
I don't like pushy attitudes.
Don't say things as if you expect me to be grateful.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The adverbial form does not modify 演技 attributively here.
The い-adjective takes no な before 演技.
ます cannot attach directly to the adjective.

en.meaning: hard to ..., hardly possible to ..., difficult to ...
en.explanation: Expresses that something is difficult or hardly possible to do. More formal than にくい and often used in written language. Emphasizes the objective difficulty or impossibility of an action.
en.formation:
動詞ます形 + がたい
動詞ます形 + 難い
en.notes: More formal than にくい. Often used in written language or formal situations.
examples[].german: His explanation is hard to understand.
It is an unforgivable act.
It's a hard-to-believe story, but it seems to be true.
His behavior is hard to understand.
It's an unforgettable memory.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます cannot attach directly to the adjective.
The adverbial form does not fit before です here.
The past form ends in かった without an extra い.

en.explanation: Similar to かたがた; expresses that one carries out a main activity and does something else on the side. This structure emphasizes that the second action accompanies or supplements the first. The main activity comes before がてら.
en.formation: Noun + がてら / Verb ます-stem + がてら
en.notes: Somewhat less formal than かたがた. The main activity comes before がてら.
examples[].german: I stopped by the post office while I was out for a walk.
I met up with a friend while I was out shopping.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a link expressing an accompanying circumstance here.
な cannot be attached here.
ます cannot be attached directly to がてら.

en.explanation: A very formal expression for "because" or "due to". Emphasizes causality and is used mainly in written language.
en.formation:
普通形 + がゆえに
Noun + (である) + がゆえに
en.notes: Very formal and literary; rare in spoken language.
examples[].german: It was a mistake born of youth.
Precisely because I lacked experience, I failed.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The causal link is completed with に.
な does not form a causal link here.
ます cannot attach directly to ゆえ.

en.explanation: Used to express the outward impression or appearance of a state or feeling. Turns adjectives into nouns that describe the appearance. Often combined with verbs of perception.
en.formation:
イ形容詞語幹 + げ
ナ形容詞語幹 + げ
名詞 + げ + な/に
en.notes: Used to describe the outward appearance of feelings or states. げな before nouns, げに as an adverb.
examples[].german: He had a lonely look on his face.
She was talking with an air of happiness.
He gave a meaningful look.
She had a sad-looking face.
The children are playing merrily.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The following な would be doubled, which is not allowed.
を does not fit before な表情 here.
ます cannot attach directly to げ.

en.explanation: A literary expression for comparisons. ごとき is used before nouns, ごとく as an adverb. Very formal; used mainly in written language, literature or formal speeches. Can also be used pejoratively.
en.formation:
名詞 + ごとき/ごとく
動詞辞書形 + ごとき/ごとく
イ形容詞 + ごとき/ごとく
en.notes: Very literary and formal. In modern everyday language, ような is used instead. Can also be humble or pejorative.
examples[].german: He left like a storm.
It is presumptuous for someone like me to give an opinion.
It is as clear as seeing fire (crystal clear).
He appeared like a storm and left again right away.
He showed demon-like strength.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The attributive form does not modify 去って行った adverbially here.
な cannot be attached here.
ます cannot attach directly to ごとく.

en.explanation: After a noun, ぐるみ means "all together, ... included". Typical in set combinations such as 家族ぐるみ (the whole family), 町ぐるみ (the whole town) or 会社ぐるみ (the whole company, often in scandals).
en.formation: Noun + ぐるみ (+ で / + の + Noun)
en.notes: Only common with a few nouns (家族, 町, 村, 地域, 会社, 組織). 会社ぐるみ and 組織ぐるみ often carry a note of criticism. Do not confuse with ～ごと (together with, e.g. 皮ごと食べる) or ぬいぐるみ (stuffed toy).
examples[].german: Our whole family is on friendly terms with the family next door.
That was fraud involving the entire company.
The whole town is preparing for the festival.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: まみれ means "covered all over with" (dirt, sweat) and does not fit with family.
だらけ means "full of" (usually something negative) and does not describe a community.
ずくめ means "consisting only of" (黒ずくめ) and does not fit with people.

en.explanation: Emphasizes that something is not limited to a single person or thing but affects others as well.
en.formation:
Noun + ひとり + だけでなく
Noun + のみならず
en.notes: Emphasizes extension beyond a single unit.
examples[].german: This is not just his problem alone, but everyone's problem.
This is not just Japan's challenge alone, but one for all of Asia.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The adverbial form of ない is なく.
な cannot be attached here.
を does not form a contrastive link here.

en.explanation: いかんでは/いかんによっては expresses that the result or consequence depends on how something is or how it is done. It emphasizes that different circumstances can lead to different results. This construction is very formal.
en.formation: Noun + のいかんでは/のいかんによっては
en.notes: Very formal. Emphasizes that the result depends on the circumstances.
examples[].german: Depending on how it's done, there is also a chance of success.
Depending on the conditions, the contract will need to be reviewed.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a dependent condition here.
な cannot connect the following clause here.
ます cannot be attached directly to いかん.

en.explanation: いかんによらず expresses that something applies regardless of particular circumstances, conditions or manner. It emphasizes that the factors mentioned have no influence on the outcome or decision. This construction is very formal and is often used in official contexts.
en.formation: Noun + のいかんによらず
en.notes: Very formal. Used in official documents and announcements.
examples[].german: Regardless of the reason, violence cannot be tolerated.
Regardless of age, anyone can take part.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This makes the statement depend on the reason instead of being independent of it.
The reference requires に.
な cannot be attached here.

en.explanation: An introductory adverb: you would like to, but the circumstances unfortunately do not allow it. Written style; from classical 如何せん, "what can one do".
en.formation: (positive clause + が／けれど,) いかんせん + obstacle
en.notes: Usually follows a が／けれど clause that names the positive point. Also written in kanji: 如何せん. Do not confuse with ～いかんで／～いかんによらず (N1, "depending on"), which go back to the same 如何.
examples[].german: I'd like to help, but unfortunately I don't have the time.
The plan is good, but unfortunately the budget isn't enough.
The food at this restaurant is delicious, but unfortunately it's far too expensive.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: いかにも ("truly, very typical") affirms and does not introduce an obstacle.
せっかく ("specially, going to the trouble") does not fit before an obstacle such as lack of time.
さすがに ("as expected; still not") does not fit an introduction expressing regret.

en.explanation: Expresses that something seems or looks like something else, often with a negative or critical connotation. Used to express that something comes across as inappropriate or unpleasant. じみた is used before nouns, じみる as a verb.
en.formation:
名詞 + じみた + 名詞
名詞 + じみる
en.notes: Usually has a negative connotation. Expresses that something seems unsuitable or inappropriate.
examples[].german: Please stop the preachy talk.
His clothes look old-fashioned / like an old man's.
Don't say such whiny things.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The stem form does not modify 話 attributively here.
The polite past requires the stem じみ.
No extra な comes before 話 here.

en.explanation: Expresses that something unexpected happens just when one had expected something else. This structure emphasizes the contrast between expectation and reality. Used to describe surprises or sudden twists.
en.formation: Verb 辞書形/た-form + かと思いきや / い-adjective + かと思いきや
en.notes: Emphasizes unexpected twists or contrasts between expectation and reality.
examples[].german: Just when I thought it was going to rain, it suddenly cleared up.
Just when I thought he was angry, he burst out laughing.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The content of the thought requires と.
な cannot be attached here.
ます cannot be attached to きや.

en.explanation: Expresses an extreme feeling or state. Often used with adjectives of emotion.
en.formation:
い-adjective + 限りだ
な-adjective + な + 限りだ
en.notes: Expresses strong feelings or evaluations.
examples[].german: His success is truly gratifying.
It is deeply regrettable that things turned out this way.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The object particle does not end the sentence.
The attributive form does not end the sentence.
ます cannot attach directly to the noun 限り here.

en.meaning: it is worth ...ing / it is not worth ...ing; worth the effort
en.explanation: Expresses whether an action or effort was or is worthwhile. 甲斐がある means that the effort bears fruit, while 甲斐がない means that the effort was in vain. Used to assess the value or benefit of an effort.
en.formation:
動詞辞書形/た形 + 甲斐がある/ない
名詞 + の甲斐がある/ない
en.notes: Often used to assess in retrospect whether an effort was successful. 〜甲斐 can also be used on its own (生き甲斐, やり甲斐).
examples[].german: All my hard work studying paid off, and I passed.
My efforts to persuade them were in vain.
It is important to find a purpose in life.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ある needs が here, not を.
The attributive past does not form a link here.
The finite form does not form a link here.

en.explanation: からして expresses that even the first or most obvious example is enough to make a judgment. Often has negative connotations. It stresses that the very first sign already says something about the whole.
en.formation: Noun + からして
en.notes: Do not confuse with からすると (standpoint). からして stresses the first sign.
examples[].german: Starting with his attitude, he's rude.
Just from the outside, this shop looks expensive.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The dictionary form does not connect with 失礼だ here.
The finite form ends the sentence.
The attributive past form does not fit before 失礼だ here.

en.meaning: from the standpoint of ..., judging from
en.explanation: からすると/からすれば expresses that something is judged from a particular perspective or on the basis of certain information. It is used to state a conclusion or opinion based on a point of view.
en.formation: Noun + からすると/からすれば
en.notes: Similar to から見ると, but more formal and often used for conclusions.
examples[].german: Judging from the way he's acting, there seems to be some kind of problem.
Based on experience, this method is the most effective.
From my point of view, this plan is unrealistic.
Judging by his appearance, he's probably around 30.
