She always acts so refined, but she's actually a very easygoing person.
Stop pretending you know when you don't.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 偉がる is not a common form; がる describes the feelings of third persons, not showing off.
偉っぽい is uncommon, and っぽい cannot be used with すぐに like a verb.
めく means "to show signs of something" (春めく) and does not combine with 偉.

en.meaning: as one would expect, just as expected
en.explanation: だけあって expresses recognition: the result matches what you would expect based on a known quality. Positive tone.
en.formation: Verb/い-Adj/な-Adj/Noun + だけあって
en.notes: Always positive/appreciative. Similar to だけに, but more strongly appreciative.
examples[].german: As you'd expect from someone who has lived in Japan for 10 years, he speaks fluent Japanese.
As you'd expect from a professional, he's really good.
As you'd expect from a professional, he works fast.
It's expensive, but the quality is correspondingly good.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The dictionary form does not link the following clause here.
The attributive past form does not link the following clause here.
The finite form ends the sentence instead of attaching the reason.

en.meaning: precisely because, as one would expect
en.explanation: だけに expresses that a result matches exactly what one would expect given the circumstances – "precisely because" the condition is what it is.
en.formation: Verb/い-adj/な-adj/noun + だけに
examples[].german: As you'd expect from a famous restaurant, the food is delicious.
Precisely because our expectations were so high, the disappointment was just as great.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を and に do not form a joint connection here.
な does not link the explanatory following clause here.
ます cannot be attached to だけ.

en.meaning: not serious enough to ...; not worth making a fuss about
en.explanation: ほどのことではない states that something is not serious or important enough to justify a certain (exaggerated) reaction: "It's not so bad that you'd need to see a doctor." Reassuring or downplaying; spoken and written.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + ほどのことではない / ほどのことはない; Noun + ほどのことではない
en.notes: ～ことはない (N2) says directly "there's no need"; ほどのことではない justifies this with the minor importance of the matter. ～までもない (N1), by contrast, means "it's unnecessary because it's obvious anyway" (言うまでもない), not "too insignificant".
examples[].german: It's just a slight cold – not bad enough that I need to go to the hospital.
It's nothing to worry about. It'll heal quickly.
There's really no need to come all the way here to apologize.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ことになる ("it ends up that") contradicts ちょっとした風邪だから.
しかない ("there's no choice but") contradicts the slight cold.
べきだ calls for a hospital visit and does not fit the reason "only a slight cold".

en.explanation: 以上は expresses that, given an existing fact, one must act accordingly. Similar to からには.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) / verb-た形 + 以上(は)
examples[].german: As long as you're a student, you should study.
Now that I've taken it on, I'll do it responsibly.
Now that I've taken it on, I'll take responsibility for it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a condition of obligation here.
な does not link to the following clause here.
ます cannot be attached to 以上.

en.explanation: 一方だ expresses that a trend or change keeps on continuing in one direction, mostly in a negative context.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + 一方だ
en.notes: Often used for negative trends, but can also be positive.
examples[].german: Prices just keep rising.
The global environment just keeps getting worse.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The statement is left without a closing predicate.
The attributive な-form does not end the sentence.
ます is not attached directly to 一方.

en.meaning: on the other hand, while, on one hand … on the other
en.explanation: 一方で contrasts two opposing aspects or situations that exist at the same time.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) / い-adj + 一方で / noun + の一方で / な-adj + な一方で
examples[].german: While things became more convenient, new problems also arose.
He's strict, but on the other hand he also has a gentle side.
While things are becoming more convenient, the dangers are increasing too.
He's kind, but he also has a strict side.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a contrastive connection here.
な does not link the two developments here.
ます cannot be attached to the noun 一方.

en.explanation: 以来 expresses that a state has continued since a certain point in time or event. It emphasizes the duration since then.
en.formation: Verb-て形 + 以来 / noun + 以来
en.notes: The state continues up to the present.
examples[].german: Ever since I came to Japan, I've been using Japanese every day.
I haven't seen him since graduation.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This refers to before coming, not since.
This means outside of or except, not since.
This refers to a time limit or boundary, not the start of an ongoing state.

en.meaning: from the standpoint of, in terms of, -wise
en.explanation: 上（じょう） as a suffix on Sino-Japanese nouns means "from the standpoint of, as far as X is concerned": 法律上 (legally), 健康上 (health-wise), 教育上 (educationally). Formal and very common in the news, administration and business. Continues with の + noun or with は/も.
en.formation: Noun (usually Sino-Japanese) + 上 / 上は / 上の + Noun
en.notes: Do not confuse with ～上で (N3, "when/after"), ～上は (N2, "now that") or ～上に (N2, "in addition"), which are read うえ. ～的 (N3), by contrast, forms な-adjectives ("-al, -ic"); 上 forms adverbial phrases or, with の, noun modifiers.
examples[].german: I decided to leave the company for health reasons.
Under the contract, we cannot disclose this information to outside parties.
That movie is said to be bad for children from an educational standpoint.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 的 forms a な-adjective and requires な before a noun (健康的な), not の.
向き means "suitable for"; a "reason suitable for health" makes no sense.
気味 means "slightly, a touch of" and does not follow 健康.

en.meaning: no sooner ... than, (almost) at the same moment
en.explanation: か～ないかのうちに describes the second action starting when the first has only just been completed (or not quite yet): "No sooner had ... than ...". The same verb appears twice. Written and narrative style; the main clause is usually in the past.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form/た-form) + か + the same verb (ない-form) + かのうちに
en.notes: Compared with ～たとたん (something surprising happens immediately afterward), か～ないかのうちに emphasizes that the first action has not even been fully completed. ～や否や (N1) is even more written-style. The main clause contains neither an intention nor a request.
examples[].german: The bell had barely started ringing when the students rushed out of the classroom.
He had barely lain down before he fell asleep.
The train had barely come to a stop when the passengers surged toward the doors.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The construction needs the second か before のうちに.
あまり expresses an excess ("out of sheer ..."), not closeness in time.
たびに marks repetition ("every time"), not a single moment.

en.explanation: かのように describes something that does not match reality but looks or feels that way. A comparison with a hypothetical situation.
en.formation: Verb/い-Adj/な-Adj + である + かのように / Noun + である + かのように
en.notes: Often combined with まるで. Literary/formal.
examples[].german: He acted as if he knew nothing.
It was an event that seemed almost like a dream.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form an adverbial comparison here.
The attributive form requires a noun instead of 振る舞った.
ます cannot be attached directly to よう.

en.meaning: if you ask whether ...; whether ... – (not necessarily)
en.explanation: かというと takes up an obvious question or conclusion in order to answer it – often to deny it: "Does that mean ...? Not necessarily." With question words (なぜかというと) it introduces an explanation. Neutral; common in argumentation.
en.formation: Sentence (plain form) / question-word sentence + かというと / かといえば; often + そうではない・～わけではない
en.notes: ～からといって (N3) directly rejects a wrong conclusion ("just because ..."); かというと first poses the question explicitly and then answers it. After なぜ/どうして, ～からだ almost always follows. Do not confuse with ～というと ("speaking of ...").
examples[].german: Are expensive restaurants always good? Not necessarily.
Why was I late? Because the trains had stopped.
Do I dislike him? That's not quite it either.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: からといって requires a conclusion in the main clause; here, however, そうではない answers a question.
かのように ("as if") compares with an appearance and does not fit そうではない.
かどうか forms an embedded question that requires a predicate such as わからない.

en.meaning: just when I thought, no sooner than
en.explanation: かと思ったら expresses that a situation changes surprisingly quickly. No sooner did you think A than B was already happening.
en.formation: Verb-た形 + かと思ったら / かと思うと
en.notes: Emphasizes the quick, surprising change.
examples[].german: One moment he was crying, and now he's already laughing.
Just when I thought it had cleared up, it started raining again.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The content of the thought needs と.
The past conditional of 思う is 思ったら.
The conditional is not formed with ますたら.

en.explanation: 限りでは limits a statement to the scope of your own knowledge or perception.
en.formation: Verb dictionary form / Verb-た形 + 限りでは
en.notes: Limits the statement to your own knowledge.
examples[].german: As far as I know, he's single.
As far as I've been able to find out, there doesn't seem to be any problem.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not limit the scope of knowledge here.
な does not link a following clause here.
ます cannot be attached to the noun 限り here.

en.explanation: かねる has two forms with opposite meanings: ～かねる means "cannot, is unable to" (a polite way of declining). ～かねない means "it cannot be ruled out that" (a warning of a negative outcome). Both are attached to the verb stem (ます-stem).
en.formation: Verb ます-stem + かねる / かねない
en.notes: かねる → polite refusal (ビジネス). かねない → warning about a negative possibility. With かねない, only for negative/undesirable outcomes.
examples[].german: I'm afraid we are unable to meet that demand.
If this is left as it is, it could well cause an accident.
I'm afraid we are unable to accommodate that request.
It's an opinion I can't agree with.
At this rate, it could lead to an accident.
It's a remark that could cause misunderstandings.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ない does not take an attached ます.
The past form is not built with ないました.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.meaning: from the standpoint of ..., judging by
en.explanation: からいうと names the yardstick or standpoint from which a judgment is made: experience, position, data, field of expertise. "Seen from X, ...". Neutral to formal; からいって sounds somewhat more categorical. It does not come directly after people (not: 私からいうと).
en.formation: Noun + からいうと / からいえば / からいって
en.notes: ～からすると/～から見ると are almost interchangeable, but can also come directly after people (私からすると). からいうと, by contrast, requires an abstract standpoint (立場, 点, 経験). Don't confuse it with ～によると ("according to"), which names a source of information, not a yardstick for judgment.
examples[].german: From my position, I can't agree with that proposal.
In terms of ability, he's the best on the team.
Judging from this data, there's a high chance the plan will fail.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: によると names a source of information ("according to"), not a standpoint for your own judgment.
をめぐって requires a point of dispute, not a yardstick for judgment.
にかけては requires a field in which someone is especially good.

en.meaning: from the standpoint of, from the perspective of
en.explanation: からみると gives the perspective from which one views or judges a situation. Similar to からすると.
en.formation: Noun + からみると / からみれば / からみて
examples[].german: From an expert's point of view, this problem is simple.
Judging from the results, this method was effective.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a viewpoint condition here.
ます is not attached to 見る.
な cannot be attached to this conditional form.

en.meaning: to do completely / to manage to / to be unable to finish
en.explanation: きる expresses that an action is carried out completely or all the way to the end. きれない means you cannot manage to do it completely.
en.formation: Verb ます-stem + きる / きれる / きれない
en.notes: きる = completely; きれない = can't be done completely.
examples[].german: I ran the marathon all the way to the end.
So much food was served that we couldn't finish it.
I ran the whole marathon.
I've completely used it all up.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This affirms that you can eat everything.
ない does not take an attached ます.
The negative polite form is not combined with ない again.

en.explanation: ことだから is used to express a guess or expectation based on a person's known character.
en.formation: Noun + の + ことだから
en.notes: Based on the person's known character.
examples[].german: Knowing how conscientious Mr. Tanaka is, he'll surely come on time.
Knowing that person, they're bound to be late again.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a reason connection with から here.
ます cannot be attached to だ.
The nominal reason connection is ことだから.

en.explanation: ことだし names one of several possible reasons that justifies the following decision, request or suggestion: "Since ..., let's ...". Friendly and colloquial; the main clause often contains ～(よ)う, ～ましょう, ～ませんか or ～ことにする.
en.formation: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + ことだし / な-adjective + な + ことだし / Noun + である + ことだし
en.notes: Compared with plain ～し, ことだし sounds softer and more considered. ～ことだから (彼のことだから), by contrast, bases a guess on a person's character. The main clause of a ことだし construction is almost never a plain statement of fact, but a decision, suggestion or request.
examples[].german: Now that the rain has stopped, shall we get going?
Since everyone is here, let's start the meeting.
The weather is nice, so why don't we go for a walk or something?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ことに only follows emotion words (驚いたことに) and does not give a reason for a suggestion.
ことなく requires the dictionary form and means "without ...ing".
ものの is concessive and cannot be followed by a suggestion like 出かけようか.

en.explanation: ことか expresses strong emotion: admiration, surprise or longing. A rhetorical exclamation.
en.formation: どんなに / どれほど / 何度 + Verb/Adj + ことか
en.notes: Often combined with どんなに, どれほど, 何度.
examples[].german: How happy I was!
How many times I thought about quitting!
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The object particle does not complete this exclamation.
な does not form a closing exclamation here.
ます cannot be attached directly to こと.

en.explanation: ことに(は) puts the speaker's feeling first, before the actual fact follows: 驚いたことに = "To my surprise ...". Only with emotion adjectives or verbs (嬉しい, 残念な, 驚いた, 困った). Rather written, but also common in speeches and narratives.
en.formation: い-adjective + ことに(は) / な-adjective + な + ことに(は) / Verb (た-form) + ことに(は)
en.notes: The construction always expresses the speaker's attitude, not that of a third person. Don't confuse it with ～ことか (N2, exclamation: どんなに嬉しいことか) or with ～ことにする/～ことになる. In English it often corresponds to an adverb like "unfortunately", "fortunately" or "surprisingly".
examples[].german: To my surprise, he was already married.
Unfortunately, the concert was canceled.
To my delight, my daughter passed the entrance exam for the university that was her first choice.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ことで names a cause or a means; the surprise did not cause the marriage.
ことから draws a conclusion from a fact, not from a feeling.
ことなく requires the dictionary form and means "without ...ing".

en.meaning: there's no need to, one doesn't have to
en.explanation: ことはない reassures the listener: there's no reason to worry or no need to do something.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + ことはない
en.notes: Reassuring function. Similar to ～なくてもいい.
examples[].german: There's no need to worry so much.
There's no need to hurry; we still have time.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This asserts that something occurs instead of a lack of necessity.
ない is not made polite by attaching ます.
ない does not take an object particle here.

en.explanation: くらいなら contrasts a highly undesirable option with another that the speaker prefers: "Rather than do X, I'd sooner do Y." The main clause usually contains ほうがいい, ～たい or ましだ. Expresses a strong personal aversion; used in speech and writing.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + くらいなら / ぐらいなら + ～ほうがいい・ましだ・～たい
en.notes: Unlike the neutral ～より(は)～ほうがいい, くらいなら expresses strong rejection of the first option ("that would be the very last thing"). Don't confuse it with ～ものなら (unrealistic condition: 戻れるものなら戻りたい) or with plain くらい ("about, to such an extent").
examples[].german: Rather than go back to a company like that, I'd be better off changing jobs.
If you're going to quit halfway, you're better off not starting at all.
Rather than ask someone else, I'd prefer to do it myself.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ものなら expresses a wish that can hardly be fulfilled ("if only I could") and does not fit ましだ.
からには means "now that ..., (I must) see it through" and contradicts the wish not to go back.
ばかりに names the cause of a regrettable result, not a comparison of two options.

en.explanation: まい expresses: 1) a strong intention not to do something (determination), 2) a guess that something will probably not happen.
en.formation: Verb dictionary form + まい (group 1) / Verb ます-stem + まい (group 2) / するまい, 来まい
en.notes: Somewhat old-fashioned/literary. Everyday language: ～ないだろう.
examples[].german: I will never make a mistake like that again.
He probably won't come anymore.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: するました wrongly combines the dictionary form with a polite ending.
The polite negative is しません, not するません.
The negative is しない, not するない.

en.explanation: まみれ is attached to nouns and forms a な-adjective describing something covered or soiled with an unpleasant substance. Almost always has a negative connotation; for positive meanings, ～だらけ (more neutral) or ～いっぱい is used.
en.formation: Noun + まみれ (+ の/だ/な)
en.notes: Typical combinations: 泥まみれ (covered in mud), 汗まみれ (covered in sweat), 血まみれ (covered in blood), 借金まみれ (deep in debt). Don't confuse with ～だらけ, which can also be used for countable things.
examples[].german: The children were playing, covered in mud.
I washed the sweat-soaked shirt.
We played until we were covered in mud.
He was lying collapsed, covered in blood.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: An object particle cannot come before になって here.
まみれなになって combines the forms incorrectly.
ます cannot be attached directly to まみれ.

en.explanation: めく is a suffix that is attached to certain nouns and forms a godan verb (めく → めいた → めいて). It expresses that something takes on the character or atmosphere of the noun. The number of combinations is limited: you cannot freely attach it to just any noun.
en.formation: Noun + めく (→ めいた + Noun / めいて)
en.notes: Common combinations: 春めく (to become spring-like), 皮肉めく (to sound ironic), 謎めく (to seem mysterious), 冗談めく (to sound like a joke). Careful: it cannot be combined freely!
examples[].german: The wind grew warmer, and spring was in the air.
His ironic-sounding way of putting things bothered me.
The weather has started to feel like spring.
His story seems mysterious.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the spring-like change that has taken place.
ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
ます is not attached to the completed past form.

en.explanation: AもVばBもV lines up two facts of the same kind, usually to stress versatility or contrasts: "He sings, and he dances too." Common in the fixed form ～もあれば～もある ("there are ... and there are also ..."). Neutral to slightly elevated; in conversation and in texts.
en.formation: Noun A + も + Verb/Adjective (ば-form) + Noun B + も + Verb/Adjective; fixed: ～もあれば～もある
en.notes: Unlike the conditional ～ば, ば here expresses no condition but links two parallel statements. ～も～し～も (N4) means the same but is more colloquial. ～も～なら～も (N2) looks similar but is a reproach aimed at both sides.
examples[].german: In life there are good times and bad times.
He sings, and he dances too.
At this place the prices are low, and the food is good too.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: どころか reverses an expectation; here good and bad times stand side by side as equals.
くせに is reproachful ("even though") and does not fit a neutral piece of life wisdom.
あまり ("out of sheer") requires a feeling or an excess as the cause.

en.explanation: も同然だ expresses that something is not yet formally the case but in fact might as well be: "It's as good as won." Stronger and more vivid than ～と同じだ. Neutral; often in conversation and in sports and business reports. Attributive: も同然の + noun.
en.formation: Noun + も同然だ / Verb (た-form) + も同然だ; Noun + も同然の + Noun
en.notes: ～のようだ/～みたいだ only compare outward appearance ("like"); も同然, by contrast, claims that the difference practically no longer matters. ～に等しい means the same but is more literary. ～かのようだ (N2) describes an appearance that does not match reality.
examples[].german: Now that we've come this far, we've as good as won the title.
We've lived together for over ten years – he's practically family.
The car was so old that it was being sold for next to nothing.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: たばかりだ means "have only just" and does not fit the condition ここまで来れば.
たことはない ("have never") contradicts the confident conclusion.
にすぎない ("merely") downplays the victory and does not fit the conclusion.

en.explanation: もかまわず describes someone doing something without regard for something one would normally pay attention to: other people's eyes, costs, rain. Usually critical, from the speaker's point of view about third parties. It follows nouns or clauses nominalized with の.
en.formation: Noun + もかまわず / Verb (plain form) + の + もかまわず
en.notes: Unlike ～にもかかわらず ("although, despite"), which neutrally states a contrast, もかまわず emphasizes a person's lack of consideration. ～を問わず ("regardless of categories such as age") contains no judgment. ～をよそに (N1) is similar but more written-style.
examples[].german: Without caring who was watching, she burst out crying loudly.
Not caring that they were getting wet in the rain, the children kept playing outside.
There are people who talk loudly on the phone on the train with no regard for how they bother others.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を問わず is used with categories such as age or gender, not with something you should be considerate of.
に沿って means "along, in line with"; you don't cry in line with other people's looks.
に応じて means "in accordance with" and contradicts the inconsiderate behavior.

en.meaning: X is no better than Y; both are equally (bad)
en.explanation: AもAならBもB criticizes two parties equally: "A is no better than B"; both are in the wrong. In the fixed form, the same noun is repeated (親も親なら子も子だ). Colloquial and clearly reproachful.
en.formation: Noun A + も + Noun A + なら + Noun B + も + Noun B + だ
en.notes: Don't confuse it with ～も～ば～も (neutral listing: 歌も歌えば踊りもする), which can also be positive. も～なら～も is almost always a reproach aimed at both sides. Similar in meaning, but more neutral: どっちもどっちだ ("both are equally to blame").
examples[].german: The husband breaks his promises, but the wife who says nothing about it is no better.
The parent is no better than the child: neither of them even says hello.
The people selling it are no better than the people buying it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: から cannot attach to the repetition 夫も夫; the copula is missing.
ほど marks a degree and does not link two equal reproaches.
ばかりか escalates from one member to the next instead of judging both equally.

en.explanation: もしない stresses, with indignation or disappointment, that someone does not even attempt something that would be a matter of course: "He didn't even look at it." も goes between the ます-stem and しない. Judgmental, mostly about other people; polite もしません, connective もせず(に).
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + もしない / もしないで / もせず(に)
en.notes: Plain ～ない only states a fact; もしない additionally expresses criticism or disappointment. ～ようとしない (N2) stresses a lack of will over a longer period, もしない the failure to do even the simplest things. ～さえしない means the same but is even more emphatic.
examples[].german: He objected without even listening to what I had to say.
My son won't even eat the food I cook.
She left the room without even looking our way.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The affirmative form ("even listened") contradicts "without listening".
がち describes a tendency and does not combine meaningfully with a one-time objection.
ぬく means "to see something through to the end" and contradicts "without listening".

en.explanation: ものだから gives a reason and is often used as an excuse or justification. The speaker explains why something happened.
en.formation: Verb/い-adj + ものだから / な-adj + な + ものだから / noun + な + ものだから
en.notes: Colloquially also もんだから. Justifying tone.
examples[].german: The roads were congested, so I ended up being late.
It was so delicious that I ate too much.
I was in a hurry, so I forgot something.
It was my first time, so I messed up.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を and から do not form a reason connection here.
ます cannot be attached to the copula だ.
The nominal reason connection is ものだから.

en.meaning: one doesn't do that, one shouldn't
en.explanation: ものではない after the dictionary form states a general norm or rule of life: "That's not something you do." Often used as a warning or piece of advice from older people to younger ones. In speech often もんじゃない; it sounds preachy.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + ものではない / もんじゃない
en.notes: ～べきではない expresses a rather logical or moral obligation, ものではない a generally accepted custom ("that's not done"). Don't confuse it with ～たものではない ("can't possibly": 食べられたものではない) or ～というものではない ("not necessarily").
examples[].german: You shouldn't speak ill of others.
You shouldn't go out alone late at night.
One should not read other people's letters without permission.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ものなら introduces a condition and cannot end the sentence.
ものの is concessive and requires a following main clause.
ものだから gives a reason and requires a following main clause.

en.explanation: ものか expresses strong negation or determination. The speaker flatly refuses.
en.formation: Verb dictionary form / い-Adj + ものか / もんか (colloquial)
en.notes: Colloquial: もんか. Strong emotional rejection.
examples[].german: I'm never going to a shop like that again!
There's no way I'm going to lose!
I'm never going to a place like that again!
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This states a typical characteristic instead of a firm refusal.
ます cannot be attached to this particle combination.
The rhetorical question uses ものか without な.

en.explanation: ながらも expresses a contradiction: despite a certain quality or situation, something contrary exists. Emphasizes the contrast.
en.formation: Verb ます-stem + ながらも / い-Adj + ながらも / Noun + ながらも
en.notes: ながら (simultaneously) vs. ながらも (although): a difference in meaning!
examples[].german: Although it's small, it's a cozy room.
Unfortunately, I can't take part this time.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a concessive link here.
ます cannot be attached to ながら.
な does not link to 居心地のいい部屋だ here.

en.explanation: ないかぎり names the only condition under which a situation would change: "As long as X doesn't happen, Y stays the same." The main clause usually describes something negative or unchanging. Neutral to formal; typical in warnings, rules and assessments.
en.formation: Verb (ない-form) + かぎり / 限り; Noun + でない限り
en.notes: ～ないことには (N3) is similar, but there the main clause is almost always negative ("without X, it won't work"). ないかぎり can also have a positive main clause (雨が降らない限り行われる). The affirmative ～限り (N3), by contrast, means "as long as / as far as": 元気な限り働きたい.
examples[].german: Unless he makes an effort himself, his grades won't improve.
Unless it rains, the match will go ahead as planned.
Please don't call this number unless it's an emergency.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ないものの is concessive ("although not ..., still"); there is no contrast between not making an effort and poor grades.
とたん requires the た-form of an affirmative verb and describes a moment, not a condition.
ついでに links a side action to a main action; not doing something offers no "opportunity".

en.meaning: isn't there some way to, can't one somehow
en.explanation: ないものか expresses a strong wish that something might be possible. The speaker is desperately looking for a solution.
en.formation: Verb-ない形 + ものか / ものだろうか
en.notes: Rhetorical; expresses frustration and a wish.
examples[].german: Can't this be done more easily somehow?
Isn't there something that can be done about it?
Isn't there some way to solve this?
Couldn't this be done more easily somehow?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ます cannot be attached to this particle combination.
The wishful question uses ものか without な.
ます cannot be attached to the question particle.

en.meaning: in one's own way, within one's means
en.explanation: なりに acknowledges that someone acts in their own way within the (limited) scope of their abilities, age or position: "Children worry in their own way." Often with 自分なり, 子どもなり, 私なり. Attributive: なりの + noun. Neutral to approving.
en.formation: Noun / Verb・い-adjective (plain form) + なりに / なりの + Noun
en.notes: ～にしては ("considering that") expresses surprise at a deviation; なりに, by contrast, expresses recognition within limits. ～らしく means "as befits X" (an ideal image), なりに "as well as X can". Do not confuse with ～なり (N1, "as soon as") or ～なり～なり ("either ... or").
examples[].german: Children, too, worry about the family in their own way.
This is the result of my thinking it over as hard as I could, in my own way.
Cheap shops have their own particular merits.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: にしては expects a deviation from the norm; "children for children" makes no comparison.
ばかりに names the cause of a regrettable result and does not fit the repetition 子どもは子ども.
をめぐって requires a point of dispute and does not fit 心配している.

en.explanation: ねばならない is the written, somewhat old-fashioned equivalent of ～なければならない: "absolutely must". It sounds determined and solemn; typical of speeches, editorials, literature and mottos. ねばならぬ sounds even more archaic. する becomes せねばならない.
en.formation: Verb (ない-stem) + ねばならない / ねばならぬ (する → せねばならない)
en.notes: Same meaning as ～なければならない (N5), but with a literary, determined ring – in casual conversation it sounds theatrical. ～ざるを得ない (N2), on the other hand, means "cannot help but", i.e. a reluctant necessity. Note: する becomes せねば, not しねば.
examples[].german: We must tackle this problem seriously.
Promises must be kept.
I must finish this report by tomorrow.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ならない cannot attach directly to the ない-form; なければ or ねば is needed.
The obligation construction requires the negative form ならない.
ずじまいだ regrets a missed chance ("in the end, never") and does not express an obligation.

en.meaning: to correspond to, to be equivalent to
en.explanation: に当たる expresses that something corresponds to a certain category or is equivalent to a certain concept.
en.formation: Noun + に当たる
examples[].german: Japan's "Obon" corresponds to Germany's "Allerheiligen" (All Saints' Day).
She is the company president's daughter (she stands in that relationship to him).
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: る cannot be attached to ます.
The verb form is not built this way.
This negates the stated correspondence.

en.explanation: にあたって is used to introduce an important event or special occasion on which special measures are taken or words are spoken.
en.formation: Noun / verb (dictionary form) + にあたって / にあたり / にあたっての + noun
en.notes: Formal; common in speeches and on official occasions.
examples[].german: At the start of the new year, I set myself some goals.
On the occasion of our departure, I would like to express my thanks to all of you.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The attributive form does not connect to 目標を立てた here.
The occasion is marked with に here.
The finite form ends the sentence instead of linking the occasion.

en.explanation: に反して expresses that something goes against what was expected or planned, or against a rule. The result is different from what was expected.
en.formation: Noun + に反して / に反する + noun / に反した + noun
examples[].german: Contrary to expectations, we won the game.
He acted against his parents' expectations.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The attributive form does not connect to the following clause here.
The polite finite form does not link the clauses here.
反する requires に for what it refers to.

en.explanation: にほかならない strongly emphasizes that something is exactly that and nothing else. It expresses conviction and emphasis.
en.formation: Noun + にほかならない / ～からにほかならない
en.notes: Very formal and emphatic.
examples[].german: Our success is nothing other than the result of hard work.
That is nothing other than his talent.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the identification instead of expressing "nothing other than".
The polite negative is not formed with ますない.
The fixed identification requires に.

en.explanation: に限らず expresses that something applies not just to one particular thing but to others as well. Broader than だけでなく.
en.formation: Noun + に限らず
examples[].german: This problem isn't limited to Japan; it's happening all over the world.
Not only men but also women can take part.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This limits the problem to Japan, the very opposite.
This asserts a limitation instead of denying it.
The scope is marked with に.

en.explanation: に限り explicitly limits a rule or offer to a particular group, time or condition: "only for X". Typical in advertising, notices and terms and conditions (本日に限り). Formal; the main clause usually describes a benefit or an exception.
en.formation: Noun + に限り / に限って (in this meaning)
en.notes: Distinguish it from ～に限って in the sense of "of all times" (忙しい日に限って…): there, annoyance comes through; with に限り it doesn't. ～に限らず is the opposite ("not only"). ～に限る at the end of a sentence means something else again: "there's nothing like".
examples[].german: Today only, everything is 20% off.
Only the first 50 people will receive a commemorative gift.
Only members can use the parking lot free of charge.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: にわたって requires a span of time; a single day is not a span.
にかけて requires a period with a starting point (～から～にかけて).
に先立って means "prior to"; the discount does not apply before today.

en.explanation: に限って expresses surprise or frustration that something unexpected happens with one particular person or in one particular situation, of all things.
en.formation: Noun + に限って
en.notes: Often used with negative surprise or irony.
examples[].german: It always rains on the very days I don't have an umbrella with me.
My child, of all people, would never do such a thing.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The attributive form does not connect to 雨が降る here.
The reference to 日 requires に here.
The finite form ends the sentence instead of linking the circumstance.

en.meaning: to depend on, to rest on
en.explanation: にかかっている expresses that a result depends decisively on one factor or person: "Success depends on your effort." It stresses the responsibility and weight of that factor. Neutral; common in speeches, sports and business, often with ～かどうかは.
en.formation: Noun + にかかっている; question clause + か(どうか) + にかかっている
en.notes: ～次第だ means the same but is more concise (努力次第だ). ～によって (N4) neutrally describes a dependence or variation (国によって違う); にかかっている stresses that everything hinges on this one factor. Do not confuse with ～にかかわる (N2, "to concern, to be at stake": 命にかかわる).
examples[].german: Whether we can win the match depends on the players' efforts.
The company's future depends on whether this new product sells.
Whether you pass depends on the coming month.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: に過ぎない ("merely") downplays something and does not name a dependence.
に違いない expresses a guess; "whether we win is surely the players' effort" makes no sense.
にわたる requires a span of time or space.

en.meaning: to concern, to be related to, to be at stake
en.explanation: にかかわる expresses that something is closely connected with an important matter or affects it.
en.formation: Noun + にかかわる
en.notes: Often used with serious, important topics.
examples[].german: It's a matter of life and death.
It's a situation that affects the company's reputation.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The affected area needs に.
The stem form cannot modify 問題 attributively here.
る cannot be attached to ます.

en.meaning: when it comes to ..., as far as ... is concerned
en.explanation: にかけては emphasizes that someone is especially good or outstanding in a particular area.
en.formation: Noun + にかけては
en.notes: Always positive; highlights a strength.
examples[].german: When it comes to cooking, there's no one who can beat him.
When it comes to speed, she's the best on the team.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This makes cooking the object of かける instead of the area of skill.
は cannot attach to the dictionary form here.
は cannot attach to the polite form here.

en.meaning: in response to, in order to meet
en.explanation: にこたえて expresses that you respond to an expectation, request or demand and meet it.
en.formation: Noun + にこたえて / にこたえる + Noun
examples[].german: In response to our customers' feedback, we developed a new product.
I'll do my best to live up to your expectations.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The cause of the response needs に here.
The attributive form does not link the following clause here.
The finite form ends the sentence instead of attaching the cause.

en.explanation: に加えて expresses that something more is added to something already there. It emphasizes the addition.
en.formation: Noun + に加えて / に加え
examples[].german: In addition to Japanese, I'm also studying Chinese.
In addition to the rain, there's a strong wind blowing too.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The attributive form does not link 中国語も here.
This makes Japanese the thing being added instead of the starting point of the addition.
ます is not attached to the dictionary form.

en.meaning: there are limits; ... really goes too far
en.explanation: にもほどがある criticizes something for exceeding the tolerable limit: "Even X has its limits!" – for example with jokes, cheekiness or carelessness. Strongly emotional and reproachful; mostly spoken, but also written in comments and letters to the editor.
en.formation: Noun / い-adjective (dictionary form) / な-adjective (stem) + にもほどがある
en.notes: ～すぎる only describes an excess; にもほどがある adds the speaker's indignation. ～極まりない (N1) belongs to written language and mainly follows Sino-Japanese な-adjectives (失礼極まりない). Do not confuse with ～ほど (N4, degree/comparison).
examples[].german: Showing up three hours late – that's outrageously rude!
There's a limit to joking around!
Cheap or not, quality this bad is going too far.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: に越したことはない ("it would be best") recommends something and does not fit the indignation.
に限る ("nothing beats") recommends something; rudeness is not being recommended.
にかけては requires a field of expertise and a main clause about special abilities.

en.meaning: toward, in preparation for; aimed at
en.explanation: に向けて names a goal that an action is directed toward: in time (the Olympics, an exam), in content (a solution, reconstruction) or as an addressee (若者に向けて発信する). Common in the news, speeches and corporate language; attributively as に向けた + Noun.
en.formation: Noun + に向けて / に向け / に向けた + Noun
en.notes: ～に向かって tends to describe a physical direction or stance (海に向かって叫ぶ), whereas に向けて describes a goal being pursued or a target group. ～向け (N3) is a suffix for target groups (子供向けの本) and attaches directly to the noun without に.
examples[].german: I'm practicing every day for next month's match.
The government announced new measures toward solving the problem.
The company president sent a message to the employees.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: にわたって requires a span of time or space; a single match is not a span.
に沿って means "along, in line with" (a plan, a guideline), not "in preparation for an event".
に反して means "contrary to" and makes no sense with the training.

en.meaning: on the occasion of, at the time of (a special occasion)
en.explanation: に際して marks a special, usually one-time occasion at or before which something is done: an opening, signing a contract, a departure. Very formal; typical of speeches, instructions and announcements. に際し is even more written-style.
en.formation: Noun + に際して / に際し / に際しての + Noun; Verb (dictionary form) + に際して
en.notes: Similar to ～にあたって, but even more formal and more strongly tied to the moment of the occasion; にあたって tends to emphasize preparing for a task. ～際に is more neutral and can also be used for everyday things (お降りの際に). For routine actions like 食事に際して, に際して sounds exaggerated.
examples[].german: Before using this, please read the following precautions.
Before going to study abroad, I had a long talk with my parents.
At the opening of the new factory, the mayor gave a speech.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: に対して marks a counterpart or a contrast, not an occasion.
にわたって requires a span of time or space; ご利用 is not a span.
に応じて means "in accordance with"; the precautions do not depend on the extent of use.

en.explanation: にせよ/にしろ acknowledges different possibilities but says the outcome stays the same in any case.
en.formation: Verb plain form / Noun + にせよ / にしろ / AにせよBにせよ
en.notes: にせよ is more formal, にしろ is more colloquial.
examples[].german: Whether you're for or against it, please give your opinion.
Whatever the reason, being late is not good.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The concessive link needs にしろ or にしても here.
This makes 何 the object of a command instead of expressing "whatever".
The verb form is not built this way.

en.meaning: from the point of view of, for (someone)
en.explanation: にしたら/にすれば puts itself in the position of a person or group and describes their feelings or point of view: "For X, this is (surely) ...". Usually about other people, often with a guess (だろう). Neutral; にしてみれば emphasizes putting yourself in their shoes even more strongly.
en.formation: Noun (person/group) + にしたら / にすれば / にしてみれば
en.notes: ～にとって describes a general evaluation (important/difficult for X) and is used for things and people; にしたら emphasizes empathizing with a person and is almost only used with people. Don't confuse it with ～にしては ("for, considering that ...") or with ～としたら (hypothetical condition).
examples[].german: For the kids, going to cram school every day must be tough.
For parents, their children's future is simply their biggest worry.
Even a service that's convenient for tourists can be a nuisance for local residents.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: にしては expresses a departure from expectations ("considering they're kids"), not a point of view.
に対して marks a counterpart; the cram school is not being evaluated toward the children.
にかけては requires a field in which someone excels.

en.meaning: even if, even though, even for
en.explanation: にしても concedes a possibility but says that the outcome still doesn't change, or expresses that something is surprising.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) / noun + にしても
examples[].german: Even if you're busy, you should eat properly.
Even as a joke, that's going too far.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a concessive connection here.
The connection requires the て-form before も.
The polite form is not combined with も here.

en.explanation: に相違ない expresses a firm conviction based on evidence: "It cannot be otherwise." Same meaning as ～に違いない, but clearly more written-style and stiffer; typical of reports, crime novels, news and formal letters.
en.formation: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + に相違ない / な-adjective・Noun + (である) + に相違ない
en.notes: In content it is like ～に違いない (N3), but in everyday conversation に相違ない sounds stilted. ～に決まっている, by contrast, is colloquial and more subjective. On official forms you come across the related formula 上記の通り相違ありません ("The above information is correct").
examples[].german: Judging from the fingerprints left at the scene, he is without a doubt the culprit.
With his ability, he is certain to pass.
There must without a doubt have been some kind of deal between the two parties.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: に過ぎない plays something down ("merely") and does not express certainty.
にかかわらず means "regardless of" and cannot end a sentence.
に越したことはない means "it would be best to" and does not fit a conclusion drawn from evidence.

en.explanation: にすぎない downplays the importance of something. It expresses that something is less important, or less, than one might think.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) / noun + にすぎない
en.notes: A modest or understating expression.
examples[].german: This is merely my personal opinion.
It has only just begun, nothing more.
That's nothing more than a rumor.
I'm just a student.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This does not create the limiting meaning "merely".
ない does not take an attached ます.
The link to the noun requires に here.

en.explanation: にとどまらず expresses that something does not stop at one point but spreads beyond it.
en.formation: Noun + にとどまらず
en.notes: Formal. Similar to に限らず, but emphasizes spreading.
examples[].german: This problem is not limited to one country; it is affecting the whole world.
His activities go beyond his home country and are spreading abroad as well.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This asserts a limitation instead of going beyond it.
This asserts a limitation in the past.
With とどまる, the scope needs に.

en.explanation: につけ expresses that a certain trigger repeatedly brings up the same feeling or thought, especially with 見る・聞く・思う. Set phrase: 何かにつけて ("at every opportunity"). As AにつけBにつけ, it means "whether A or B, in either case".
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + につけ(て) / Noun + につけ(て); Aにつけ Bにつけ (pairs of opposites)
en.notes: Unlike ～たびに, which neutrally counts each repetition, につけ almost always links the trigger with an inner reaction (思い出す, 感じる, 心配になる); with pure actions like 行くにつけ it sounds unnatural. Don't confuse it with ～につれて (proportional change: 年をとるにつれて).
examples[].german: Whenever I look at this photo, I'm reminded of my hometown.
He complains at every opportunity.
Rain or wind, my mother is always worrying about the field.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: とたん requires the た-form (見たとたん) and describes a single moment, not a repetition.
あげく follows the た-form and marks a bad end result, not a recurring memory.
ものの is concessive ("although ..., still"); there is no contrast between the photo and the memory.

en.explanation: につき has two meanings: 1) a formal reason on signs, notices and announcements (工事中につき = "due to construction work"), 2) distribution, "per, each" (一人につき3枚). The first meaning is typically written and official; in conversation you say ～ので or ～のため.
en.formation: Noun + につき (reason); quantity/Noun + につき + amount (per)
en.notes: Don't confuse it with ～について ("about, regarding"). As a reason, につき only follows nouns and sounds official; for personal reasons in everyday life it sounds stiff. In the meaning "per", it is interchangeable with ～あたり (一人あたり).
examples[].german: Today is our regular day off, so we are closed.
The participation fee is 1,000 yen per person.
This road is closed due to construction work.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: について means "about, regarding" and does not give a reason for the closure.
に対して marks a counterpart or a contrast, not a reason.
にかけて requires a period of time (～から～にかけて).

en.explanation: によっては highlights that under certain circumstances a particular, often unexpected or unfavorable result can occur: "Depending on the case, it may even be ..." Typical: 場合によっては, 人によっては. Neutral to formal; popular in notices and business texts.
en.formation: Noun + によっては
en.notes: Plain ～によって (N4, "depending on") describes general differences (国によって文化が違う); によっては singles out an individual case and often ends with ～こともある / ～場合がある. ～次第では is similar in meaning but stresses more strongly that the result depends on the factor.
examples[].german: Depending on the weather, the game may be canceled.
For some people, this medicine can cause drowsiness.
Depending on the circumstances, we may need to revise the contract.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: にとっては requires an affected person or group; the weather does not judge anything.
に対しては marks a counterpart; the game is not canceled toward the weather.
にしては expresses a deviation from expectations, not a condition.

en.explanation: のもとで expresses that something happens under certain conditions or under someone's guidance or influence.
en.formation: Noun + のもとで / のもとに
examples[].german: I did research under a famous professor.
I'm working under harsh conditions.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The setting of the research requires で here.
の requires a following noun instead of 研究を行った.
The link to the professor requires の.

en.explanation: 抜きで expresses that something is left out or excluded. Something takes place without a particular element.
en.formation: Noun + 抜きで / 抜きに / 抜きの + noun
en.notes: を抜きにして is an alternative form.
examples[].german: Let's talk without joking around (seriously).
I went out without breakfast.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: で is not attached to 抜く here.
The attributive form requires a noun.
This ends the sentence instead of modifying 話しましょう.

en.explanation: ぬきにして expresses that you deliberately leave out or set aside a particular aspect.
en.formation: Noun + (は)ぬきにして / ぬきにしても
examples[].german: Joking aside, let's talk seriously.
No flattery: it really is a wonderful work.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The expression uses ぬきにする.
The dictionary form does not link the following clause here.
The finite polite form ends the sentence.

en.meaning: after a long …, at the end of, finally
en.explanation: 末に expresses that after a long process, a lot of effort or deliberation, a result was finally reached.
en.formation: Verb-た形 + 末(に) / noun + の末(に)
en.notes: Emphasizes the long, hard process before the result.
examples[].german: After long discussions, an agreement was reached.
After much agonizing, I decided to change jobs.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not link the eventual result here.
末 is not a な-adjective here.
ます cannot be attached directly to 末.

en.explanation: たものではない (colloquially たもんじゃない) is a strongly negative judgment: something is so bad that you can't even bring yourself to do it, e.g. eat it or look at it. Usually used with the potential form (食べられた, 見られた). Emotional, mostly spoken language.
en.formation: Verb (potential form, た-form) + ものではない / もんじゃない
en.notes: Don't confuse it with ～ものではない without た (dictionary form), which expresses a norm ("one shouldn't do that": 人の悪口を言うものではない). たものではない is a subjective judgment about poor quality. Stronger and more emotional than ～わけがない or ～っこない.
examples[].german: This dish is so spicy that it's impossible to eat.
His handwriting is so messy that it's impossible to read.
I can't possibly let anyone hear a song sung this badly.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: たものだ recalls the past ("I often used to ...") and contradicts 辛すぎて.
たばかりだ means "just did" and does not fit とても and the judgment about the spiciness.
どころではない follows the dictionary form or a noun, not the た-form.

en.meaning: I would (really) like to ...; I do hope
en.explanation: たいものだ and てほしいものだ intensify a wish and give it a reflective, often solemn tone: "That is something I would truly wish for." Common with long-term wishes or with hopes directed at people in general. Often もんだ in speech.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + たいものだ / Verb (て-form) + ほしいものだ
en.notes: The ものだ forms (N3) have several functions: norm (するものだ), reminiscence (したものだ) and amazement. たいものだ belongs to the emotional meaning and must not be confused with the reminiscence form ～たものだ ("I often used to ..."). It is unsuitable for spontaneous, concrete wishes (水が飲みたい).
examples[].german: Even just once, I'd really love to see the northern lights.
I truly hope the children will cherish their own dreams.
I do hope the world becomes a peaceful place soon.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: たものだ recalls the past ("often used to") and contradicts 一度でいいから.
たがる describes a third person's wish, not one's own.
A statement about experience does not fit 一度でいいから ("even just once").

en.meaning: can't just keep doing ..., have to act differently
en.explanation: てばかりはいられない expresses that you cannot remain in a state forever and have to take action.
en.formation: Verb-て形 + ばかりはいられない / ばかりもいられない
examples[].german: I can't just keep crying. I have to move forward.
I can't just keep playing around; I should start working soon.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This affirms that it is possible to just keep crying.
ない does not take an attached ます.
After 泣い, this ongoing action needs the て-connection.

en.meaning: even if one has to ...; at any cost
en.explanation: てでも expresses strong determination: to reach a goal, one is ready to use even an extreme means – "if need be, even ...". The main clause usually contains a wish or intention (～たい, ～つもりだ, ～なければならない). Spoken and written.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + でも + wish / intention / obligation
en.notes: Counterpart of ～てまで: てまで often appears with criticism or negation ("I wouldn't go that far"), てでも with a positive intention ("I'd even ... for that"). Do not confuse with ～ても (N4, "even if"), which only concedes without expressing determination.
examples[].german: I want to keep this shop going, even if I have to borrow money.
I intend to protect my family, whatever it takes.
Even if I have to stay up all night, I've got to finish these documents by tomorrow.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: たきり ("and since then no longer") makes no sense with the wish to keep going.
あげく describes a bad result that has already occurred and cannot end with a wish (～たい).
とたん requires an event that happened immediately, not a wish in the main clause.

en.meaning: only after, for the first time through
en.explanation: てはじめて expresses that you only recognize or understand something for the first time through an experience.
en.formation: Verb-て形 + はじめて
examples[].german: It was only when I got sick that I understood the value of good health.
It was only after coming to Japan that I ate real sushi.
I ate sushi for the first time after coming to Japan.
Only after losing it did I realize how important it was.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The link to the moment of first realization needs the て-form.
The past form does not connect with 健康のありがたさが分かった here.
The finite polite form ends the sentence.

en.explanation: てからというもの emphasizes that a noticeable, lasting change has taken place since a particular event.
en.formation: Verb-て形 + からというもの
en.notes: Stronger and more emotional than ～て以来.
examples[].german: Ever since our child was born, every day has been hectic.
Ever since I came to Japan, I've been eating nothing but Japanese food.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The set phrase links the expression with と.
ます cannot be attached directly to もの.
な does not link a following clause here.

en.meaning: even going so far as to ...; at the cost of
en.explanation: てまで expresses that someone resorts to an extreme or inappropriate means to reach a goal: "even going as far as X". The speaker often views this critically or asks whether it is worth it (～てまで～たくない). Neutral, spoken and written.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + まで
en.notes: With nouns, plain まで is used ("even": 子どもまで知っている). てまで, by contrast, emphasizes the price you pay. ～てでも is similar but expresses determination more ("whatever it takes": 借金してでも行きたい), while てまで often comes with a negative or criticism.
examples[].german: I don't want to buy designer goods if it means going into debt.
He even stayed up all night to finish that job.
I don't want to make money if it means deceiving people.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: てこそ ("only when") positively highlights a necessary condition and does not fit the refusal.
てばかり requires a following いる and describes a habit.
たきり ("not since") makes no sense with the sentence expressing a wish.

en.meaning: to demonstrate; to show everyone, to be determined to
en.explanation: てみせる means 1) to demonstrate something or to put on a show of an attitude, 2) to announce with strong determination that you will manage something: "I'll prove it to you!". Meaning 2 uses the dictionary form, often with 必ず or きっと.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + みせる
en.notes: Don't confuse it with ～てみる ("to try"): with てみる the outcome is open, whereas てみせる in meaning 2 is a self-confident announcement to others. The determination meaning is limited to the first person; みせる always presupposes an (imagined) audience.
examples[].german: I'm definitely going to pass the next exam: I'll show everyone.
The teacher actually demonstrated how to cook the dish.
He put on a calm face, but he must really have been scared.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: てある requires a transitive verb and describes a state, not a resolution.
ておく means "to do in advance" and does not fit passing an exam.
てばかりいる describes a constant habit and does not fit 次の試験 and 必ず.

en.explanation: てしょうがない expresses that a feeling is so strong that you can't do anything about it. More colloquial than てならない.
en.formation: Verb-て形 / い-Adj-くて + しょうがない / な-Adj + で + しょうがない
en.notes: しかたがない is the more formal version. Colloquial: しょうがない.
examples[].german: I'm so hungry I can't stand it.
I can't stop thinking about it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ない needs が here instead of を.
ない does not take an attached ます.
The connection after 空い needs the て-form.

en.meaning: can't keep on, can't afford to
en.explanation: てはいられない expresses that you cannot continue a certain state because the situation does not allow it.
en.formation: Verb-て形 + はいられない / てもいられない
examples[].german: I can't wait forever.
I can't afford to take it easy; the deadline is close.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This affirms that it is possible to keep waiting.
ない does not take an attached ます.
After 待っ, this connection needs the て-form.

en.explanation: てはならない expresses a strict prohibition or a moral duty to refrain from something: "This must not happen." More formal and more general than ～てはいけない – typical of laws, rules, speeches and editorials. In speech it sounds solemn or preachy.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + はならない / はなりません
en.notes: Easily confused with ～てならない (N3, without は): 心配でならない means "I'm terribly worried" and expresses an uncontrollable feeling. てはならない, by contrast, is a prohibition. In everyday life ～てはいけない is enough; てはならない sounds like a principle.
examples[].german: We must never forget this tragedy.
The content of the meeting must not be leaked to outsiders.
Human life must not be treated lightly.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 決して requires a negation; てもかまわない gives permission.
てたまらない expresses an unbearable feeling and does not fit 決して.
決して requires a negation; てばかりいる describes a habit.

en.meaning: at the same time as, simultaneously
en.explanation: と同時に expresses that two things happen at exactly the same time, or that something has two qualities at once.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) / verb-た形 / noun + と同時に
examples[].german: The moment the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.
He is a doctor and at the same time also a writer.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not link simultaneous events here.
な does not link a following clause here.
ます cannot be attached to 同時.

en.explanation: といっても qualifies a previous statement: what was said is true, but it is not as extreme as you might think.
en.formation: Sentence (plain) + といっても
en.notes: Corrects a possible exaggeration in the previous statement.
examples[].german: I can speak Japanese, but only enough for greetings.
It may be called spacious, but it's only six tatami mats.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The quoted content needs と.
The concessive link needs 言っても.
も is not attached to the polite form here.

en.meaning: ... or ..., or rather; how shall I put it
en.explanation: というか～というか lines up two spontaneous descriptions because neither alone seems accurate enough: "It was – bold, or maybe reckless." Expresses hesitation or amazement; the sentence often ends with a summarizing judgment. Colloquial.
en.formation: Noun / な-adjective (stem) / Verb・い-adjective (plain form) + というか + same + というか
en.notes: ～やら～やら (N2) lists several things or feelings side by side ("what with ... and ..."); というか～というか searches for the right description of a single thing. A single ～というか makes a vague correction ("or rather"), similar to ～というより. More formal: ～といおうか～といおうか.
examples[].german: His behavior was bold, or maybe reckless – anyway, I was stunned.
The food at that place is nostalgic, or maybe simple – somehow it's a comforting taste.
I was surprised, or maybe appalled – either way, I was at a loss for words.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: にしろ～にしろ would have to appear in both parts; mixed with というか it is ungrammatical.
After a な-adjective, だけに would need な (大胆なだけに), and it gives a reason, not a description.
After a な-adjective, だからといって would be needed, and it requires a negated conclusion.

en.explanation: ということだ has two meanings: 1) hearsay (I've heard that), 2) conclusion (so that means).
en.formation: Sentence (plain) + ということだ
en.notes: Hearsay or logical conclusion, depending on context.
examples[].german: I hear he's getting married next month.
So that means everyone agrees, right?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The reported content takes と.
ます cannot be attached directly to こと.
The attributive な-form does not end the sentence here.

en.meaning: it is not necessarily the case that
en.explanation: というものではない rejects a simplified or absolute statement. Reality is more complex.
en.formation: Verb plain form / い-Adj / な-Adj + というものではない
en.notes: Corrects an overly simple view.
examples[].german: Having money doesn't automatically make you happy.
Eating a lot isn't necessarily a good thing.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This confirms the equation instead of rejecting it.
ない does not take an attached ます.
The quoted content needs と.

en.meaning: that doesn't mean that; it's not that
en.explanation: というわけではない denies an obvious conclusion. You correct a misunderstanding or a hasty assumption.
en.formation: Sentence (plain form) + というわけではない
en.notes: Extended form of わけではない. Especially used with conclusions.
examples[].german: Just because you live in Japan doesn't mean your Japanese is perfect.
It's not that I'm against it, but I'd like to think about it a little more.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This confirms the conclusion instead of qualifying it.
ない does not take an attached ます.
The nominal negation requires ではない.

en.explanation: とみえる infers a guess from an observed fact: "Evidently ..." The clue is usually stated directly. Literary/narrative in style; with とみえて, the guess and the observed result are linked ("apparently ..., since ...").
en.formation: Sentence (plain form) + とみえる / とみえて / とみえ
en.notes: ～らしい / ～ようだ (N4) are neutral forms of conjecture; とみえる puts more stress on the visible clue and sounds more written. Unlike ～そうだ (appearance), とみえる follows complete sentences, often in the past. Do not confuse with the verb 見える ("to be visible").
examples[].german: Something good must have happened to him – he's been in a good mood all morning.
The children must be really tired. They're sound asleep.
It must have rained during the night – the road is wet.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: としても ("even if") concedes an assumption; the good mood would then be illogical.
とはいえ ("although ..., still") requires a contrast; a good mood after something nice is not one.
ばかりに names the cause of a regrettable result; a good mood is not regrettable.

en.meaning: I hear that; (someone) says to tell you that
en.explanation: とのことだ passes on information or a message you have received: "I've been told that ...". More polite and more formal than ～そうだ (伝聞); typical in business communication, emails and when passing on messages (田中さんから、遅れるとのことです).
en.formation: Sentence (plain form) + とのことだ / とのことです
en.notes: Unlike ～そうだ (hearsay), とのこと can also pass on requests and messages word for word and sounds more formal. ～ということだ (N2) can also express a conclusion ("that means, so"); とのことだ is only used for passing things on.
examples[].german: The department manager says he'll be a little late for the meeting.
According to the weather forecast, there will be heavy snow tomorrow.
The other party said they would like us to send the documents by tomorrow.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ことです without との expresses advice ("you should"), not a passed-on message.
ように cannot be closed directly with です.
とのことで requires a following clause and cannot end the sentence.

en.explanation: としたら sets up a hypothetical assumption and asks what would happen or be true in that case.
en.formation: Verb/い-Adj/な-Adj/Noun + だ + としたら / とすれば / とすると
en.notes: としたら/とすれば/とすると are largely interchangeable.
examples[].german: Supposing you won the lottery, what would you spend it on?
If what he says is true, that's a serious matter.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The assumed statement needs と.
The conditional form of する is したら.
The conditional is not formed with ますたら.

en.meaning: together with, along with, as well as
en.explanation: とともに has three meanings: 1) together with (a person/thing), 2) at the same time as a change, 3) as well as, and also.
en.formation: Noun + とともに / verb (dictionary form) + とともに
examples[].german: I spent a happy time together with my family.
Along with the development of technology, our lives have changed too.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form an accompaniment phrase here.
The attributive form requires a noun.
ます cannot be attached to ととも.

en.meaning: although, even though it is true that
en.explanation: とはいえ concedes a fact but adds contrasting or qualifying information. More formal than けど.
en.formation: Sentence (plain) + とはいえ / Noun + とはいえ
en.notes: Formal written language.
examples[].german: Although it's spring, there are still cold days.
Although I passed, I can't let my guard down.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The quoting link needs と.
The finite polite form does not form a concessive link here.
な cannot be attached to this combination.

en.meaning: although ..., still; even though it is said that
en.explanation: とはいうものの concedes a fact or statement and immediately qualifies it: "It's true that ..., but in reality ...". Also common at the start of a sentence as a conjunction. Written language and speeches; somewhat more formal than ～といっても.
en.formation: Noun / Sentence (plain form) + とはいうものの / というものの; sentence-initial: とはいうものの、～
en.notes: Very close to ～とはいえ (N2); とはいえ is more concise and somewhat more literary. ～ものの (N3) comes directly after a sentence without と(は)いう and concedes a fact of one's own. ～といっても rather stresses that something is less than expected ("a vacation – but only two days").
examples[].german: It may be spring, but mornings and evenings are still cold.
Although I've lived in Japan for ten years, I still find keigo difficult.
I've started a diet. That said, I can't give up sweets.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: というより corrects a description ("rather than"); "spring rather than cold" makes no sense.
After a noun, だからといって would be needed, and the main clause would have to deny a conclusion.
とすれば ("assuming that") is hypothetical and contradicts the actual cold.

en.explanation: Sentence-final とか passes on information one has heard, tentatively and in passing: "He's getting married, I hear." The speaker keeps a slight distance from whether it is true. Colloquial, but also common in polite conversation (～とかで / ～とか聞きました).
en.formation: Sentence (plain form) + とか / とかで / とか聞いた
en.notes: ～そうだ (伝聞, N4) passes on hearsay matter-of-factly; とか sounds vaguer and more casual, almost like "or something". Do not confuse with listing ～とか～とか (N4, "for example ... and ..."). ～とのことだ is the formal, precise equivalent.
examples[].german: I hear Mr. Tanaka is getting married next month.
Apparently the department manager is off with a cold, so today's meeting was postponed.
They say this summer is going to be hotter than usual.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ことか is an exclamation of amazement (どんなに～ことか) and does not pass on news.
ことに requires an emotion word before it and a clause after it.
ばかりか requires a following clause with も and cannot end the sentence.

en.meaning: just as, at the very moment when
en.explanation: ところに describes something unexpected happening at a particular moment (in the middle of an action, or just before or after it).
en.formation: Verb-ている / verb-た / verb-よう としている + ところに
en.notes: ところを = catching or interrupting someone in the middle of something.
examples[].german: Just as I was about to go out, a friend came over.
A phone call came while I was sleeping.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Two such case particles cannot be combined here.
な does not link 友達が来た here.
ます cannot be attached to ところ.

en.meaning: judging from the fact that ...; inferring from that
en.explanation: ところを見ると infers a guess from a concrete observation: "The way he's smiling, it must have gone well." The main clause usually ends with らしい, ようだ, に違いない or だろう. Neutral; spoken and written.
en.formation: Verb / い-adjective (plain form) + ところを見ると / ところからすると; main clause with らしい・ようだ・に違いない
en.notes: ～からすると (N2) names a general basis for a judgment (話し方からすると); ところを見ると requires a concretely observed action or situation. Do not confuse with ～ところを (N1, apologetic: お忙しいところを) or ～ところに ("just as").
examples[].german: Judging by how happy he looks, he seems to have passed the exam.
Since the lights are off, it looks like no one is here anymore.
Judging from the fact that he says nothing, he's probably against it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ところに ("just as") requires an event that comes along, not a guess.
In this meaning ところで follows the た-form ("even if") and does not fit らしい.
くせに ("even though", reproachful) requires a contrast; being happy and passing do not contradict each other.

en.explanation: ったら takes up a familiar person as the topic, someone the speaker is annoyed, puzzled or amused by: "My mother, honestly – she's always ...". Also used as an exclamation after a name (お母さんったら！). Very colloquial, typical among family and friends.
en.formation: Noun (usually a person) + ったら
en.notes: ～ときたら (N1) is similar, but almost always sharply critical and somewhat cruder; ったら can also sound affectionately exasperated. Do not confuse with the conditional ～たら or with ～ったら for emphasis in requests (早くしてったら！ "come on, hurry up!").
examples[].german: My mom, honestly – no matter how many times I tell her, she keeps telling the same stories.
That Tanaka, honestly – it looks like he got the meeting time wrong again.
Geez, big brother, honestly!
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ばかりか requires an escalation with も in the following clause, not a topic.
につき is an official way of giving a reason ("due to") and does not fit a complaint about one's mother.
をめぐって requires a dispute over something; the mother is the topic here, not the point of dispute.

en.meaning: doesn't count as, can hardly be called
en.explanation: うちに入らない downplays something: it doesn't meet the criteria to count as X: "That's not really X at all." Often used with amounts or achievements (料理, 運動, 残業), modestly or dismissively. Colloquial; うち here means "circle, range".
en.formation: Noun + の + うちに入らない / い-adjective・Verb (dictionary form) + うちに入らない
en.notes: Unlike ～に過ぎない ("nothing more than"), which classifies something matter-of-factly, うちに入らない expresses that something doesn't even reach the threshold of a category. Don't confuse it with ～うちに (N3, "while, as long as": 若いうちに).
examples[].german: Just walking for 30 minutes doesn't count as exercise.
What I make can hardly be called cooking.
Cold like this doesn't even count as cold.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The affirmative form contradicts くらいでは ("only this little").
に過ぎない comes directly after the noun, not after の.
最中だ means "right in the middle of" and does not fit the evaluation with くらいでは.

en.meaning: in addition to, on top of that, moreover
en.explanation: 上に expresses that something more is added to an existing quality or situation. Often used when piling up positive or negative points.
en.formation: Verb/い-adj + 上に / な-adj + な上に / noun + の上に / である上に
en.notes: Similar to し, but more formal. It strengthens the list.
examples[].german: This restaurant is cheap, and on top of that, the food is good.
It rained, and on top of that, the wind got stronger.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The additive connection is 上に.
上 does not need a な connection here.
The past-tense copula does not link the qualities here.

en.explanation: 上は expresses that, given an existing fact or decision, one should act accordingly. It implies determination.
en.formation: Verb-た形 / verb (dictionary form) + 上は
en.notes: Similar to からには and 以上は.
examples[].german: Now that I've taken it on, I intend to see it through to the end.
Once you've made a promise, you have to keep it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not form a conditional connection here.
な does not link to the following clause here.
This ends the sentence instead of linking the obligation.

en.meaning: to be possible / to be impossible
en.explanation: 得る (うる/える) expresses that something is possible, 得ない (えない) that it is impossible. Formal.
en.formation: Verb ます-stem + 得る(うる/える) / 得ない(えない)
en.notes: 得る can be read うる or える. 得ない is always read えない.
examples[].german: That kind of thing is impossible.
It's something that could quite possibly happen.
It's entirely possible that this could happen.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This asserts possibility instead of impossibility.
ない does not take an attached ます.
This combines two incompatible negative endings.

en.explanation: は別として takes a point or case out of the following statement: "X aside, ... holds true". Unlike with はともかく, X is not dismissed as unimportant but treated as a special case. Neutral to formal; often with question clauses (～かどうかは別として).
en.formation: Noun + は別として / は別にして; question clause + か(どうか) + は別として
en.notes: Close to ～はともかく: はともかく puts X aside as secondary, は別として objectively sets X apart as a special case. ～を除いて (N2) excludes an element from a set even more formally and typically appears with universal statements (全員, 毎日).
examples[].german: Apart from a few specialists, hardly anyone knows about this problem.
Whether you like it or not, this job has to be done.
Price aside, the design is flawless.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: はもちろん includes the specialists ("of course, and also") and contradicts ほとんどいない.
に限って singles out the specialists as "of all people" and makes no sense with the rest of the sentence.
をはじめ names the first example of a group that then does something together, not an exception.

en.meaning: it goes without saying; not to mention
en.explanation: は言うまでもない states that something is so obvious that it really wouldn't need to be mentioned. As は言うまでもなく it links something self-evident with a further example: "X of course, and also Y". Formal; typical in speeches and essays.
en.formation: Noun + は言うまでもない / は言うまでもなく; Sentence + の / こと + は言うまでもない
en.notes: The general form ～までもない (N1) means "there's no need to ..." and occurs with many verbs (説明するまでもない); は言うまでもない is the fixed, very common expression derived from it. ～はもちろん (N2) means the same as は言うまでもなく but is less formal.
examples[].german: It goes without saying that health is important.
He can speak French, not to mention English.
It goes without saying that in an earthquake it is important to make sure any fires are put out.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: はともかく requires a following main clause and cannot end the sentence.
The connective form requires a continuation with a further example.
はずがない cannot follow the topic marker は and would negate the statement.

en.explanation: はもちろん highlights that something goes without saying and adds that further things apply as well.
en.formation: Noun + はもちろん(、noun + も)
examples[].german: He can speak Japanese, of course, but English too.
I'm busy on weekends, of course, but on weekdays too.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: もちろん does not form an attributive な-connection here.
を cannot be attached to the emphasis here.
ます cannot be attached directly to もちろん.

en.meaning: not to mention; naturally … and beyond that
en.explanation: はもとより is the more formal version of はもちろん. It stresses that something goes without saying and that further things come on top of it.
en.formation: Noun + はもとより
en.notes: More formal than はもちろん. Mainly used in written language.
examples[].german: He is famous not only at home but abroad as well.
This hospital has not only good facilities but also highly qualified staff.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: な does not link the two areas here.
を does not link 海外でも here.
ます cannot be attached to もとより in this way.

en.explanation: はともかく deliberately sets one point aside in order to highlight the more important one: "X may be as it may; what matters is Y." Often used in evaluations (見た目はともかく味はいい). Neutral to slightly colloquial; はともかくとして is somewhat more formal.
en.formation: Noun + はともかく(として); question clause + か(どうか) + はともかく
en.notes: ～はさておき (N1) is very similar but is used more often to change the subject (それはさておき). ～はもちろん, by contrast, means "not only X but also Y" and includes X, whereas はともかく sets X aside. ～ならともかく means "if it were X, that would be one thing".
examples[].german: Looks aside, it tastes really good.
Regardless of the result, what matters is that you kept going until the end.
Whether or not it can actually be done, it's an interesting idea.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: はおろか escalates to an extreme and requires も/さえ, usually with a negative; that does not fit 味はとてもいい.
につき gives a formal reason ("due to"); the looks are not the reason for the taste.
をめぐって requires a dispute or discussion in the main clause.

en.meaning: there's no way that, it's impossible that
en.explanation: わけがない expresses a strong negation: it is absolutely impossible, or there's no logical reason, for something to be so.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) / い-adj + わけがない / な-adj + な + わけがない
en.notes: Colloquially: わけない. Shows the speaker's strong conviction.
examples[].german: There's no way he would do something like that.
