examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: しか requires a negative verb form.
へ does not mark an exclusive activity here.
から does not express "nothing but games" here.

en.explanation: べきだ: a strong recommendation or duty.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形) + べきだ
en.notes: する→すべき/するべき. Negative: ～べきではない.
examples[].german: You should keep your promises.
I should have said so sooner.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: No な is inserted after the verb.
The attributive form does not end the sentence here.
を does not come before this copula.

en.explanation: ～ちゃいけない is the spoken short form of ～てはいけない: ては becomes ちゃ, では becomes じゃ. You often hear it from parents, teachers or among friends. Even more casual is ～ちゃだめ. The meaning remains a clear prohibition.
en.formation: Verb (て-form): ～ては → ～ちゃ / ～では → ～じゃ + いけない / だめ
en.notes: て → ちゃ (食べては → 食べちゃ), で → じゃ (飲んでは → 飲んじゃ). Don't confuse it with ～ちゃう/～じゃう (← てしまう): 食べちゃった = ate it all up, 食べちゃいけない = must not eat. With ～なくちゃ (← なくては), on the other hand, you get "must": 食べなくちゃ.
examples[].german: You mustn't swim here.
You can't eat yet.
You mustn't play games until late at night.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 泳ぐ has the て-form 泳いで; では becomes じゃ, not ちゃ.
Permission would be ～でもいい; じゃいい is not a form.
The prohibition ends in いけない, not いかない.

en.explanation: だけでなく expresses that not just one thing applies, but another one as well.
en.formation: Noun/Verb/Adj + だけでなく ～も
en.notes: Casual: ～だけじゃなくて. Formal: ～のみならず.
examples[].german: I can speak not only Japanese but also Chinese.
It's not only cheap but also tasty.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: しか requires a negative ending.
の cannot connect to the following clause here.
This leaves the contrastive link to the additional language incomplete.

en.explanation: だろう (casual) and でしょう (polite): a supposition or expectation.
en.formation: Verb/Adj/Noun + だろう/でしょう
en.notes: でしょう? (with rising intonation) = right? / isn't it?
examples[].german: It will probably be sunny tomorrow.
He has probably gone home already.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The copula でした does not attach to a verb here.
ます is not attached to the dictionary form.
No な is inserted after the verb.

en.explanation: 出す as a suffix: the sudden start of an action.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + 出す
en.notes: Emphasizes the sudden start. Compare ～始める (start in general).
examples[].german: Suddenly it started to rain.
The baby suddenly started crying.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This marks the end rather than the beginning.
This negates the onset.
This is not a past form.

en.explanation: A noun of sensory perception + がする describes something you perceive involuntarily: 音がする (a sound can be heard), においがする (there's a smell), 味がする (it tastes of). The perception is the subject, marked with が – not the person perceiving it.
en.formation: 音 / 声 / におい / 味 / 感じ + がする; with a description in front: noun + の / adjective + perception noun + がする
en.notes: Typical nouns: 音, 声, におい (pleasant: 匂い, unpleasant: 臭い), 味, 香り, 感じ, 寒気 (chills), 吐き気 (nausea). With 気 you get ～気がする ("I have a feeling that …", N3). Comparison: 音が聞こえる emphasizes the hearing, 音がする the fact that a sound is there.
examples[].german: There's a nice smell coming from the kitchen.
A strange noise came from the next room.
This soup tastes of ginger.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Perceptions like におい take が with する, not を.
いる is only used for living beings, not for a smell.
で marks a place or means and does not make a sentence with します here.

en.explanation: がち: a (usually negative) tendency.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + がち / Noun + がち
en.notes: Behaves like a な-adj: ～がちな + noun.
examples[].german: Lately I tend to catch colds.
Mostly cloudy weather continues.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: A たい expression does not take だ.
An い-adjective does not take だ.
The adverbial form cannot come before だ.

en.explanation: がる: outward signs of a feeling in a third person.
en.formation: い-Adj (without い) + がる
en.notes: 欲しい→欲しがる, 怖い→怖がる. Godan verb.
examples[].german: The child is showing fear.
She wants new clothes.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The final い is dropped before がる.
This negates the fear being shown.
The て-form is 怖がって.

en.explanation: As a suffix, 始める expresses the beginning of an action.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + 始める
en.notes: Also a standalone verb: 始める = to begin.
examples[].german: It started to rain.
I started studying Japanese.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This marks the end rather than the beginning.
This negates the beginning.
The past is 始めた.

en.explanation: はずだ: a strong expectation or logical conclusion.
en.formation: Verb/い-Adj + はずだ / な-Adj + なはずだ
en.notes: はずがない = impossible.
examples[].german: It should have arrived by now.
He should know.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: No な is inserted after the verb.
This does not end the sentence here.
を does not come before this copula.

en.explanation: はずがない: a strong denial of a possibility.
en.formation: Verb/Adj (plain form) + はずがない
en.notes: Stronger than ～ないだろう. Opposite: ～はずだ (should be).
examples[].german: There's no way he would do something like that.
It can't possibly be this cheap.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This asserts an expectation rather than an impossibility.
No な is inserted after the verb.
The negation uses が, not を.

en.explanation: ほど～ない: a negative comparison.
en.formation: A は B ほど + Adj (ない形)
en.notes: Negative comparison. Positive: ～より～のほうが.
examples[].german: Tokyo is not as hot as Osaka.
Japanese is not as difficult as Chinese.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This claims Tokyo is hotter.
The negative form is 暑くない.
This does not negate the comparison.

en.explanation: ほど expresses degree or extent. Often used in comparisons and in ～ば～ほど (the more ..., the more ...).
en.formation: Verb (辞書形) + ほど / Noun + ほど
en.notes: ～ば～ほど = the more ..., the more .... Negative: ～ほど～ない = not as ... as.
examples[].german: I was so happy I wanted to cry.
The more you study, the more interesting it gets.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ながら follows the verb stem, not たい.
泣きたいすぎて is not a correct connection.
This makes the wish to cry the reason rather than the degree of happiness.

en.explanation: The imperative form is a direct command. It is rarely used in everyday speech and sounds rough.
en.formation: Godan: u→e (書く→書け) / Ichidan: る→ろ (食べる→食べろ)
en.notes: する→しろ, 来る→来い (こい). Often used for cheering someone on: 頑張れ! Negative form: ～な (するな = don't do it).
examples[].german: Hurry up!
Be quiet.
Go for it!
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This reports the past rather than giving an order.
This negates the action.
This is not an imperative form.

en.explanation: A question with a question word can be embedded in a larger sentence: plain form + か + 知っている / わかる / 教えてください. This works like English embedded questions with "what", "when" or "where" ("I don't know when it starts"). For questions without a question word, use ～かどうか.
en.formation: Question word … verb / い-adj (plain form) + か / … noun・な-adj (without だ) + か
en.notes: だ is dropped before か: 何が好きか (not *好きだか), 誰の傘か. A particle after か (を/が) is usually left out. The embedded part stays plain even in polite speech: not *何時に始まりますか知っていますか. Without a question word: 来るかどうかわからない.
examples[].german: Do you know what time the meeting starts?
Please tell me where I should buy a ticket.
I don't know yet who's coming.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: かどうか is only used for questions without a question word; here there's already 何時.
と quotes statements; a question with a question word needs か.
A verb in the plain form cannot take を directly.

en.explanation: かどうか: a yes/no question as a subordinate clause.
en.formation: Verb/Adj (plain form) + かどうか
en.notes: Questions with a question word: just か (何時に来るか分からない).
examples[].german: I can't decide whether to go.
Please check whether it's correct.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The embedded yes/no question begins with か.
が does not replace the embedding か.
No な is inserted after the verb.

en.meaning: to start to; to half do
en.explanation: かける: an action was started but not finished.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + かける
en.notes: 死にかける = to come close to death. 食べかけ = half-eaten.
examples[].german: I have a book I've started reading.
I started to say something and stopped.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 読みますの is not a suitable noun modifier here.
読みた is not a form of 読む.
読みかける would modify 本 directly, without の.

en.explanation: かな and かしら come at the end of a sentence and express wondering aloud: "I wonder if …". You are asking yourself rather than the other person, so it sounds soft and unobtrusive. かな is neutral; かしら sounds traditionally feminine and is less common today.
en.formation: Verb / い-adj (plain form) + かな / な-adj・noun (without だ) + かな; かしら works the same way
en.notes: With a negative, かな becomes an indirect wish: 早く来ないかな = If only he'd come soon! ～てくれないかな is a soft request. After nouns and な-adjectives, だ is dropped (学生かな, not *学生だかな). With superiors, it's better to use ～でしょうか.
examples[].german: I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.
I wonder if these clothes are a bit too flashy.
I wonder if Mr. Tanaka has arrived yet.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: だ cannot come directly after a verb like 晴れる.
The order is reversed; the ending is かな.
です cannot come directly after the dictionary form of a verb.

en.explanation: こそ is an emphatic particle that gives special emphasis to the word before it.
en.formation: Noun + こそ
en.notes: Very common: こちらこそ (likewise / the pleasure is mine).
examples[].german: Likewise, nice to meet you.
This year I really want to pass.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not express an emphatic reply.
へ marks a direction rather than "likewise".
しか does not fit the positive ending.

en.explanation: 辞書形 + ことがある: something happens occasionally.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形) + ことがある
en.notes: 辞書形 = sometimes. た形 = experience.
examples[].german: Sometimes I don't eat breakfast.
Occasionally I'm late.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ある does not take an object with を here.
No な is inserted after the verb.
This negates occasionally skipping it.

en.meaning: it has been decided that; it turns out that
en.explanation: ことになる expresses that a decision was made by others or that things turned out that way.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形/ない形) + ことになる
en.notes: ～ことになっている = an existing rule/arrangement.
examples[].german: It has been decided that I'll be transferred to Osaka starting next month.
It was decided that the meeting would be canceled.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: なる requires に here, not を.
This negates the decision that was made.
ます is not attached to なる.

en.explanation: ことにする expresses an active, personal decision.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形/ない形) + ことにする
en.notes: ～ことにしている = a regular habit based on your own decision.
examples[].german: I decided to go to Japan next year.
I decided not to eat sweets.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The decision construction requires に.
This negates the decision.
する forms the past tense した.

en.explanation: ことは～が: concedes something, but then qualifies it.
en.formation: Verb/Adj + ことは + Verb/Adj + が
en.notes: The same verb/adjective is repeated.
examples[].german: I did eat it, but it wasn't tasty.
It is expensive, but the quality is good.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the action that is explicitly conceded.
The concession requires は.
ので gives a reason rather than the conceded contrast.

en.explanation: くする (い-adj) and にする (な-adj): actively bringing about a change.
en.formation: い-Adj: い→くする / な-Adj: ～にする
en.notes: Compare ～くなる/～になる (to become, by itself).
examples[].german: I made the room brighter.
Please tidy up the room.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Before する, an い-adjective needs the く-form.
This negates making it brighter.
This is not a past form of する.

en.explanation: までに: a deadline by which something has to be done.
en.formation: Point in time/Verb (辞書形) + までに
en.notes: までに = by (deadline). まで = until (continuously).
examples[].german: Please hand in the report by Friday.
Let's buy our tickets before the train comes.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means from Friday on rather than by Friday at the latest.
This means after Friday.
This means later than Friday.

en.meaning: as it is, in the state of
en.explanation: まま: a state remains unchanged.
en.formation: Verb (た形) + まま / Noun + のまま
en.notes: そのまま = as it is.
examples[].german: Don't come in with your shoes on.
I fell asleep with the light on.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ながら does not attach to 履いた.
履いたてから is not a valid verb connection.
No な is inserted after the verb.

en.explanation: みたいだ: the casual variant of ようだ.
en.formation: Verb/Adj/Noun + みたいだ
en.notes: Before nouns: みたいな, before verbs: みたいに.
examples[].german: It looks like it's going to rain.
That person seems to be a teacher.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: No な is inserted after the verb.
This form needs a following noun.
This form needs a following predicate.

en.explanation: など lists examples and implies that there are more. More formal than とか.
en.formation: Noun + など
en.notes: Casual variant: なんか. Often with や: AやBなど.
examples[].german: I like fruit such as apples and bananas.
Someone like me still has a long way to go.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: しか does not fit the positive predicate.
への would mark a destination rather than examples of fruit.
からの marks an origin rather than a set of examples.

en.explanation: ～ないといけない means "must" and is the most common way to say it in spoken Japanese. Literally: "If you don't do it, it won't do." It usually expresses a necessity arising from the concrete situation. In conversation いけない is often dropped: もう行かないと。
en.formation: Verb (ない-form) + と + いけない / いけません
en.notes: Instead of いけない you also hear だめ: 早く寝ないとだめだよ. The short form ～ないと without いけない sounds like a half-spoken thought – typical when reminding yourself or saying goodbye. Regulations and official texts tend to use ～なければならない.
examples[].german: I have to hand in the report by Friday.
It's already ten. I should be heading home soon.
In Japan, you have to take off your shoes before entering a house.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: なくてもいい means "don't have to" – the opposite of the statement.
ないでください asks someone not to do something; it does not express your own obligation.
と belongs between ない and いけない; ないは is ungrammatical.

en.explanation: ～なくてはいけない and ～なくてはならない mean "must" – literally "if you don't do it, it won't do". They mean the same as ～なければならない but sound a bit more conversational. いけない fits personal obligations better, ならない general rules.
en.formation: Verb (ない-form: ない → なくて) + は + いけない / ならない
en.notes: Spoken short form: ～なくては → ～なくちゃ (いけない), often shortened all the way: 行かなくちゃ! ～なきゃ (from ～なければ) is equivalent. The meaning stays the same; only the register changes: なければならない (written, official) > なくてはならない > なくてはいけない > ないといけない > なくちゃ/なきゃ (casual). Opposite: ～なくてもいい (don't have to).
examples[].german: I have to get up early tomorrow.
You have to take this medicine every day.
I've got to go home now.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 起きてはいけません is a prohibition ("must not get up"), not an obligation.
なくてもいい means "don't have to" – the opposite of the statement.
The obligation form is built on なくて; ないでは is ungrammatical here.

en.explanation: ～なきゃ is the spoken short form of ～なければ, and ～なくちゃ that of ～なくては. Usually the following いけない／ならない is dropped: 行かなきゃ = "I have to go". Only used in conversation with friends and family.
en.formation: Verb (ない-form: ない → なきゃ / なくちゃ) (+ いけない / ならない)
en.notes: Register from formal to casual: なければならない > なくてはいけない > ないといけない > なきゃ／なくちゃ. Opposite: ～なくてもいい (don't have to). Don't confuse it with ～ちゃいけない (must not).
examples[].german: It's already ten. I should get going home.
I have to write the report by tomorrow.
Oh, I have to buy milk.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 帰らない means "I won't go home" – a negation, not an obligation.
なくてもいい means "don't have to" and contradicts the hint about the late hour.
帰られる is passive/potential and expresses no necessity.

en.explanation: 直す as a suffix: repeating an action in order to improve it.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + 直す
en.notes: やり直す (to redo), 考え直す (to reconsider), 見直す (to look over again).
examples[].german: Please do it over again.
I rewrote this sentence.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The request requires the て-form.
ます cannot come before ください here.
This asks not to redo the action.

en.explanation: なら: picks up a topic and responds to what has been said.
en.formation: Verb/Adj/Noun + なら
en.notes: Often responds to information from the other person.
examples[].german: If you're going to Japan, I recommend Kyoto.
If it's fish you want, this restaurant is good.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 行くたら is not a conditional form.
行くれば is not a conditional form.
No な is inserted after 行く.

en.explanation: なさい is a more polite command form, often used by parents, teachers or superiors.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + なさい
en.notes: More polite than 命令形, but still authoritative. Only used toward people of lower status.
examples[].german: Go to bed early.
Do your homework.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: なさい follows the stem, not the dictionary form.
なさい does not follow the た-form.
This reports not sleeping rather than giving an instruction.

en.explanation: に対して expresses whom an action is directed at, or a contrast between two things.
en.formation: Noun + に対して
en.notes: Before a noun: ～に対する + noun (e.g. 学生に対する態度).
examples[].german: Please speak politely to customers.
My older brother likes sports, whereas my younger brother likes reading.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The attributive form needs a noun after it.
This marks a point of view, not the customers being addressed.
This marks a news source, not the people being spoken to.

en.meaning: for (from the point of view of)
en.explanation: にとって expresses from whose perspective something is judged.
en.formation: Noun + にとって
en.notes: Don't confuse with ～のために (for the purpose of). にとって = subjective perspective.
examples[].german: For me, family is the most important thing.
Kanji are difficult for foreigners.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This marks a quoted source of information rather than one's own standard of value.
の needs a following head noun here.
をとって is not the perspective construction.

en.explanation: について: indicates the topic that is being talked about.
en.formation: Noun + について
en.notes: Before a noun: ～についての + noun.
examples[].german: I'm researching Japanese culture.
Let's discuss this problem.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: の would modify a noun instead of the verb.
This marks a standard of value, not a research topic.
This names a source, not the topic being researched.

en.explanation: によると: indicates the source of a piece of information.
en.formation: Noun + によると
en.notes: Often with ～そうだ or ～ということだ.
examples[].german: According to the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow.
According to the news, there was an accident.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: の does not form a source expression before the following clause here.
A weather forecast is a source of information here, not a standard of value.
の needs a head noun.

en.meaning: by, by means of; depending on
en.explanation: によって has several meanings: means (by means of), the agent in the passive (by), and variation depending on the situation.
en.formation: Noun + によって
en.notes: Before a noun: ～による + noun. ～によると = according to.
examples[].german: This novel was written by Natsume Sōseki.
Culture differs from country to country.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: による modifies a noun, not the following verb.
This marks a perspective rather than the author.
This would make the author the subject matter of the novel.

en.explanation: As a suffix, にくい expresses that something is hard to do.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + にくい
en.notes: Conjugates like an い-adjective. Similar: ～づらい (with emotional difficulty).
examples[].german: This handwriting is hard to read.
These shoes are hard to walk in.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means easy to read.
An い-adjective does not end with だ.
だ does not go after the past of an い-adjective.

en.meaning: the reason is; it is ... that
en.explanation: のは～だ/からだ: emphasizing or explaining the reason.
en.formation: Clause + のは + Noun/Adj + だ/からだ
en.notes: Emphasizes the reason or the key element.
examples[].german: The reason I was late was the train.
The reason I was surprised was that the price was high.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not nominalize the clause as a topic.
に does not nominalize the clause as a topic.
After the verb, なは is not a valid connection.

en.explanation: のように (formal) and みたいに (casual) express a comparison.
en.formation: Noun + のように / Noun + みたいに
en.notes: Before a noun: のような/みたいな: 夢のような話 = a dreamlike story.
examples[].german: I want to fly through the sky like a bird.
He's playing like a child.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Before the verb, the adverbial form with に is needed.
After a noun, の is used here.
This does not form an adverbial comparison.

en.explanation: のに expressing purpose: says what something is needed for.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形) + のに + necessary/useful/etc.
en.notes: Don't confuse with ～のに (although). Here: purpose/use.
examples[].german: This book is useful for studying.
Learning Japanese takes time.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The verb clause first has to be nominalized.
The order is のに.
After the verb, なに does not express purpose here.

en.explanation: おかげで: a positive cause, expressing gratitude.
en.formation: Verb/Adj + おかげで / Noun + のおかげで
en.notes: Positive: おかげで. Negative: せいで.
examples[].german: Thanks to my teacher, I passed.
Thanks to the medicine, I got better.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means before the teacher, not thanks to them.
This means instead of the teacher, not thanks to them.
せいで assigns negative blame; the translation "thanks to" calls for positive appreciation.

en.explanation: As a suffix, 終わる expresses that an action has been brought to an end.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + 終わる
en.notes: Also standalone: 終わる = to end.
examples[].german: I finished reading the book.
I finished writing my homework.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This marks the beginning rather than the completion.
This negates the completion.
This is not a polite past form.

en.explanation: The potential form expresses ability or possibility. The object is often marked with が instead of を.
en.formation: Ichidan: ～られる / Godan: u→eru
en.notes: Godan: 書く→書ける, 読む→読める. Ichidan: 食べる→食べられる. する→できる, 来る→来られる. Colloquial: 食べれる (dropping the ra).
examples[].german: I can speak Japanese.
Can you read this kanji?
Can you come tomorrow?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the ability.
This reports an action rather than the ability.
ます is not attached to the dictionary form.

en.explanation: っぽい: casual; expresses that something gives the impression of something else.
en.formation: Noun/verb stem + っぽい
en.notes: Often slightly negative. Conjugates like an い-adj: っぽくない, っぽかった.
examples[].german: This color is whitish.
He gets angry easily.
That's childish behavior.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: An い-adjective does not take だ.
This is not an adjective form.
An い-adjective does not take ます.

en.explanation: The passive form expresses that the subject undergoes an action. Japanese also has the "suffering passive" (迷惑の受身).
en.formation: Ichidan: ～られる / Godan: ～あれる (u→areru)
en.notes: Godan: 書く→書かれる, 読む→読まれる. Ichidan: 食べる→食べられる. する→される, 来る→来られる.
examples[].german: I was praised by the teacher.
Someone stepped on my foot on the train.
I got caught in the rain.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This is active rather than passive.
This negates the praise.
This is not a past form.

en.explanation: らしい: a supposition based on hearsay or inference.
en.formation: Verb/Adj/Noun + らしい
en.notes: Conjugates like an い-adj.
examples[].german: Apparently it's going to rain tomorrow.
That restaurant is supposed to be good.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: After the noun, 雨のようだ would be correct.
The adverbial form does not end the sentence.
だ does not follow らしい.

en.explanation: らしい as a suffix: typical, characteristic.
en.formation: Noun + らしい
en.notes: Don't confuse with ～らしい (supposition).
examples[].german: Typical spring weather today, isn't it?
She is very feminine.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: らしい modifies nouns without an extra な.
The adverbial form does not modify the noun here.
The attributive form does not need の.

en.explanation: In Japanese, relative clauses come before the noun. No relative pronoun is needed.
en.formation: Verb/Adj (plain form) + Noun
en.notes: Simply put the clause in front of the noun.
examples[].german: The book I bought yesterday is very interesting.
The teacher who teaches Japanese is Mr. Tanaka.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The plain form is used here before the head noun.
A verbal relative clause does not need の before 本.
This is not a verb form.

en.explanation: さ turns adjectives into nouns.
en.formation: い-Adj (without い) + さ / な-Adj + さ
en.notes: 高さ, 長さ, 深さ, 大きさ, 便利さ, etc.
examples[].german: How many meters high is this mountain?
I really felt how difficult Japanese is.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 高い does not turn the measurable height into a noun here.
The く-form is not a noun for height here.
This would be the past rather than a measurable height.

en.explanation: さえ emphasizes an extreme case and implies that everything else goes without saying.
en.formation: Noun + さえ / Verb (ます-stem) + さえする
en.notes: さえ～ば means "if only / as long as": お金さえあれば = If only I had money.
examples[].german: Even children know that.
I don't even remember the name.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: しか requires a negative verb form.
子供でから is not a suitable connection.
子供でを is not a suitable particle combination.

en.explanation: A combination of causative and passive. Expresses that you are forced to do something.
en.formation: Ichidan: ～させられる / Godan: ～あせられる
en.notes: Godan short form: ～される (e.g. 行かされる instead of 行かせられる).
examples[].german: I was made to eat vegetables I don't like.
I'm made to work overtime every day.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means making someone eat, not being forced to eat yourself.
This negates the compulsion.
The causative passive is formed from the stem.

en.explanation: The causative form expresses that someone makes or lets another person do something.
en.formation: Ichidan: ～させる / Godan: ～あせる (u→aseru)
en.notes: Godan: 書く→書かせる, 読む→読ませる. Ichidan: 食べる→食べさせる. する→させる, 来る→来させる.
examples[].german: The mother made her child eat vegetables.
The teacher made the students stand up.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This is passive/potential, not the action being caused.
This negates making the child eat.
する is not attached to the dictionary form.

en.meaning: to be allowed to, to take the liberty of
en.explanation: させてもらう: asking for and receiving permission to do something.
en.formation: Verb (させ-form) + てもらう
en.notes: Polite: ～させていただく. Very common in business Japanese.
examples[].german: I'll take the liberty of leaving early today.
I'd like to take the liberty of saying a word.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: もらう follows the て-form.
This negates making use of the permission.
The polite form is もらいます.

en.explanation: させてください is a polite request for permission to do something. A combination of the causative and ください.
en.formation: Verb (させ-form) + てください
en.notes: Very polite. Often used in business contexts.
examples[].german: Please let me do it.
Please let me think about it for a moment.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The request requires the て-form.
ます cannot come before ください here.
This asks not to be allowed to think.

en.explanation: せいで: a negative cause, assigning blame.
en.formation: Verb/Adj + せいで / Noun + のせいで
en.notes: Opposite: おかげで (positive).
examples[].german: The game was canceled because of the rain.
I was late because I overslept.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means before the rain, not because of the rain.
This means instead of the rain, not because of it.
This would praise the cancellation as something to be grateful for; what is meant is an unfavorable cause.

en.explanation: し: lists several reasons or qualities.
en.formation: Verb/い-Adj + し / な-Adj + だし
en.notes: Also with just one reason: 疲れたし、帰ろう.
examples[].german: It's cheap and tasty, simply the best.
No time, no money, so I can't go.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: An い-adjective does not take な here.
安いの does not link the parallel reason here.
を does not coordinate reasons here.

en.meaning: to have no choice but to …
en.explanation: Verb in the dictionary form + しかない means that only one option is left: "the only thing to do is …". It sounds resigned or determined. Unlike noun + しか～ない (only X), here a whole action comes before しか.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + しかない / しかありません
en.notes: Comparison: noun + しか～ない (百円しかない = only 100 yen) vs. verb + しかない (待つしかない = all you can do is wait). More literary: ～ほかない / ～よりほかない (N3), even stronger: ～ざるを得ない. Positive and determined: やるしかない! = Time to get to it!
examples[].german: There are no more trains, so I have no choice but to take a taxi home.
If nobody will help me, I'll just have to do it alone.
Now that we've come this far, all we can do is keep going.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: だけ does not combine with ない to mean "no choice but".
しか always requires a negative form.
After the dictionary form comes しかない; しかしない is ungrammatical here.

en.explanation: そうだ (様態/yōtai) expresses an impression based on appearance. It is based on your own observation.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + そうだ / い-Adj (without い) + そうだ / な-Adj + そうだ
en.notes: Exceptions: いい→よさそう, ない→なさそう. Don't confuse with ～そうだ (hearsay).
examples[].german: It looks like it's going to rain.
This cake looks delicious.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The attributive form needs a noun after it.
The adverbial form needs a following predicate.
そう expressing appearance does not connect with のだ.

en.explanation: そうだ (伝聞): reports what you have heard or read.
en.formation: Clause (plain form) + そうだ
en.notes: Hearsay: plain form + そうだ. Appearance: stem + そうだ.
examples[].german: According to the weather forecast, it will be sunny tomorrow.
I hear that movie is interesting.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The attributive form needs a following noun.
The adverbial form needs a following predicate.
No な is inserted after the verb.

en.explanation: ふりをする: to feign, to put on an act.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形/ない形) + ふりをする / Noun + のふりをする
en.notes: Always deliberate pretending.
examples[].german: I pretended not to know.
He's pretending to be asleep.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the pretending.
No な is inserted after the verb.
The fixed expression for pretending is ふりをする.

en.explanation: たほうがいい: advice or a recommendation.
en.formation: Verb (た形) + ほうがいい / Verb (ない形) + ほうがいい
en.notes: た形 = recommending. ない形 = advising against.
examples[].german: You'd better go to bed early.
You'd better not drink.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The evaluation requires が.
This advises against going to bed early.
を does not fit the comparative evaluation.

en.explanation: たばかり expresses that an action has only just been completed.
en.formation: Verb (た-form) + ばかり
en.notes: Don't confuse with ～ばかり (only / nothing but).
examples[].german: I've only just come to Japan.
I only just ate, but I'm already hungry.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means constantly coming rather than having just arrived.
来る is read くる, not きる; besides, it does not express a completed arrival.
No な is inserted after ばかり before です.

en.explanation: たがる: expresses the wish of a third person. ～たい can only be used for yourself.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + たがる
en.notes: Your own wish: ～たい. Third persons: ～たがる. Godan conjugation.
examples[].german: The child wants to go outside.
He wants to go to Japan.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The final い of たい is dropped before がる.
This negates the wish being shown.
The て-form is たがって.

en.explanation: ために: purpose (辞書形) or reason (た形/noun).
en.formation: Verb (辞書形) + ために / Noun + のために
en.notes: Purpose: 辞書形. Reason: た形/noun.
examples[].german: I came to Japan to study Japanese.
The trains stopped because of the typhoon.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The purpose expression needs に, not な.
No な is inserted after a verb.
を does not form a purpose expression here.

en.explanation: たらどう: a casual suggestion or piece of advice.
en.formation: Verb (たら) + どう(ですか)
en.notes: Depending on the tone, it can also sound impatient.
examples[].german: Why don't you go see a doctor?
How about getting more rest?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 行っれば is not a verb form.
行っます is not a verb form.
The suggestion requires the conditional form たら.

en.explanation: ていただけませんか: a very polite request.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + いただけませんか
en.notes: てください < てもらえませんか < ていただけませんか.
examples[].german: Could you please wait a moment?
Could you explain it once more?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: いただく follows the て-form here.
The polite form is いただけません.
This is not a polite question form.

en.explanation: てくださいませんか: a polite request, between てください and ていただけませんか.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + くださいませんか
en.notes: てください < てくださいませんか < ていただけませんか.
examples[].german: Would you please help me for a moment?
Would you please take a photo?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The request requires the て-form.
The polite form of くださる is くださいません.
This is not a question form.

en.explanation: ちゃう and じゃう: contracted forms of てしまう and でしまう.
en.formation: Verb (て→ちゃう) / Verb (で→じゃう)
en.notes: Very common in everyday speech. て→ちゃ, で→じゃ.
examples[].german: I ate it all.
I left something on the train.
You mustn't drink that.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 食べてしまった becomes 食べちゃった, not 食べじゃった.
The past is ちゃった.
This negates eating it all.

en.meaning: to be enough; to get out of having to
en.explanation: てすむ: something is enough. ずにすむ/ないですむ: you get away without having to do it.
en.formation: Verb (て) + すむ / Verb (ず) + にすむ
en.notes: ないですむ = more casual than ずにすむ.
examples[].german: I got away without having to take medicine.
A thousand yen was enough.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The past of 済む is すんだ.
This negates that taking it could be avoided.
済む is connected with に here.

en.explanation: ～てよかった expresses relief or joy about something that happened: "Good that …". It looks back on an action or situation that turned out well. The opposite – regret about something you didn't do – is expressed by ～ばよかった.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + よかった / い-adj (～くて) / な-adj・noun (～で) + よかった; negative: ～なくてよかった
en.notes: Contrast: 行ってよかった (I went – luckily) vs. 行けばよかった (I didn't go – too bad). Often used to show sympathy: 無事でよかったですね (I'm so glad everything turned out all right). With a negative: 雨が降らなくてよかった (good thing it didn't rain).
examples[].german: I'm glad I came to Japan.
Thank goodness I made it in time!
It's a good thing it wasn't a serious injury.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: よかった attaches to the て-form, not to the た-form.
The past of いい/よい is よかった.
No particle が goes between the て-form and よかった.

en.explanation: てあげる expresses that you do someone the favor of doing something for them.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + あげる
en.notes: Can sound condescending. More polite: ～て差し上げる. Don't use it toward people of higher status about things you do for them.
examples[].german: I taught my friend Japanese.
Shall I carry your luggage for you?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: あげる follows the て-form here.
This negates the help given.
あげる forms the past tense あげた.

en.explanation: てある expresses that a deliberate action has been carried out and its result still remains.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + ある
en.notes: Difference from ～ている: てある emphasizes deliberate preparation, ている the current state.
examples[].german: The window has been opened (and is still open).
A note has been written on the table.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ある follows the て-form here.
ある is negated with ない, not あらない.
ます cannot come before ある.

en.meaning: to want someone to do something
en.explanation: てほしい expresses the wish that another person does something.
en.formation: Person に + Verb (て-form) + ほしい
en.notes: Negative: ～ないでほしい (I want you not to do it).
examples[].german: I want you to come soon.
I want you to study more.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Wanting someone else to act requires the て-form.
This negates the wish.
ます cannot come before ほしい.

en.meaning: to go and ...; from now on
en.explanation: ていく expresses movement away from the speaker or a change that continues into the future.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + いく
en.notes: Opposite of ～てくる. Toward the future: だんだん暑くなっていく (it's going to get hotter and hotter).
examples[].german: I'll keep doing my best from now on, too.
I'll take a bento box with me.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 持った行く is not a valid verb connection.
This negates taking it along.
持っます is not a verb form.

en.explanation: てくれる expresses that someone does something for the speaker or the speaker's group. It implies gratitude.
en.formation: Person が + Verb (て-form) + くれる
en.notes: Polite: ～てくださる. Request: ～てくれませんか (Could you please ...?).
examples[].german: My mother made me a bento.
My friend took me to the station.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This makes the mother the recipient rather than the one acting.
This negates the action.
くれる follows the て-form.

en.meaning: to come and ...; up to now
en.explanation: てくる expresses movement toward the speaker or a change from the past up to now.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + くる
en.notes: Opposite of ～ていく. Up to now: だんだん寒くなってきた (it has been getting colder).
examples[].german: It has started to rain.
I have been studying Japanese for three years.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the rain starting.
くる follows the て-form here.
The past of くる is きた.

en.meaning: it's fine if …; feel free to …
en.explanation: ～ても構わない expresses permission or indifference: "It doesn't matter if …". It corresponds to ～てもいい but sounds a little more formal and stresses that the speaker has no problem with it. As a question (～ても構いませんか) it politely asks for permission.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + も構わない / い-adj (～くても) / な-adj・noun (～でも) + 構わない
en.notes: 構う means "to mind, to care about" and is used almost only in the negative: 構わない = "don't mind". Politeness levels when asking for permission: ～てもいい？ (casual) < ～てもいいですか < ～ても構いませんか < ～てもよろしいでしょうか (very polite). As a short reply: 構いませんよ = No problem.
examples[].german: Feel free to read the books in this room.
"May I open the window?" "Yes, please go ahead."
As long as it's cheap, I don't mind if it's old.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ではいけません is a prohibition – the opposite of permission.
構う is only used in the negative in this expression; the affirmative makes no sense.
The permission form is ～ても構わない; 構わない cannot be combined with たら.

en.meaning: to have something done by someone
en.explanation: てもらう expresses that you receive the favor of someone doing something for you.
en.formation: Person に + Verb (て-form) + もらう
en.notes: Polite: ～ていただく. Request: ～てもらえませんか (Could you please ...?).
examples[].german: My friend helped me (I received help).
The teacher explained it to me.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This reverses the direction of the help.
This negates the help received.
もらう follows the て-form.

en.meaning: to do in advance, to prepare
en.explanation: ておく expresses that an action is done as preparation or in advance.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + おく
en.notes: Colloquial: ～とく (買っとく = buy it and have it ready).
examples[].german: I'll cook the food ahead of the party.
Please get ready for tomorrow.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: おく needs the て-connection.
This negates the preparation.
作っます is not a verb form.

en.explanation: てはいけない: a prohibition.
en.formation: Verb (て-form) + はいけない
en.notes: Colloquial: ～ちゃだめ.
examples[].german: You may not take photos here.
You must not sleep in class.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This allows sleeping.
This tells you to sleep.
The prohibition requires the て-form.

en.explanation: と: a natural, automatic or habitual consequence.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形/ない形) + と
en.notes: Used for laws of nature, habits and giving directions.
examples[].german: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
When you press this button, the door opens.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: なるたら is not a conditional form.
なるれば is not a conditional form.
ながら requires the stem なり.

en.explanation: という: identifies or defines something, or introduces indirect speech.
en.formation: Noun/Clause + という + Noun
en.notes: Colloquial: っていう. ～ということだ = that means.
examples[].german: Do you know the kanji called "sakura"?
I heard that there's a test tomorrow.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The quoted name needs と.
に does not replace the quotation particle here.
The relative structure modifies 漢字 without an extra の.

en.explanation: とか: casual listing of examples.
en.formation: Noun + とか + Noun + とか
en.notes: More casual than ～など.
examples[].german: On weekends I do things like watching movies and shopping.
Buy some apples or bananas or something.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: しか requires a negative ending.
へ does not list leisure activities.
が makes movies the subject rather than an item in the list.

en.explanation: 時に: indicates the point in time when something happens.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形/た形) + 時 / Noun + の時
en.notes: 辞書形+時 = before you do it. た形+時 = after you have done it.
examples[].german: When I went to Japan, I saw temples.
When you have a problem, please come and talk to us.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ながら requires the verb stem.
前に requires 行く here and means before the trip.
行ったてから is not a valid verb connection.

en.explanation: ところだ: the point in time of an action (before/in the middle of it/after).
en.formation: 辞書形+ところ / ている+ところ / た形+ところ
en.notes: 辞書形 = about to. ている = right now, in the middle of it. た形 = just now.
examples[].german: I'm just about to go out.
I've just finished eating.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This does not end the sentence here.
No な is inserted after the verb.
を does not come before です here.

en.explanation: ～とく is the spoken contraction of ～ておく: て + おく merges into とく, で + おく into どく. The meaning stays the same – doing something in advance or deliberately leaving it as it is. Among friends and family the short form is much more common than the full form.
en.formation: Verb (て-form): ～ておく → ～とく / ～でおく → ～どく; conjugates like a godan verb: とく, といて, といた
en.notes: Examples: 買っておく → 買っとく, 見ておいて → 見といて, 飲んでおく → 飲んどく. Don't confuse it with 解く (とく, to solve) or どく (to move out of the way). Like ～ちゃう (← てしまう), ～とく belongs to casual speech; in emails to superiors or in essays, stick with ～ておきます.
examples[].german: I put the beer in the fridge already.
I'll go ahead and copy the documents for tomorrow's meeting.
Read this book by the end of the week, OK?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The past of ～とく is ～といた, not ～とった.
どく only comes from でおく (読んどく); 入れて has て, so it's とく.
とく forms its past like 書く → 書いた, so it's といた.

en.explanation: として indicates the function or capacity in which someone or something is regarded.
en.formation: Noun + として
en.notes: Common with job titles and roles.
examples[].german: I came to Japan as an exchange student.
This town is famous as a tourist destination.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: の would have to modify a noun, not 日本に来ました.
This marks a point of view rather than the role in which the person came to Japan.
This names a source of information rather than a role.

en.meaning: to continue to, to keep doing
en.explanation: As a suffix, 続ける expresses that an action continues.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + 続ける
en.notes: Also standalone: 続ける = to continue.
examples[].german: I kept walking for three hours.
Don't give up, and keep making an effort.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates continuing to walk.
This is not a past form.
ます is not inserted before 続けた.

en.explanation: って: colloquial と (quotation particle).
en.formation: Sentence + って
en.notes: ～って言ってた = said that. ～っていう = called, named.
examples[].german: Tanaka says he's not coming.
What does "sumimasen" mean?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: No な is inserted after 来ない for a quotation.
をって is not a quotation connection.
を cannot end the quotation here without a further predicate.

en.explanation: The volitional form expresses intention, a suggestion or an invitation. It corresponds to "Let's ..." or "I'll ...".
en.formation: Ichidan: ～よう / Godan: u→ō
en.notes: Godan: 書く→書こう, 読む→読もう. する→しよう, 来る→来よう. ～ようと思う = I intend to.
examples[].german: Let's watch a movie.
I think I'll get up early tomorrow.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 見る forms 見よう, not 見ろう.
見るよう is not a standalone suggestion to do something together.
This negates watching.

en.explanation: わけだ: a logical conclusion.
en.formation: Verb/Adj (plain form) + わけだ
en.notes: わけがない = impossible. わけではない = not necessarily.
examples[].german: He practices every day, so no wonder he's good.
No wonder it's cheap.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not come before this copula.
This does not end the sentence here.
上手なようだ can express a guess; the given sentence, however, explains the established skill as no wonder.

en.explanation: わけにはいかない: not possible for moral or social reasons.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形) + わけにはいかない
en.notes: A social/moral impossibility, not a physical one.
examples[].german: I promised, so I can't very well not go.
I can't just give up here.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This would present not going as possible.
No な is inserted after the verb.
The fixed construction uses に.

en.explanation: 忘れる as a suffix: you forget to carry out an action.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + 忘れる
en.notes: 言い忘れる (to forget to say), 買い忘れる (to forget to buy).
examples[].german: I forgot to lock the door.
Don't forget to take your medicine.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the forgetting.
This is not a past form.
ます is not inserted before 忘れた.

en.explanation: As a suffix, やすい expresses that something is easy to do or that there is a tendency.
en.formation: Verb (ます-stem) + やすい
en.notes: Conjugates like an い-adjective: やすくない, やすかった.
examples[].german: This book is easy to read.
Glass breaks easily.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means hard to read.
An い-adjective does not end with だ.
This is not an adjective form.

en.explanation: より = the thing being compared against, のほうが = the element that has more of the quality.
en.formation: A より B のほうが + Adj
en.notes: 思ったより難しい (harder than I thought).
examples[].german: The bus is cheaper than the train.
I like winter better than summer.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: まで sets a limit rather than a standard of comparison.
へ marks a direction.
を does not mark a standard of comparison here.

en.explanation: ようだ: a supposition based on your own observation.
en.formation: Verb/い-Adj + ようだ / な-Adj + なようだ / Noun + のようだ
en.notes: More formal than みたいだ.
examples[].german: He seems to be busy.
I seem to have caught a cold.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: No な is inserted after an い-adjective.
The attributive form requires a following noun.
The adverbial form requires a following statement.

en.explanation: ような (formal) and みたいな (casual) before nouns.
en.formation: Noun + のような/みたいな + Noun
en.notes: のような = formal, みたいな = casual.
examples[].german: It was a dreamlike day.
I want to become someone like him.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Before a noun, ような is used.
だ is not an attributive connection here.
夢のような requires な before 一日.

en.meaning: to come to (be able to), to reach the point where
en.explanation: ようになる expresses a gradual change or development: something that was not possible before becomes possible.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形/ない形) + ようになる
en.notes: Negative: ～なくなる (to stop doing): 食べなくなった = stopped eating.
examples[].german: I've become able to speak Japanese.
I've started eating vegetables.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The change requires に.
This negates the ability that was gained.
なるました is not a verb form.

en.explanation: ように: an indirect purpose, used with the potential form or the ない-form.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形/ない形) + ように
en.notes: ために = direct purpose. ように = indirect purpose.
examples[].german: I'll write it down so that I don't forget.
Speak loudly so people can hear you.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Before the verb, an adverbial form is needed.
を does not form a purpose expression here.
No な is inserted after the verb.

en.meaning: to make a point of, to keep up a habit
en.explanation: ようにしている: a conscious habit you make a point of keeping.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形/ない形) + ようにしている
en.notes: ようにする = to try on one occasion. ようにしている = a regular habit.
examples[].german: I make a point of eating vegetables every day.
I make a point of not eating late at night.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The habit you aim for requires に.
No な is inserted after the verb.
This negates the effort.

en.meaning: to try to, to make sure to
en.explanation: ようにする expresses that you make a conscious effort to do or avoid something.
en.formation: Verb (辞書形/ない形) + ようにする
en.notes: ～ようにしている = a regular habit you make a point of keeping.
examples[].german: I make a point of exercising every day.
Please make sure not to be late.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The habit you aim for is connected with に.
This negates the effort.
しますて is not a て-form.

en.meaning: I'm planning to …; I'm thinking of …
en.explanation: Volitional form + と思う expresses your own intention: "I'm planning to …". ～ようと思います sounds like a decision made at the moment of speaking, ～ようと思っています like a plan you've had for a while. It is softer and more personal than ～つもりだ.
en.formation: Verb (volitional form: ～よう / ～おう) + と思う / と思っている
en.notes: Only for your own intention. About third parties: 彼は留学しようと思っているらしい. ～つもりだ sounds firmer and more planned, ～ようと思う more like a thought or a fresh decision. ～ようと思ったら often means "just as I was about to …". Related: ～ようとする (to try, to be about to).
examples[].german: I'm thinking of going to Hokkaidō during the summer vacation.
This year I'm finally going to quit smoking.
Just as I was about to make a call, a friend called me.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The content of a thought is linked with と, not に.
The volitional form of 行く is 行こう; ～かろう belongs to い-adjectives.
思う forms the continuing state with ている, not てある.

en.meaning: to try to, to be about to
en.explanation: ようとする: making an attempt or being just about to do something.
en.formation: Verb (volitional form) + とする
en.notes: ～ようとしている = to be just about to.
examples[].german: I tried to open the door, but it wouldn't open.
Just as I was about to go out, the phone rang.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The intention uses 開けよう.
The attempt construction requires と.
This negates the attempt.

en.explanation: ずに is the formal variant of ないで. Both express that one action is not done while another takes place.
en.formation: Verb (ない-stem) + ずに / Verb (ない-form) + で
en.notes: する→せずに (exception). ずに is more typical of written language than ないで.
examples[].german: I went to school without eating breakfast.
I was able to read it without a dictionary.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This means after breakfast.
This means after breakfast.
This means while eating.

en.explanation: ずつ expresses equal distribution or gradual change.
en.formation: Number/quantity + ずつ
en.notes: 少しずつ (little by little) is especially common.
examples[].german: I study a little every day.
Please hand out two to each person.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: しか requires a negative.
へ does not divide studying into small amounts.
をに is not a quantity particle combination here.

en.explanation: To describe a verb more closely, an い-adjective becomes ～く (早い → 早く) and a な-adjective becomes ～に (静か → 静かに). This is how 'quick' becomes 'quickly' and 'quiet' becomes 'quietly' (as in 'speak quietly'). The adverb comes before the verb.
en.formation: い-adj.: い → く + Verb (早い → 早く) / な-adj. + に + Verb (静か → 静かに) / Exception: いい → よく
en.notes: Irregular: いい → よく (よくできました = well done). Watch out with きれい and 有名: they are な-adjectives, so きれいに, not *きれく. The same form appears in ～くなる/～になる (to become) and ～くする/～にする (to make). Some adverbs are words in their own right: とても, ゆっくり, すぐ.
examples[].german: Please speak quietly in the library.
I get up early every morning.
I wrote the kanji neatly.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: な only goes between a な-adjective and a noun (静かな部屋), not before a verb.
静かで is the て-form and links clauses, but does not describe the speaking.
～く is the adverb form of い-adjectives; 静か is a な-adjective.

en.explanation: あまり comes before a negated verb or adjective and softens the negation: 'not particularly, not often, not much'. This makes a negative statement sound soft and polite. In this meaning, あまり always needs a negative form.
en.formation: あまり + Verb (ない / ません) / あまり + い-adj. (～くない) / あまり + な-adj. (～じゃない)
en.notes: Degrees: 全然～ない (not at all) is stronger than あまり～ない (not particularly). Colloquially often あんまり. To questions like 好きですか, answering あまり… is an evasive, polite alternative to a blunt いいえ. With a positive form, あまり(に) means 'far too much' – a different, more advanced use.
examples[].german: This movie wasn't very interesting.
I don't drink much alcohol.
It's not very cold today, is it?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: とても intensifies positive statements; before a negative it does not give 'not particularly'.
たくさん expresses a quantity and cannot grade an adjective.
よく means 'often' or 'well' and does not fit before おもしろくなかった.

en.meaning: throughout, all over (じゅう) · in progress (ちゅう)
en.explanation: Read じゅう, 中 means 'whole, throughout': 一日中 (all day long), 世界中 (all over the world). Read ちゅう, it means 'in the middle of, in progress': 電話中 (on the phone right now), 会議中. Which reading applies depends on the word.
en.formation: Time period / place + 中 (じゅう) / Action noun + 中 (ちゅう)
en.notes: Rule of thumb: じゅう with time periods and places (一年中, 日本中, 家中), ちゅう with ongoing activities (授業中, 食事中, 工事中). On signs: 営業中 (open), 準備中 (in preparation). 今日中に (きょうじゅうに) means 'by the end of today'. Don't confuse it with 中 (なか) = 'in, inside'.
examples[].german: Mr. Tanaka is on the phone right now.
Yesterday it rained all day.
This song is famous all over the world.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 間 (かん) comes after durations like 三日間 and does not form 'in the middle of a phone call'.
ごろ makes points in time approximate and does not fit an activity.
たち forms the plural of people and does not fit 電話.

en.explanation: Noun + でも softens a suggestion or invitation: お茶でも飲みませんか = 'Shall we have some tea or something?'. でも hints that it could just as well be something else and leaves the other person some leeway. It replaces は, が or を.
en.formation: Noun + でも + suggestion / invitation / wish (～ませんか, ～ましょう, ～どうですか)
en.notes: Don't confuse it with でも at the start of a sentence ('but') or with noun + でも meaning 'even' (子供でもわかる = even a child understands that). In a suggestion, でも sounds modest because you don't commit to anything. Colloquially also ～なんか: コーヒーなんかどう？
examples[].german: Would you like to have some tea or something?
Let's go see a movie or something on Sunday.
It's hot, isn't it? How about something cold?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ても attaches to the て-form of verbs and adjectives, not to a noun like お茶.
飲む takes its object with を; with が the sentence becomes ungrammatical.
に marks a destination or a time, not a drink that you drink.

en.explanation: ごろ is attached to a time expression and makes it approximate: 三時ごろ = around three o'clock. It only works with points in time such as clock times, days, months or years, not with durations or amounts. It can be followed by に, but this is often dropped.
en.formation: Point in time + ごろ (+ に)
en.notes: ごろ = approximate point in time, ぐらい/くらい = approximate amount or duration: 三時ごろ (around three o'clock) vs. 三時間ぐらい (about three hours). In everyday speech you also hear 三時ぐらい, but the textbook form for points in time is ごろ. Don't combine it with durations (*二時間ごろ). As a word on its own it is ころ: 子供のころ (when I was a child).
examples[].german: I go to bed around eleven every night.
I'd like to go to Japan around April.
Let's meet at the station around noon.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: After a time expression, the suffix is voiced: ごろ.
ずつ distributes amounts evenly and does not fit a clock time.
しか requires a negative form and means 'only'.

en.explanation: か between two options means 'or': AかB. When two clauses with か follow each other (…か…か), you get 'whether ... or ...' for something that is still open. Unlike や, か names alternatives of which only one applies.
en.formation: Noun + か + Noun / Clause (plain form) + か + Clause (plain form) + か
en.notes: AかB: only one of the two. AやB: examples from a larger set. AとB: both, a complete list. With two clauses, か comes at both ends (行くか行かないか); the second か must not be left out. For 'whether or not' there is also the shorter form ～かどうか (N4).
examples[].german: I haven't decided yet whether I'll go to the party or not.
Every morning I eat bread or rice.
I'll call on Monday or Tuesday.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: と joins nouns ('and'), but not two clauses as alternatives.
や only lists nouns and cannot come after a verb.
With が you do not get 'whether ... or'; the sentence becomes ungrammatical.

en.meaning: here / there (near you) / over there / where
en.explanation: ここ, そこ, あそこ and どこ are place words following the こ-そ-あ-ど system: ここ is the place near the speaker, そこ the place near the listener, あそこ a place far from both. どこ asks about the place. They behave like nouns and take particles such as に, で or へ.
en.formation: ここ / そこ / あそこ / どこ + particle (は, に, で, へ, から …) or + です
en.notes: The polite equivalents are こちら/そちら/あちら/どちら – common in shops and on the phone (お手洗いはどちらですか). Colloquial: こっち/そっち/あっち/どっち. そこ also refers to a place the other person has just mentioned: 「京都に住んでいます。」「そこはどんな所ですか。」
examples[].german: Where is the restroom?
May I take pictures here?
The station is over there.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: どの needs a following noun and cannot stand alone before です.
いつ asks about time, not place.
だれ asks about a person, not a place.

en.meaning: this ... / that ... (near you) / that ... (over there) / which ...
en.explanation: この, その, あの and どの always come directly before a noun and specify it – like 'this' and 'that' in 'this book' or 'that book'. The distance follows the same こ-そ-あ system as これ/それ/あれ. どの asks which thing out of a group is meant.
en.formation: この / その / あの / どの + Noun
en.notes: この/その/あの/どの can never stand alone: not *このは…, but これは…. To talk about something both speakers know but can't see at the moment, you use あの: あの店、おいしかったね (That place back then was good, wasn't it?). あのう… is also a typical filler when addressing someone.
examples[].german: Who is that person over there?
This book is very interesting.
Which train are you taking?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: あれ stands alone and cannot directly modify a noun like 人.
あそこ is a place word and cannot come directly before a noun like 人.
あちら is a direction/place word and cannot come directly before 人.

en.meaning: this / that (near you) / that (over there) / which one
en.explanation: These demonstrative pronouns stand alone in place of a noun. こ- points to something near the speaker, そ- to something near the listener, and あ- to something far from both. どれ asks which thing out of three or more is meant.
en.formation: これ / それ / あれ / どれ + particle (は, が, を …) – with no noun after it
en.notes: これ/それ/あれ/どれ are never directly followed by a noun: not *これ本, but この本 (→ この/その/あの/どの). As the subject of a question, どれ takes が, not は: どれがいいですか. When there are only two options, you ask with どちら/どっち. To the question それは何ですか you answer with これは…, because the perspective switches.
examples[].german: Which one is your bag?
This is Japanese tea.
Excuse me, I'd like that one (near you), please.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: どの must come directly before a noun (どのかばん) and cannot stand alone.
どんな asks about the kind of thing and needs a following noun.
だれ asks about a person, not a bag.

en.explanation: With the negative question ～ませんか you invite someone politely: 一緒に行きませんか = 'Won't you come along?'. The negation sounds reserved and leaves the other person a choice. This is more considerate than ～ましょう, which already assumes agreement.
en.formation: Verb stem (ます-form without ます) + ませんか
en.notes: Typical exchange: invitation with ～ませんか, acceptance with いいですね、～ましょう. Refusals are indirect: 土曜日はちょっと… (Saturday is a bit …). Don't invite with ～たいですか – it asks directly about the other person's wishes and comes across as pushy. Informal: 行かない？ with rising intonation.
examples[].german: Would you like to watch a movie together this weekend?
Shall we take a short break?
"Would you like to go out to eat tonight?" – "Sounds good. Let's go!"
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ませんでした negates the past ('didn't watch') and is not an invitation.
ましたか asks whether someone did something instead of inviting them.
ないでください asks someone not to do something – the opposite of an invitation.

en.meaning: some- (何か, どこか) / nothing, nobody (何も～ない)
en.explanation: Question words combine with particles to form new words: + か gives "some-" (何か = something, 誰か = someone, どこか = somewhere), + も with a negative gives "nothing, nobody, nowhere" (何も～ない, 誰も～ない). These forms are very common in everyday speech.
en.formation: 何 / 誰 / どこ / いつ + か / 何 / 誰 + も + negative / どこ + へ・に + も + negative
en.notes: The answer to 何か食べましたか is: いいえ、何も食べませんでした. Other particles go before も: 誰とも話さなかった (didn't talk to anyone), どこにもない (nowhere). Careful: いつも means "always", and どれも/どちらも with a positive verb means "every one/both" – "no/none" only comes about with a negative.
examples[].german: There's nothing in the fridge.
I'd like to drink something.
I didn't go anywhere on Sunday.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 何か means "something" and with ありません does not give the statement "nothing".
何が asks about the subject; without a final か, the sentence is ungrammatical.
ある does not take an object with を.

en.explanation: たち is attached to pronouns and words for people to turn them into a group: 私たち (we), 子供たち (the children). Japanese nouns otherwise have no plural, so たち is optional and is used almost only for people and animals.
en.formation: Pronoun / word for a person / name + たち
en.notes: After a name, たち means 'X and their group': 田中さんたち are not several Tanakas. たち is not normally used for objects (*本たち) – the noun stays unchanged. Respectful for others: ～がた (先生がた, あなたがた); casual: ～ら (僕ら).
examples[].german: We're in the same class.
The children are playing in the park.
Tanaka and the others have already gone home.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: さん is an honorific suffix for others and is never attached to 私.
がた is respectful and is only used for others (あなたがた), not for yourself.
ごろ makes points in time approximate and does not fit people.

en.explanation: 全然 (ぜんぜん) strengthens a negation to 'not at all'. It comes before a negated verb or adjective and is very common in conversation. In formal texts, まったく～ない is preferred.
en.formation: 全然 + Verb (ない / ません) / 全然 + い-adj. (～くない) / 全然 + な-adj. (～じゃない)
en.notes: In today's colloquial Japanese you also hear 全然 with positive statements: 全然大丈夫 (totally fine) – usually to ease the other person's worry. In exams and polite speech, however, the rule is 全然 + negative. Degrees: 全然～ない > あまり～ない. Written language: まったく～ない.
examples[].german: This curry isn't spicy at all.
I don't watch TV at all.
I didn't understand the test at all.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: とても comes before positive adjectives; with 辛くない it does not make a natural sentence.
いっぱい expresses a quantity and cannot intensify an adjective.
よく means 'often' or 'well' and cannot intensify 辛くない.

en.explanation: To negate a な-adjective, じゃないです or ではありません is used after the adjective stem. The conjugation is the same as for negating nouns.
en.formation: な-adjective + じゃないです / ではありません
en.notes: じゃないです is more colloquial, ではありません is more formal. Both are correct.
examples[].german: This room isn't clean.
Japanese isn't easy.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This says the room is clean.
Despite the い at the end, きれい is a な-adjective.
This is the affirmative past.

en.explanation: For the past form of a な-adjective, でした is used after the adjective stem. The conjugation is the same as the past form of nouns.
en.formation: な-adjective + でした
en.notes: The conjugation of な-adjectives follows the same pattern as Noun + です/でした/じゃない/じゃなかった.
examples[].german: The party was lively.
He was well. / He was doing fine.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: な-adjectives do not form the past with かった.
This is not a negative form of a な-adjective.
This says the party was not lively.

en.explanation: For the negative past form of a な-adjective, じゃなかったです or ではありませんでした is used.
en.formation: な-adjective + じゃなかったです / ではありませんでした
en.notes: Here too: じゃなかったです is more colloquial, ではありませんでした is more formal.
examples[].german: I wasn't free yesterday.
That shop wasn't famous.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This says there was free time.
暇 is a な-adjective.
暇 does not form its negative like an い-adjective.

en.explanation: な-adjectives need な when they come directly before a noun. As a predicate, they are used with です like nouns. They do not conjugate like い-adjectives.
en.formation: な-adjective + な + Noun / な-adjective + です
en.notes: な-adjectives behave like nouns when conjugating: they use じゃない, でした, じゃなかった instead of changing their ending.
examples[].german: It's quiet here.
That's a lively child, isn't it?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 静か is a な-adjective and doesn't take い.
The negative of a な-adjective does not use くない.
This means "not quiet".

en.explanation: ～ながら expresses that two actions are done at the same time by the same person. The main action comes at the end of the sentence, the secondary action before ながら.
en.formation: Verb stem + ながら + main action
en.notes: Both actions must be done by the same person. For different people you use ～間に (aida ni).
examples[].german: I study while listening to music.
Please don't eat while watching TV.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 聞きて is not a て-form; besides, it would mean "only afterwards".
聞きた is not a た-form.
聞きない is not a negative form.

en.explanation: ～ないで means "without doing something". It expresses that one action is not carried out while another takes place.
en.formation: Verb ない-form + で
en.notes: ～ないで can also express a request when ください is added: 食べないでください (Please don't eat).
examples[].german: I went to school without eating breakfast.
I read it without using a dictionary.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This says breakfast was eaten beforehand.
This describes eating at the same time instead of going without breakfast.
This says "after breakfast".

en.explanation: ～ないでください is a polite request not to do something. It is the negative form of ～てください.
en.formation: Verb ない-form + でください
en.notes: The ない-form is built from the dictionary form: group 1 (godan): う-row → あ-row + ない (書く → 書かない), group 2 (ichidan): る → ない (食べる → 食べない).
examples[].german: Please don't take photos here.
Please don't worry.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The negative request needs ないで, not なく.
ません does not connect directly with ください.
The negative past does not form a request.

en.explanation: ～なければならない means "must" or "have to". It expresses an obligation or necessity. There are several short forms of it.
en.formation: Verb ない-form (without い) + ければならない
en.notes: Short forms: ～なければならない → ～なければいけない → ～なきゃいけない → ～なきゃ (shortest, colloquial). They all have the same meaning.
examples[].german: I have to take medicine every day.
I have to do my homework.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This explicitly removes the obligation.
This advises against taking it.
The obligation needs the negative ending いけません.

en.explanation: ～なくてもいい expresses that it is not necessary to do something. It is the opposite of ～なければならない. The polite form is ～なくてもいいです.
en.formation: Verb ない-form (without い) + くてもいい
en.notes: How it's formed: Verb ない-form → ない becomes なくて: 食べない → 食べなくてもいい. Don't confuse it with ～てもいい (permission).
examples[].german: You don't have to come tomorrow.
You don't have to eat all of it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This obliges the person to come instead of releasing them from it.
This obliges the person to come.
いい is an adjective and does not take ます here.

en.explanation: ね is used at the end of a sentence to seek agreement or express a shared opinion. It is like English "isn't it?" or "right?".
en.formation: Sentence + ね
en.notes: ね is often used in conversation to create a friendly atmosphere and signal agreement.
examples[].german: Nice weather, isn't it?
This movie is interesting, isn't it?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を cannot close the copula as a sentence-final particle.
に is not a sentence-final particle that seeks agreement here.
ですます doubles the polite ending, which is not allowed.

en.meaning: direction / point in time / place of existence
en.explanation: に has many functions: it marks the destination of a movement, a point in time, the place where something exists, and the indirect recipient. It is one of the most versatile particles in Japanese.
en.formation: Noun + に
en.notes: With days of the week and specific clock times you use に, but with relative time expressions such as 今日、明日、来週, に is not used.
examples[].german: I go to school.
I get up at seven o'clock.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The school is a destination, not a route you pass through.
の cannot link the destination to 行きます.
The school is not the subject of the movement.

en.explanation: ～に行く expresses the purpose of a movement: you go somewhere in order to do something. Instead of 行く you can also use 来る or 帰る.
en.formation: Verb stem + に行く / に来る / に帰る
en.notes: You use the verb stem (masu-stem), not the dictionary form: 食べに行く (correct), 食べるに行く (wrong). With する-verbs: 買い物しに行く.
examples[].german: I'm going to see a movie.
Won't you come over for lunch?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: A purpose after the verb stem is marked with に.
が does not connect the verb stem as a purpose.
で does not attach to 見 as a purpose here.

en.explanation: の connects two nouns and shows belonging, possession or a closer description. It often corresponds to English 's or "of". の can also replace a noun when it is clear from context.
en.formation: Noun + の + Noun
en.notes: の can also be used as a nominalizer: 食べるのが好きです (I like eating).
examples[].german: It's my book.
He/She is a Japanese teacher.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not create a possessive relation to the following noun.
A direction is not a statement of possession.
に cannot directly mark 本 as someone's possession here.

en.meaning: to like doing / to be good at / to be bad at
en.explanation: With ～のが, verbs can be nominalized so they can be combined with adjectives such as 好き (to like), 上手 (good at), 下手 (bad at).
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + のが + 好き/上手/下手 + です
en.notes: 上手 and 下手 are not used about yourself in polite speech. About yourself, you'd rather say 得意 (tokui, good at) or 苦手 (nigate, bad at).
examples[].german: I like cooking.
I'm bad at singing.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The verb needs to be nominalized with の or こと here.
This means "don't like cooking".
好き requires が here, not を.

en.explanation: ～のほうが marks the preferred or highlighted side in a comparison. It is often combined with ～より.
en.formation: Noun + のほうが + Adjective
en.notes: どちらのほうが (dochira no hō ga) is used in questions: コーヒーとお茶とどちらのほうが好きですか。 (Which do you like better, coffee or tea?)
examples[].german: I like winter better than summer.
This one is cheaper.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 好き requires が here, not を.
に does not mark the preferred item in the comparison here.
のほどが is not the comparative construction asked for.

en.explanation: ～のは～です nominalizes part of a sentence with の and makes it the topic. It lets you talk about actions or situations as nouns. It is often used for explanations and definitions.
en.formation: Verb/Sentence + のは + Noun/Adjective + です
en.notes: の turns a sentence into a noun. Similar constructions: ～のが好き (to like doing), ～のを忘れる (to forget to do).
examples[].german: Studying Japanese is fun.
Getting up early in the morning is hard.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を does not nominalize the activity.
に does not nominalize the activity.
と does not form a nominalized topic here.

en.meaning: because; since (more polite than から)
en.explanation: ～ので gives a reason and is more polite and objective than から. It is often used in more formal situations or in writing.
en.formation: Verb/い-adj. (plain form) + ので / な-adj. + なので / Noun + なので
en.notes: ので sounds more polite and less direct than から. With requests and apologies, ので is preferred. The plain form comes before ので (na-adj. + なので).
examples[].german: I'm sick, so I'll take the day off.
Since the train was delayed, I was late.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 病気なから is not a form; the correct one would be 病気だから.
病気なため is not a correct noun connection.
病気なけど is not a correct connection.

en.explanation: ～のに expresses a contradiction or disappointment. It means "although" or "even though" and shows that the result is different from what was expected.
en.formation: Verb/い-adj. (plain form) + のに / な-adj. + なのに / Noun + なのに
en.notes: のに often expresses disappointment or frustration. It is more subjective than けれども and implies that the result is unwelcome.
examples[].german: Even though I studied a lot, I failed the test.
Even though he promised, he didn't come.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This claims a reason instead of the contrast.
This makes the studying the reason for failing.
This gives a cause or purpose instead of the unexpected contrast.

en.explanation: ～しか～ない means "only" and stresses that something is little or limited. It is always used with the negative verb form and often expresses disappointment or regret.
en.formation: Noun + しか + Verb (negative)
en.notes: しか replaces は、が and を, but is added on to other particles: にしか、でしか. Difference from だけ: しか stresses the limit more strongly.
examples[].german: I only have a hundred yen.
I can only speak Japanese.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: しか requires a negative form.
This means "exactly a hundred yen are missing".
This claims a large amount instead of only a hundred yen.

en.explanation: ～すぎる expresses that something is excessive. It can be used with verbs and adjectives and means "too much" or "too". すぎる itself conjugates as a group 2 (ichidan) verb.
en.formation: Verb stem + すぎる / い-adj. (without い) + すぎる / な-adj. + すぎる
en.notes: With い-adjectives the い drops: 高い → 高すぎる. With な-adjectives the な drops: 静か → 静かすぎる.
examples[].german: I ate too much yesterday.
This bag is too expensive.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The completed action yesterday needs the past.
This negates the overeating.
すぎる is a verb and forms its polite past with ました.

en.explanation: ～たことがある expresses that you have experienced something before. It refers to experiences in the past. The polite form is ～たことがあります.
en.formation: Verb た-form + ことがある
en.notes: The negative is ～たことがない (I have never...). This form refers to your whole life experience, not to a specific event.
examples[].german: I have been to Japan before.
Have you ever eaten sushi?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This negates the experience.
Experience requires the た-form.
A ます-form does not go before こと here.

en.explanation: ～たい expresses the speaker's wish to do something. It is conjugated like an い-adjective. You only use it for your own wishes, not for other people's.
en.formation: Verb stem + たい
en.notes: たい is only used for yourself. For others you say ～たがっている. The object can be marked with を or が: 水を飲みたい / 水が飲みたい.
examples[].german: I want to drink some water.
I want to go to Japan.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 飲みますです doubles the polite ending, which is not allowed.
飲みませんです is not a desire form here.
飲みましたです is not a desire form here.

en.explanation: ～たら expresses a condition: "If/When A happens, then B". It can also mean "after". The form is made from the た-form + ら.
en.formation: Verb た-form + ら / い-adj. → ～かったら / な-adj./Noun → だったら
en.notes: たら is the most versatile conditional form. It can be used for hypothetical and real conditions. Unlike ～と, たら is also used for one-time situations.
examples[].german: If it rains, I'll stay at home.
If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 降っれば is not a conditional form.
降っなら is not a valid connecting form.
降っても means "even if" instead of the neutral condition.

en.explanation: ～たり～たりする lists example actions. It means "to do things like ... and ..." and implies that other actions also take place. The final form is always する.
en.formation: Verb た-form + り + Verb た-form + り + する
en.notes: The list must always end with する (in the appropriate tense). It also works with adjectives: 大きかったり小さかったり.
examples[].german: On weekends I do things like read books and watch TV.
On my days off I did things like shopping and cooking.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 読む forms 読んだり, not 読んたり.
見る forms 見たり, not 見だり.
たり requires the た-form of the verbs.

en.explanation: The て-form can link clauses and express a sequence in time. It means "and then" or "and". The last verb in the sentence determines the tense.
en.formation: Verb て-form + next action
en.notes: The て-form used as a link often implies a sequence in time. The last verb in the sentence determines the politeness level and tense for the whole sentence.
examples[].german: In the morning I get up, wash my face and eat breakfast.
I take the bus and go to school.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 起きたて is a noun-like "freshly ..." form and does not link the action here.
The て-form is not attached to ます.
This says "without getting up" and contradicts the sequence.

en.explanation: The て-form is one of the most important verb forms in Japanese. It is used as the basis for many grammatical constructions, such as ～ている, ～てください and ～てもいい. How it is formed depends on the verb group.
en.formation: Group 1 (godan): う・つ・る → って, む・ぶ・ぬ → んで, く → いて, ぐ → いで, す → して / Group 2 (ichidan): る → て / Group 3 (irregular): する → して, くる → きて
