en.notes: The て-form on its own is not a complete sentence. One exception: 行って (as a short form of 行ってください = Go!). You have to memorize how the て-form is formed.
examples[].german: I'm reading a book.
I ate and went to sleep.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 読む forms the voiced connective 読んで.
読んた is not a form of 読む.
読んだ cannot come directly before います.

en.explanation: ～ている expresses an ongoing action (progressive) or a resulting state. The polite form is ～ています. With some verbs it describes a state rather than an activity.
en.formation: Verb て-form + いる / います
en.notes: With state verbs such as 知る, 結婚する, 持つ, ている describes the resulting state: 知っています (I know it), not an ongoing action.
examples[].german: I'm reading a book right now.
I live in Tokyo.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The translation stresses the action going on right now.
This negates the reading.
This describes finished reading instead of reading in progress.

en.explanation: ～てから emphasizes the order of two actions: first the first action is completed, then the second begins. It stresses more strongly than 後で that the first action must be finished first.
en.formation: Verb て-form + から
en.notes: てから emphasizes the sequence more strongly than 後で. With てから, the first action must be completed before the second begins.
examples[].german: Please wash your hands first and then eat.
After coming to Japan, I started studying Japanese.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: This gives a reason instead of the order for the request.
洗っます is not a verb form.
洗っない is not a verb form.

en.explanation: ～てください is a polite request to do something. It corresponds to English "Please do...". It is one of the most common forms in everyday life.
en.formation: Verb て-form + ください
en.notes: てください is polite, but it is still an instruction. For even more polite requests you use ていただけませんか.
examples[].german: Please write your name here.
Please say it once more.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: 書く forms 書いて, not 書いで.
ください does not attach to the た-form.
ください does not attach to the ます-form.

en.explanation: ～てみる means "to try something out" or "to do something as a test". It expresses that you do something for the first time or to see what it's like. The polite form is ～てみます.
en.formation: Verb て-form + みる
en.notes: てみる stresses trying something out, not "trying" in the sense of making an effort. For "to make an effort" you would rather use ～ようとする.
examples[].german: Please try this dish.
I'll try speaking in Japanese.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: A ます-form does not go before ください.
Trying something out needs 食べて, not 食べた.
The request needs みてください, not みたください.

en.meaning: to do accidentally / to do completely
en.explanation: ～てしまう has two meanings: doing something unintentionally or regrettably, or completing an action fully. The polite form is ～てしまいます. In colloquial speech it is shortened to ～ちゃう.
en.formation: Verb て-form + しまう
en.notes: Colloquial: ～てしまう → ～ちゃう (食べてしまう → 食べちゃう), ～でしまう → ～じゃう (飲んでしまう → 飲んじゃう).
examples[].german: Unfortunately, I forgot my wallet.
I finished reading the whole book.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: しまう attaches to the て-form.
The polite past ends in ました.
This negates the forgetting.

en.explanation: ～ても expresses that something holds true despite a certain condition. It means "even if". The result doesn't change, whether or not the condition occurs.
en.formation: Verb て-form + も / い-adj. (～くても) / な-adj. (～でも) / Noun (～でも)
en.notes: い-adjectives: 高い → 高くても. な-adjectives: 静か → 静かでも. Nouns: 雨 → 雨でも. Don't confuse it with ～てもいい (permission).
examples[].german: Even if it rains, I'll go.
Even if it's expensive, I want to buy it.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: "Even if" needs ても, not たも.
降っれば is not a conditional form.
降っない is not a negative form.

en.meaning: may; it is all right to...
en.explanation: ～てもいいです expresses permission. It means "you may..." or "it's okay if...". As a question, it is used to ask for permission.
en.formation: Verb て-form + もいいです
en.notes: The negative "you must not" is ～てはいけません, not ～てもよくないです.
examples[].german: May I take photos here?
You may go home.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: Permission attaches to the て-form.
いい does not form its past with でした.
いい, as an adjective, does not take ます.

en.meaning: must not; it is forbidden to...
en.explanation: ～てはいけません expresses a prohibition. It means "you must not..." or "it is not allowed to...". It is stronger than a simple request.
en.formation: Verb て-form + はいけません
en.notes: In colloquial speech, ～ちゃだめ or ～ちゃいけない is used. ～てはいけません is the more formal variant.
examples[].german: You must not smoke here.
You must not eat in the classroom.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: The prohibition needs the て-form before は.
This explicitly allows smoking.
This tells someone to smoke.

en.explanation: と has two main meanings: it joins nouns in a list ("and") or marks someone you do something with ("with"). In a list, all items are named (a complete list).
en.formation: Noun + と + Noun / Noun + と + Verb
en.notes: と lists all items completely. For an incomplete list ("and so on") you use や.
examples[].german: I bought bread and milk.
I watched a movie with a friend.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: へ does not join items that were bought.
で would mark bread as a means instead of as another item bought.
が makes bread the subject instead of the second item bought.

en.explanation: ～と思います expresses your own opinion or assumption. It corresponds to English "I think (that)...". For other people's opinions, you use ～と思っています.
en.formation: Sentence (plain form) + と思います
en.notes: The plain form comes before と思います, not the ます-form: 行くと思います (correct), 行きますと思います (wrong).
examples[].german: I think it will rain tomorrow.
I think this book is interesting.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: A complete thought is quoted with と.
に does not link a quoted sentence here.
が does not replace the quotation particle here.

en.explanation: ～時 (とき) means "when" and indicates a point or period in time. It can be used with verbs, adjectives and nouns.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary/た-form) + 時 / い-adj. + 時 / な-adj. + な + 時 / Noun + の + 時
en.notes: Dictionary form + 時 = "when you are going to do something"; た-form + 時 = "after you have done something". The difference is subtle and depends on context.
examples[].german: When I went to Japan, I took a lot of photos.
What do you do when you have free time?
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ながら requires the stem, not 行った.
前に requires the dictionary form here, not 行った.
てから cannot also be attached to 行った.

en.explanation: ～つもり expresses a firm intention or plan. It means "I plan to..." or "I intend to...". The negative can be formed in two ways.
en.formation: Verb (dictionary form) + つもりです / Verb ない-form + つもりです
en.notes: つもり expresses a personal intention. For other people's plans, you use ～予定 (yotei) or ask directly.
examples[].german: I plan to go to Japan next year.
I intend not to drink alcohol anymore.
I'm not going to eat sweets anymore.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: ながら requires the verb stem and does not form a noun before です here.
行くてから is not a correct connection.
行くましたです is not a verb form.

en.explanation: は marks the topic of a sentence, i.e. what is being talked about. It is always pronounced "wa", even though it is the hiragana character "ha". The topic does not have to be the grammatical subject.
en.formation: Noun + は
en.notes: Don't confuse it with が (ga). は emphasizes the topic, が emphasizes the subject. が is used for new information, は for topics that are already known.
examples[].german: I am a student.
Tokyo is big.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を marks an object; the copula has none here.
で does not form a noun-predicate statement here.
へ indicates a direction, not an identity.

en.explanation: を marks the direct object of a sentence, i.e. what the action affects. It is pronounced "o". It is also used to mark a place that you move through.
en.formation: Noun + を + Verb
en.notes: を is only used with transitive verbs (verbs that take an object). With verbs of motion such as 歩く、走る, を marks the place you pass through.
examples[].german: I eat bread.
I walk through the park.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: に does not mark the thing being eaten.
Bread is not a destination of movement here.
With active 食べます, bread is the object, not the one eating.

en.explanation: や joins nouns in an incomplete list. It means "and (among other things)" and shows that there are further items that are not mentioned.
en.formation: Noun + や + Noun (+ など)
en.notes: や is often combined with など (and so on). Unlike と (complete list), や suggests that the list is not complete.
examples[].german: I bought apples and mandarins (among other things).
There are books, notebooks and so on.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: へ does not list items that were bought.
が would make the apples the subject.
This makes the apples a modifier of the mandarins instead of listing both.

en.explanation: よ is used at the end of a sentence to share new information or to emphasize a statement. It signals to the listener that you are saying something new or important.
en.formation: Sentence + よ
en.notes: よ sounds more assertive than ね. Using it too often can come across as pushy. よね combines both particles (emphasis + confirmation).
examples[].german: This is delicious, I'm telling you!
It's already late!
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: を is not a suitable sentence-final particle after です.
に does not close this copula sentence.
へ is a direction particle, not an emphasizer.

en.explanation: ～より is used for comparisons and marks what something is compared with. It corresponds to English "than" in comparisons.
en.formation: B + より + A + のほうが + Adjective
en.notes: より marks the "loser" in the comparison. The full structure is: B より A のほうが ～. You can also use just より: 東京は大阪より大きい.
examples[].german: Tokyo is bigger than Osaka.
Trains are faster than buses.
examples[].cloze.quiz.distractors[].reas: まで sets a limit, not a standard of comparison.
から does not express a comparison of size here.
へ indicates a direction, not a comparison of size.
